sections.markdown:
A building and timber-pest inspection puts eyes on the actual house: what could be seen, what could be reached, and what sat outside the scope. Decide what the property and transaction warrant, whether an existing report gives you reliance rights, and which unresolved signals need specialist follow-up. The checks below move from early triage to more specific investigation:

**The common checks, at a glance**

| Check | What it catches | When it's worth it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Section 32 / contract review | Legal, title, zoning, disclosure risk | Always |
| Desktop / pre-inspection read | Likely repair exposure, what to ask, what to inspect | Early, before spending on a physical inspection |
| Building & pest inspection | Visible defects, pests, moisture, structural signs | Before you commit, and before any unconditional offer |
| Specialist (structural, electrical) | A specific suspected defect | When an earlier check flags something |

An apartment is two purchases in one: the lot itself, and a share of a building run by its owners corporation. The physical inspection covers the unit; the owners-corporation records cover the building's finances and the special levies that can land on you after settlement. guides.contentMarkdown:
# How to check a property’s condition: the complete Australian guide

A home becomes much easier to understand when you read three things together: what the documents say, what the building is showing you and what the likely work could cost. Start with the records you can get, use them to sharpen the inspection, then turn the findings into a short list of decisions and follow-up questions.

## Research note
The sequence below reflects official buyer guidance: read the contract and disclosure material early, then commission the physical and specialist checks the property warrants. See the [NSW inspection guidance](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/buying-and-selling-property/buying-property-nsw/inspecting-a-property/inspection-reports) and [Victoria's due-diligence checklist](https://www.consumer.vic.gov.au/housing/buying-and-selling-property/checklists/due-diligence).

## Opening
### Three views of the same home
- **Documents:** What the paperwork says the home is
- **Building:** What the building itself is telling you
- **Decision:** What it will cost, when, and what to ask next

_Read together, they show what you are buying and what is coming._

## The order to do things in
Working through it in sequence is cheaper and calmer than doing everything at once on a single property. A workable order: read whatever documents exist first (cheap or free), form a view of the building's likely exposure early, then spend on a physical inspection when it matters. If you are buying, settle your finance and price limit before any auction.

## Start with the available documents
Start with the legal and property records that exist for the address. Every state runs seller disclosure its own way. Victoria hands you a Section 32, NSW builds the disclosure into the contract itself, Queensland now requires a Form 2, and the rest each have arrangements of their own. Titles, searches, plans, permits and owners-corporation records can expose legal or shared-building issues outside a visual inspection. Have the contract and required disclosure reviewed for the property's jurisdiction.

See the dedicated guide: [how to read a Section 32 (Vendor's Statement)](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/reading-a-section-32).

## Then read the building, and decide how hard
A building and timber-pest inspection puts eyes on the actual house: what could be seen, what could be reached, and what sat outside the scope. Decide what the property and transaction warrant, whether an existing report gives you reliance rights, and which unresolved signals need specialist follow-up. The checks below move from early triage to more specific investigation:

**The common checks, at a glance**

| Check | What it catches | When it's worth it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Section 32 / contract review | Legal, title, zoning, disclosure risk | Always |
| Desktop / pre-inspection read | Likely repair exposure, what to ask, what to inspect | Early, before spending on a physical inspection |
| Building & pest inspection | Visible defects, pests, moisture, structural signs | Before you commit, and before any unconditional offer |
| Specialist (structural, electrical) | A specific suspected defect | When an earlier check flags something |

Guides for each: [desktop and physical reports](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/desktop-vs-physical-report), [what an inspection costs](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/building-and-pest-inspection-cost), [whether one is worth it before auction](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/building-inspection-before-auction), and [which kind of condition report you need](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/what-is-a-property-condition-report). For damp, mould and indoor-environment questions, see [building biologist scope and cost](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/building-biologist-cost). Buying interstate? Read [NSW's contract for sale](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/reading-a-contract-for-sale-nsw) or [Queensland's Form 2](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/seller-disclosure-qld).

## Match the checks to the property
### Risk clusters by era

Risk clusters by construction and era. A 1970s brick veneer, a 1920s weatherboard and a 2015 apartment each create different inspection priorities. See [red flags by era](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/red-flags-by-era) and [the wall-crack guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/cracks-structural-or-cosmetic).

### Apartments add a financial dimension

An apartment is two purchases in one: the lot itself, and a share of a building run by its owners corporation. The physical inspection covers the unit; the owners-corporation records cover the building's finances and the special levies that can land on you after settlement. For apartments, read both: [buying an apartment](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/buying-an-apartment-strata).

## If you are buying, your method changes your protections
How you buy matters as much as what you buy. A private-treaty purchase usually lets you make the offer conditional and gives a short cooling-off period; an **auction is generally unconditional, with no cooling-off to fall back on**, so every check gets finished before you bid. Know which you are in: [cooling-off periods by state](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/cooling-off-period-by-state) and [auction-day due diligence](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/auction-day-due-diligence).

## Continue the record through ownership
Keep the condition picture current through ownership. It helps plan repairs, supports insurance and prepares the evidence for a future sale. Continue with [what your home needs by decade](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/what-your-home-needs-by-decade), [the maintenance that prevents the big bills](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/the-maintenance-that-prevents-the-big-bills), and [keeping a record of your home](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/keeping-a-record-of-your-home).

> Note: Homechecker combines public signals, visible property evidence and supplied documents into an independent read of likely needs and worthwhile next checks. Keep it current as the property changes.

## Frequently asked questions
### What checks should I do before buying a house in Australia?
At minimum, arrange contract and disclosure review plus a building and pest inspection before an unconditional offer. A desktop read can triage earlier questions. Auction and private-treaty rules create different deadlines and protections.

### What order should I do the checks in?
Read the disclosure documents first, form an early view of the building’s likely exposure (a desktop read does this cheaply), then commission a physical inspection on the property you are serious about, and settle your finance and price limit before any auction.

### How much do pre-purchase checks cost?
It depends on the property, the state and the scope. Start with inexpensive steps such as documents and desktop triage, then commission the physical and specialist inspections the property warrants. See the building and pest inspection cost guide.

### Do I need a building inspection if the vendor provides one?
Read the report and its fine print: when it was done, what areas were reached, who inspected, whether they carry insurance, and whether you are allowed to rely on it. Commission your own inspection when those answers leave a material gap.

### How does condition evidence help during ownership?
It turns guesswork into a plan: what to maintain and when, what to tell the insurer, what a renovation will run into, and what a future buyer will ask. Keep it current as the house changes.

## Method
We took the official buyer guidance and arranged it in the order a buyer meets it: documents first, then the building, then the specialists, with a deep-dive waiting at each step.

## Limitations
General Australian guidance only. Contracts, statutes, policies, site conditions and professional scopes vary; obtain advice for the property and decision in front of you.

## Sources
- [Inspection reports before buying property](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/buying-and-selling-property/buying-property-nsw/inspecting-a-property/inspection-reports) — NSW Government; accessed 2026-07-19
- [Due diligence checklist for home buyers](https://www.consumer.vic.gov.au/housing/buying-and-selling-property/checklists/due-diligence) — Consumer Affairs Victoria; accessed 2026-07-19

guides.title: How to read a Section 32 vendor's statement in Victoria
guides.summary: A Section 32 tells a Victorian buyer important things about the land before they sign. This guide helps you find the clauses that deserve a question, a search or legal advice.
guides.answer: The seller must give you the Section 32 before you sign the contract. Check that it describes the right land and seller, then work through easements, covenants, planning controls, outgoings, owners-corporation records, notices, permits and services. It tells you about the legal side of the property; a separate inspection tells you what is happening in the building itself.
guides.methodology: Written against the current Sale of Land Act and Victoria’s own consumer guidance, and updated for the July 2026 Home Warranty changeover.
guides.limitations: This provides Victorian legal orientation. A Victorian conveyancer or solicitor should read the statement and contract before you sign anything.
guides.researchNote: Consumer Affairs Victoria says the seller must provide the Section 32 before the buyer signs and recommends legal review. The statement covers legal disclosure. Arrange a separate physical inspection for the building's condition. Read the [official Section 32 overview](https://www.consumer.vic.gov.au/housing/buying-and-selling-property/selling-property/conveyancing-and-contracts-for-sellers) alongside the contract.

sections.heading: Opening
sections.markdown:
### Read the land, then inspect the building
- **Title:** Who owns it, and what the title lets or forbids
- **Planning:** What the zone and overlays will let you do
- **Outside the statement:** The roof, the damp, the pests: none of it is in here

_The statement covers the land. Someone still has to look at the house._

sections.heading: What the statement covers
sections.markdown:
Section 32 of Victoria's [Sale of Land Act 1962](https://www.legislation.vic.gov.au/in-force/acts/sale-land-act-1962/173) requires prescribed information to be disclosed before the buyer signs. [Consumer Affairs Victoria recommends that a legal practitioner or conveyancer prepare and review it](https://www.consumer.vic.gov.au/housing/buying-and-selling-property/selling-property/conveyancing-and-contracts-for-sellers). The statement records the legal and administrative position of the land; the contract sets the terms of the deal; and the building’s actual condition belongs to a separate, physical inspection. Three documents, three different jobs.

The Act groups the required material across sections 32A to 32I. Section 32N also makes a contractual term void to the extent that it tries to exclude, modify or restrict the operation of this disclosure division.

> Important: The statement must be provided before the buyer signs. Auction buyers should obtain and review the statement and contract before bidding because cooling-off is generally unavailable.

sections.heading: The sections 32A to 32I contents map
sections.markdown:
**Use the statutory structure to navigate the bundle**

| Act section | What it covers | Question to ask |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 32A | Financial matters, including rates, taxes, charges and other prescribed liabilities | Are the amounts current, and how will each item be adjusted at settlement? |
| 32B | Insurance details required for applicable owner-builder work | Which work is covered, under which scheme, and is the evidence current? |
| 32C | Land-use matters, including easements, covenants and planning information | Where does each restriction apply, and what does it mean for the intended use or works? |
| 32D | Notices, orders, declarations, reports and proposals affecting the land | What action is outstanding, by when, and who bears it under the contract? |
| 32E | Particulars of building permits issued in the preceding seven years | Do the permits and completion records match the visible work? |
| 32F | Owners-corporation certificate and prescribed information where applicable | What do the plan, minutes, funds, insurance and future works say together? |
| 32G | Growth Areas Infrastructure Contribution information where applicable | Does a current or deferred liability affect this land or settlement? |
| 32H | Whether the prescribed services are connected | Do the service statements match what the property appears to use? |
| 32I | Evidence of the vendor’s title to the land | Do the seller, title reference, lot and plan match everything offered for sale? |

sections.heading: Map the title material against the home
sections.markdown: Map each easement and covenant against the house, garage, deck, drains and any proposed extension. If the plan is hard to reconcile with what stands on the land, ask the conveyancer whether a survey or further title work is warranted.

sections.heading: See what the overlays mean for this address
sections.markdown: A zone sets the broad planning framework. Overlays add controls for matters such as heritage, flooding, vegetation or bushfire. Follow the schedule, maps and local provisions to establish the permit pathway. For the Victorian heritage pathway, see [living in a Heritage Overlay](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/living-in-a-heritage-overlay).

sections.heading: Make visible work prove itself
sections.markdown: Compare permit and owner-builder material with visible additions and renovations. Section 32E covers building permits issued in the preceding seven years. Ask for completion evidence and have your legal representative, council or a building professional resolve gaps between the records and the property.

sections.heading: Owner-builder work needs its own document check
sections.markdown:
[Consumer Affairs Victoria says an owner-builder selling within six years and six months of completing the work must provide a defects inspection report that is no more than six months old](https://www.consumer.vic.gov.au/housing/building-and-renovating/checklists/owner-builders), together with the applicable insurance information. The requirement can cover extensions, renovations, garages and verandas.

Victoria moved from Domestic Building Insurance to Home Warranty for new eligible work on 1 July 2026. [The Building and Plumbing Commission says the scheme depends on when the building contract was signed and the cover issued](https://www.bpc.vic.gov.au/home-owners/insurance-for-domestic-building-work/domestic-building-insurance-and-home-warranty). Ask the conveyancer to identify the work, completion date, builder status, policy or notice of cover and any transitional issue for this sale.

sections.heading: For apartments, read the scheme as a second property
sections.markdown: Use the owners-corporation certificate as the entry point. Reconcile the registered plan, lot liability and entitlement, fees, insurance, maintenance plan, fund position, minutes, defects, disputes and proposed works. Compare the money with the building's planned obligations. Continue with [how to read owners-corporation records](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/reading-your-owners-corporation-report).

sections.heading: Inspect the building separately
sections.markdown: The Section 32 may disclose notices or permits connected with work. Use a [building and pest inspection](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/building-and-pest-inspection-cost) for accessible evidence about the roof, subfloor, drainage, wiring, plumbing, termites, cracking and moisture. Use specialist advice for flagged issues.

sections.heading: A fast review before you send it to your conveyancer
sections.markdown:
1. **Confirm the identifiers:** address, title, lot, plan and seller.
2. **Mark every encumbrance:** easement, covenant, mortgage and restriction.
3. **Write down the planning controls:** zone, overlays and any use or design question they create.
4. **Reconcile money and shared-building material:** outgoings, owners-corporation certificate, funds and planned works.
5. **Compare records with the building:** visible extensions, decks, wet areas, sheds and service connections.
6. **Send the PDF with your questions:** your intended use and concerns help the conveyancer target the review.

sections.heading: What a Section 32 looks like
sections.markdown: A Section 32 usually arrives as a document bundle. It may include a title search, plan, certificates, planning material, service information, notices, permit particulars and owners-corporation documents. File names and page order vary. Start with the title and plan, then mark off each statutory category in the contents map above. Send the whole bundle to your conveyancer with your questions attached; a bundle that arrives with questions gets a sharper hour of review than one that arrives cold.

sections.heading: When a disclosure problem may support rescission
sections.markdown:
Section 32K of the [Sale of Land Act 1962](https://www.legislation.vic.gov.au/in-force/acts/sale-land-act-1962/173) may allow a purchaser to rescind in specified circumstances where the statement was not provided or contained false or incomplete information. The section also contains a vendor protection where the court is satisfied that the vendor acted honestly and reasonably and the purchaser is substantially in the same position as if the requirements had been met. Timing, materiality, knowledge and the contract matter. Get legal advice immediately if a problem appears.

> Important: This guide provides Victorian legal orientation. A Section 32 can be defective, amended or supplemented, and contractual consequences depend on the facts. Have a Victorian conveyancer or solicitor review the statement and contract before signing or bidding.

faqs.question: What does a Section 32 look like?
faqs.answer: It is usually a bundle containing the title search, plan, certificates, planning and service information, notices, permit particulars and owners-corporation material where applicable. The page order varies, so use sections 32A to 32I as the contents map.

faqs.question: When must a Section 32 be given to a buyer?
faqs.answer: Before the buyer signs the contract. Auction buyers should obtain and review it well before bidding because an auction purchase generally has no cooling-off period.

faqs.question: How far back does the building-permit disclosure go?
faqs.answer: Section 32E requires particulars of building permits issued in the preceding seven years. Compare those particulars with visible additions and renovation records.

faqs.question: Can a buyer rescind if the Section 32 is wrong?
faqs.answer: Section 32K may provide a right in specified circumstances, with statutory qualifications and a vendor defence. Obtain immediate advice from a Victorian conveyancer or solicitor.

faqs.question: Does a Section 32 show building defects?
faqs.answer: It provides legal and administrative disclosure. Investigate roof, damp, pest, service and structural condition separately.

faqs.question: What should I look at first?
faqs.answer: Confirm you are looking at the right land and the right seller. Then map the easements and covenants against the block, read the planning controls, reconcile the money and any owners-corporation material, and compare the permits with the work visible at the property.

faqs.question: Is an owners-corporation certificate enough for an apartment?
faqs.answer: It is the starting document. Read it with the plan, minutes, budgets, funds, insurance, maintenance plan, defects, disputes and future works.

faqs.question: Can I read a Section 32 without a conveyancer?
faqs.answer: Use the statement to form questions. A Victorian conveyancer or solicitor should assess its legal effect, omissions, interaction with the contract and any remedy before you commit.

- **Title:** Who owns it, and what the title lets or forbids
- **Planning:** What the zone and overlays will let you do
- **Outside the statement:** The roof, the damp, the pests: none of it is in here

_The statement covers the land. Someone still has to look at the house._

## What the statement covers
Section 32 of Victoria's [Sale of Land Act 1962](https://www.legislation.vic.gov.au/in-force/acts/sale-land-act-1962/173) requires prescribed information to be disclosed before the buyer signs. [Consumer Affairs Victoria recommends that a legal practitioner or conveyancer prepare and review it](https://www.consumer.vic.gov.au/housing/buying-and-selling-property/selling-property/conveyancing-and-contracts-for-sellers). The statement records the legal and administrative position of the land; the contract sets the terms of the deal; and the building’s actual condition belongs to a separate, physical inspection. Three documents, three different jobs.

The Act groups the required material across sections 32A to 32I. Section 32N also makes a contractual term void to the extent that it tries to exclude, modify or restrict the operation of this disclosure division.

> Important: The statement must be provided before the buyer signs. Auction buyers should obtain and review the statement and contract before bidding because cooling-off is generally unavailable.

## The sections 32A to 32I contents map
**Use the statutory structure to navigate the bundle**

| Act section | What it covers | Question to ask |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 32A | Financial matters, including rates, taxes, charges and other prescribed liabilities | Are the amounts current, and how will each item be adjusted at settlement? |
| 32B | Insurance details required for applicable owner-builder work | Which work is covered, under which scheme, and is the evidence current? |
| 32C | Land-use matters, including easements, covenants and planning information | Where does each restriction apply, and what does it mean for the intended use or works? |
| 32D | Notices, orders, declarations, reports and proposals affecting the land | What action is outstanding, by when, and who bears it under the contract? |
| 32E | Particulars of building permits issued in the preceding seven years | Do the permits and completion records match the visible work? |
| 32F | Owners-corporation certificate and prescribed information where applicable | What do the plan, minutes, funds, insurance and future works say together? |
| 32G | Growth Areas Infrastructure Contribution information where applicable | Does a current or deferred liability affect this land or settlement? |
| 32H | Whether the prescribed services are connected | Do the service statements match what the property appears to use? |
| 32I | Evidence of the vendor’s title to the land | Do the seller, title reference, lot and plan match everything offered for sale? |

## Map the title material against the home
Map each easement and covenant against the house, garage, deck, drains and any proposed extension. If the plan is hard to reconcile with what stands on the land, ask the conveyancer whether a survey or further title work is warranted.

## See what the overlays mean for this address
A zone sets the broad planning framework. Overlays add controls for matters such as heritage, flooding, vegetation or bushfire. Follow the schedule, maps and local provisions to establish the permit pathway. For the Victorian heritage pathway, see [living in a Heritage Overlay](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/living-in-a-heritage-overlay).

## Make visible work prove itself
Compare permit and owner-builder material with visible additions and renovations. Section 32E covers building permits issued in the preceding seven years. Ask for completion evidence and have your legal representative, council or a building professional resolve gaps between the records and the property.

## Owner-builder work needs its own document check
[Consumer Affairs Victoria says an owner-builder selling within six years and six months of completing the work must provide a defects inspection report that is no more than six months old](https://www.consumer.vic.gov.au/housing/building-and-renovating/checklists/owner-builders), together with the applicable insurance information. The requirement can cover extensions, renovations, garages and verandas.

Victoria moved from Domestic Building Insurance to Home Warranty for new eligible work on 1 July 2026. [The Building and Plumbing Commission says the scheme depends on when the building contract was signed and the cover issued](https://www.bpc.vic.gov.au/home-owners/insurance-for-domestic-building-work/domestic-building-insurance-and-home-warranty). Ask the conveyancer to identify the work, completion date, builder status, policy or notice of cover and any transitional issue for this sale.

## For apartments, read the scheme as a second property
Use the owners-corporation certificate as the entry point. Reconcile the registered plan, lot liability and entitlement, fees, insurance, maintenance plan, fund position, minutes, defects, disputes and proposed works. Compare the money with the building's planned obligations. Continue with [how to read owners-corporation records](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/reading-your-owners-corporation-report).

## Inspect the building separately
The Section 32 may disclose notices or permits connected with work. Use a [building and pest inspection](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/building-and-pest-inspection-cost) for accessible evidence about the roof, subfloor, drainage, wiring, plumbing, termites, cracking and moisture. Use specialist advice for flagged issues.

## A fast review before you send it to your conveyancer
1. **Confirm the identifiers:** address, title, lot, plan and seller.
2. **Mark every encumbrance:** easement, covenant, mortgage and restriction.
3. **Write down the planning controls:** zone, overlays and any use or design question they create.
4. **Reconcile money and shared-building material:** outgoings, owners-corporation certificate, funds and planned works.
5. **Compare records with the building:** visible extensions, decks, wet areas, sheds and service connections.
6. **Send the PDF with your questions:** your intended use and concerns help the conveyancer target the review.

## What a Section 32 looks like
A Section 32 usually arrives as a document bundle. It may include a title search, plan, certificates, planning material, service information, notices, permit particulars and owners-corporation documents. File names and page order vary. Start with the title and plan, then mark off each statutory category in the contents map above. Send the whole bundle to your conveyancer with your questions attached; a bundle that arrives with questions gets a sharper hour of review than one that arrives cold.

## When a disclosure problem may support rescission
Section 32K of the [Sale of Land Act 1962](https://www.legislation.vic.gov.au/in-force/acts/sale-land-act-1962/173) may allow a purchaser to rescind in specified circumstances where the statement was not provided or contained false or incomplete information. The section also contains a vendor protection where the court is satisfied that the vendor acted honestly and reasonably and the purchaser is substantially in the same position as if the requirements had been met. Timing, materiality, knowledge and the contract matter. Get legal advice immediately if a problem appears.

> Important: This guide provides Victorian legal orientation. A Section 32 can be defective, amended or supplemented, and contractual consequences depend on the facts. Have a Victorian conveyancer or solicitor review the statement and contract before signing or bidding.

## Frequently asked questions
### What does a Section 32 look like?
It is usually a bundle containing the title search, plan, certificates, planning and service information, notices, permit particulars and owners-corporation material where applicable. The page order varies, so use sections 32A to 32I as the contents map.

### When must a Section 32 be given to a buyer?
Before the buyer signs the contract. Auction buyers should obtain and review it well before bidding because an auction purchase generally has no cooling-off period.

### How far back does the building-permit disclosure go?
Section 32E requires particulars of building permits issued in the preceding seven years. Compare those particulars with visible additions and renovation records.

### Can a buyer rescind if the Section 32 is wrong?
Section 32K may provide a right in specified circumstances, with statutory qualifications and a vendor defence. Obtain immediate advice from a Victorian conveyancer or solicitor.

### Does a Section 32 show building defects?
It provides legal and administrative disclosure. Investigate roof, damp, pest, service and structural condition separately.

### What should I look at first?
Confirm you are looking at the right land and the right seller. Then map the easements and covenants against the block, read the planning controls, reconcile the money and any owners-corporation material, and compare the permits with the work visible at the property.

### Is an owners-corporation certificate enough for an apartment?
It is the starting document. Read it with the plan, minutes, budgets, funds, insurance, maintenance plan, defects, disputes and future works.

### Can I read a Section 32 without a conveyancer?
Use the statement to form questions. A Victorian conveyancer or solicitor should assess its legal effect, omissions, interaction with the contract and any remedy before you commit.

## Method
Written against the current Sale of Land Act and Victoria’s own consumer guidance, and updated for the July 2026 Home Warranty changeover.

## Limitations
This provides Victorian legal orientation. A Victorian conveyancer or solicitor should read the statement and contract before you sign anything.

- [Sale of Land Act 1962, version 173](https://www.legislation.vic.gov.au/in-force/acts/sale-land-act-1962/173) — Victorian Legislation; accessed 2026-07-19

guides.contentMarkdown:
# Buying in NSW: how to read the contract for sale

In NSW, prescribed disclosure forms part of the contract for sale. Before marketing, the contract must include documents such as the title search, deposited plan, drainage diagram and council planning certificate under section 10.7. Read these with your conveyancer for title, encumbrance, zoning, drainage and planning issues, and arrange a separate inspection to understand the building's condition.

## Research note
A NSW residential property must have a contract available before marketing, and the NSW Government recommends requesting it early for legal review. See [contracts and deposits when buying in NSW](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/buying-and-selling-property/buying-property-nsw/contracts-and-deposits).

## Opening
### Read it before you exchange
- **Read early:** Ask for the contract the day the listing appears
- **Change before exchange:** Anything you want changed, agree it before exchange
- **Inspect separately:** The building gets its own inspection, on its own merits

_Exchange is the moment it becomes real. Arrive ready._

## The disclosure is the contract
Under section 52A of the *Conveyancing Act 1919* and its regulations, a NSW residential property must have a contract with prescribed documents before marketing. Ask for it the day the listing appears. It has to exist by then. The vendor also gives implied warranties about adverse matters affecting the land. Missing prescribed documents or a breached warranty may create a rescission right within 14 days of exchange. Have a conveyancer assess the specific contract and facts.

## What must be attached
**The prescribed documents, and where to spend your attention**

| Document | What to scrutinise |
| --- | --- |
| Title search | The seller matches the registered owner; every mortgage, caveat, easement and covenant listed against the title |
| Deposited plan | The lot’s boundaries and any easements, checked against fences and proposed work |
| Drainage / sewerage service diagram | The sewer route, including any conflict with an extension, pool or garage |
| Section 10.7 planning certificate | Zoning, heritage, road widening, flood and bushfire-prone land information |
| Documents for title interests | The full terms of each easement or restrictive covenant |
| Swimming pool documents (where there is a pool) | The available compliance, occupation or non-compliance certificate |

## The 10.7 certificate is the story of the land
The planning certificate, formerly called the s149, records zoning, heritage, flood-prone or bushfire-prone land, road-widening proposals and relevant planning controls. It is where future works, insurance and site-risk questions get their first honest answers.

## The drainage diagram is the easement tell
Map the sewer route against anywhere you might one day build: the extension, the pool, the garage. Building over or near it can mean water-authority consent, a redesigned plan, or relocating the asset at your cost.

## Cooling off, waivers, and auctions
A NSW residential private-treaty purchase usually carries a five-business-day cooling-off period, with withdrawal costing 0.25% of the price. A **section 66W certificate** from the buyer's solicitor or conveyancer can waive that period. Complete checks before providing one. Cooling-off is generally unavailable at auction; use [the auction-day guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/auction-day-due-diligence) and [the state comparison](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/cooling-off-period-by-state).

## Check building condition separately
The contract discloses the land's legal position. Use a [building and pest inspection](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/building-and-pest-inspection-cost) for accessible building condition, informed by an [independent desktop read](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/desktop-vs-physical-report). For strata, add the owners-corporation records using [the apartment checklist](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/buying-an-apartment-strata).

> Note: Victoria uses the [Section 32](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/reading-a-section-32) and Queensland uses the [Form 2 seller disclosure](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/seller-disclosure-qld). Use the guide for the property's jurisdiction.

> Important: Contract terms and standard conditions can be amended. Have a NSW solicitor or conveyancer review the contract and any 66W certificate before signing.

## Frequently asked questions
### What documents must be attached to a contract for sale in NSW?
Under section 52A of the Conveyancing Act 1919 and its regulations: the title search, the deposited plan, a drainage (sewerage service) diagram, the council’s section 10.7 planning certificate, documents for easements and covenants on title, and, where there is a pool, the swimming pool compliance documents. The contract must exist with these attached before the property is offered for sale.

### What is a section 10.7 certificate?
The council’s planning certificate for the land (formerly the s149): zoning, heritage listings, flood-prone and bushfire-prone notations, road-widening proposals and the planning controls that apply. It is where you learn what the land is allowed to become, and what constraints any future works would face.

### Is there a cooling-off period when buying in NSW?
For residential private-treaty purchases, it is usually five business days, with withdrawal costing 0.25% of the purchase price. A section 66W certificate can waive it. Cooling-off is generally unavailable at auction.

### What is a section 66W certificate?
A certificate from your solicitor or conveyancer that waives the cooling-off period and makes the signed contract binding. Complete inspection, contract and finance checks before providing one.

### Can I get out of a contract if the disclosure documents are missing in NSW?
Possibly. A purchaser may be able to rescind within 14 days of exchange where prescribed documents were absent or a vendor warranty was breached. Have a conveyancer assess the contract and facts.

### Does the contract for sale tell me about the building’s condition?
It discloses the land’s legal position, title, encumbrances, planning and drainage. Use a building and pest inspection for physical condition and a desktop read for earlier triage.

## Method
Built from the NSW Government’s guidance on contracts, cooling-off and inspections, read as one purchase sequence.

## Limitations
This is NSW legal orientation. A licensed conveyancer or Australian legal practitioner should review amendments and certificates.

## Sources
- [Contracts and deposits when buying property in NSW](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/buying-and-selling-property/buying-property-nsw/contracts-and-deposits) — NSW Government; accessed 2026-07-19
- [Inspection reports before buying property](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/buying-and-selling-property/buying-property-nsw/inspecting-a-property/inspection-reports) — NSW Government; accessed 2026-07-19

guides.question: What does Queensland's seller disclosure statement (Form 2) include?
guides.title: Queensland seller disclosure: how to read the Form 2
guides.summary: Queensland Form 2 gives buyers important information before they sign. Pair it with the building, flood and approval checks that still belong on your list.
guides.answer: Queensland's seller disclosure scheme applies to contracts entered into from 1 August 2025. In most covered sales, the seller must give the buyer a completed Form 2 and prescribed certificates before the buyer signs. Auctions have their own make-available process before the hammer falls. The bundle covers land, title, encumbrances, planning and specified notices. You will still need separate checks for building condition, flood history and previous approvals.
guides.methodology: Built from the Queensland Government’s own scheme guide and its current cooling-off guidance, written while the scheme is still new enough to surprise people.
guides.limitations: This is Queensland legal orientation. Whether a defective Form 2 lets you out depends on the Act, the defect and your circumstances, which is exactly the question for your solicitor.
guides.researchNote: Queensland's scheme applies to contracts entered from 1 August 2025. The official guide explains delivery timing, prescribed certificates, exclusions, the over-$10 million waiver and the buyer's conditional termination right: read the [seller disclosure scheme](https://www.qld.gov.au/housing/buying-owning-home/seller-disclosure-scheme) before relying on a Form 2.

cluster.blurb: Read the disclosure bundle for the right jurisdiction, then arrange the physical and specialist checks the property warrants.

sections.heading: Opening
sections.markdown:
### What the disclosure gives you
- **Statement:** What the seller must now tell you, in the approved form
- **Certificates:** Title, plan and the prescribed paperwork behind it
- **Buyer checks:** Condition, pests and flood are still yours to check

_A wrong Form 2 may open an exit. The statutory test decides._

sections.heading: The scheme in one page
sections.markdown:
The *Property Law Act 2023* introduced a mandatory pre-contract disclosure system for many Queensland sales from 1 August 2025. The [Queensland Government's scheme guide](https://www.qld.gov.au/housing/buying-owning-home/seller-disclosure-scheme) covers houses, townhouses, units, commercial property and vacant land, subject to statutory exceptions. The seller is responsible for the disclosure even when an agent or solicitor handles delivery.

For an ordinary private sale, the completed Form 2 and required certificates must be given before the buyer signs. Keep the contract and disclosure together: one describes the bargain; the other puts prescribed facts about the property on the table.

sections.heading: What to extract from the bundle
sections.markdown:
**A buyer’s reading order for Queensland seller disclosure**

| Part | Evidence to reconcile | Decision question |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Property identity | Seller, address, lot and plan | Does the legal parcel match everything presented as part of the property? |
| Title and encumbrances | Current title, registered, unregistered and statutory encumbrances | Where is each restriction or right, and how does it affect use or building? |
| Occupation | Any required tenancy or rooming-accommodation disclosure | Will possession and the proposed settlement work as expected? |
| Planning and environment | Zoning, resumptions, transport notices, contaminated-land status, tree matters and heritage listing | Does any control or proposal change the intended use or risk? |
| Buildings and structures | Pool information and specified notices under building and planning legislation | What action, certification or continuing obligation is attached? |
| Community title | Community management statement and body-corporate certificate where prescribed | What do boundaries, by-laws, money, insurance and works say together? |

The Government itself calls its online list an incomplete summary, which is worth taking at face value. For the actual transaction, rely on the approved Form 2, the prescribed certificates and legal advice.

sections.heading: The condition gaps are deliberate
sections.markdown:
The official guidance excludes [structural soundness, flooding history and previous building or development approvals](https://www.qld.gov.au/housing/buying-owning-home/seller-disclosure-scheme) from the general disclosure requirements. Arrange a qualified building and pest inspection, local flood and hazard checks, and approval searches where the visible work or intended use warrants them.

For a unit, read the body-corporate certificate with minutes, budgets, insurance, maintenance, defects, disputes and proposed levies. Continue with [buying an apartment or strata property](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/buying-an-apartment-strata).

sections.heading: Auction delivery is different
sections.markdown: At auction, the Queensland Government says the seller must give or make available the disclosure statement and prescribed certificates before the hammer falls. Cooling-off is generally unavailable after a successful bid, so obtain the documents early enough for legal review.

sections.heading: The over-$10-million waiver
sections.markdown: The scheme contains exceptions for some government or listed-corporation buyers, related parties and particular statutory sales. For a sale over $10 million, the official summary requires **the buyer to waive disclosure**. Have the transaction's solicitor confirm the full exception and valid-waiver requirements.

sections.heading: When a buyer may be able to terminate
sections.markdown:
The official guidance says a buyer may have a right to terminate before settlement if disclosure was absent, inaccurate or incomplete. For inaccurate or incomplete information, the buyer must show materiality, lack of prior knowledge and that the truth would have changed the decision to sign. Another Act may control the consequence for some failures.

> Important: Timing, delivery, materiality, prior knowledge, statutory interaction and the contract all matter. Have a Queensland solicitor assess the disclosure bundle and facts before acting.

sections.heading: A practical buyer workflow
sections.markdown:
1. **Get the Form 2, certificates and contract together**, early enough for review before signing or bidding.
2. **Map title and plan information** against the structures, access, services and future work you expect.
3. **List the remaining questions**: structure, pests, flood, approval history and concealed condition.
4. **Commission the missing checks**, including building and pest inspection and any council, body-corporate or specialist search.
5. **Escalate any mismatch straight away** if the disclosure, the listing, what the agent said and what you can see do not agree. Resolve it before signing or settlement, while there is still time to act.

faqs.question: When did Queensland seller disclosure start?
faqs.answer: The mandatory scheme applies to relevant contracts entered into from 1 August 2025 under the Property Law Act 2023.

faqs.question: Must the Form 2 be given before the buyer signs?
faqs.answer: For an ordinary covered private sale, yes: the completed statement and prescribed certificates must be given before the buyer signs. Auctions use specific rules requiring the material to be given or made available before the hammer falls.

faqs.question: Does the Form 2 disclose structural condition or flood history?
faqs.answer: Queensland Government guidance excludes structural soundness, flooding history and previous building or development approvals from the general requirements.

faqs.question: Can a buyer terminate for a wrong Form 2?
faqs.answer: A conditional right may arise before settlement under a specific legal test. The seriousness of the error, what the buyer already knew and whether the truth would have changed the decision to sign all matter. Get legal advice before acting.

faqs.question: How does the over-$10-million exception work?
faqs.answer: The official summary describes a sale price over $10 million where the buyer waives disclosure. Have the waiver requirements checked for the transaction.

# Queensland seller disclosure: how to read the Form 2

Queensland's seller disclosure scheme applies to contracts entered into from 1 August 2025. In most covered sales, the seller must give the buyer a completed Form 2 and prescribed certificates before the buyer signs. Auctions have their own make-available process before the hammer falls. The bundle covers land, title, encumbrances, planning and specified notices. You will still need separate checks for building condition, flood history and previous approvals.

## Research note
Queensland's scheme applies to contracts entered from 1 August 2025. The official guide explains delivery timing, prescribed certificates, exclusions, the over-$10 million waiver and the buyer's conditional termination right: read the [seller disclosure scheme](https://www.qld.gov.au/housing/buying-owning-home/seller-disclosure-scheme) before relying on a Form 2.

## Opening
### What the disclosure gives you
- **Statement:** What the seller must now tell you, in the approved form
- **Certificates:** Title, plan and the prescribed paperwork behind it
- **Buyer checks:** Condition, pests and flood are still yours to check

_A wrong Form 2 may open an exit. The statutory test decides._

## The scheme in one page
The *Property Law Act 2023* introduced a mandatory pre-contract disclosure system for many Queensland sales from 1 August 2025. The [Queensland Government's scheme guide](https://www.qld.gov.au/housing/buying-owning-home/seller-disclosure-scheme) covers houses, townhouses, units, commercial property and vacant land, subject to statutory exceptions. The seller is responsible for the disclosure even when an agent or solicitor handles delivery.

For an ordinary private sale, the completed Form 2 and required certificates must be given before the buyer signs. Keep the contract and disclosure together: one describes the bargain; the other puts prescribed facts about the property on the table.

## What to extract from the bundle
**A buyer’s reading order for Queensland seller disclosure**

| Part | Evidence to reconcile | Decision question |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Property identity | Seller, address, lot and plan | Does the legal parcel match everything presented as part of the property? |
| Title and encumbrances | Current title, registered, unregistered and statutory encumbrances | Where is each restriction or right, and how does it affect use or building? |
| Occupation | Any required tenancy or rooming-accommodation disclosure | Will possession and the proposed settlement work as expected? |
| Planning and environment | Zoning, resumptions, transport notices, contaminated-land status, tree matters and heritage listing | Does any control or proposal change the intended use or risk? |
| Buildings and structures | Pool information and specified notices under building and planning legislation | What action, certification or continuing obligation is attached? |
| Community title | Community management statement and body-corporate certificate where prescribed | What do boundaries, by-laws, money, insurance and works say together? |

The Government itself calls its online list an incomplete summary, which is worth taking at face value. For the actual transaction, rely on the approved Form 2, the prescribed certificates and legal advice.

## The condition gaps are deliberate
The official guidance excludes [structural soundness, flooding history and previous building or development approvals](https://www.qld.gov.au/housing/buying-owning-home/seller-disclosure-scheme) from the general disclosure requirements. Arrange a qualified building and pest inspection, local flood and hazard checks, and approval searches where the visible work or intended use warrants them.

For a unit, read the body-corporate certificate with minutes, budgets, insurance, maintenance, defects, disputes and proposed levies. Continue with [buying an apartment or strata property](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/buying-an-apartment-strata).

## Auction delivery is different
At auction, the Queensland Government says the seller must give or make available the disclosure statement and prescribed certificates before the hammer falls. Cooling-off is generally unavailable after a successful bid, so obtain the documents early enough for legal review.

## The over-$10-million waiver
The scheme contains exceptions for some government or listed-corporation buyers, related parties and particular statutory sales. For a sale over $10 million, the official summary requires **the buyer to waive disclosure**. Have the transaction's solicitor confirm the full exception and valid-waiver requirements.

## When a buyer may be able to terminate
The official guidance says a buyer may have a right to terminate before settlement if disclosure was absent, inaccurate or incomplete. For inaccurate or incomplete information, the buyer must show materiality, lack of prior knowledge and that the truth would have changed the decision to sign. Another Act may control the consequence for some failures.

> Important: Timing, delivery, materiality, prior knowledge, statutory interaction and the contract all matter. Have a Queensland solicitor assess the disclosure bundle and facts before acting.

## A practical buyer workflow
1. **Get the Form 2, certificates and contract together**, early enough for review before signing or bidding.
2. **Map title and plan information** against the structures, access, services and future work you expect.
3. **List the remaining questions**: structure, pests, flood, approval history and concealed condition.
4. **Commission the missing checks**, including building and pest inspection and any council, body-corporate or specialist search.
5. **Escalate any mismatch straight away** if the disclosure, the listing, what the agent said and what you can see do not agree. Resolve it before signing or settlement, while there is still time to act.

## Frequently asked questions
### When did Queensland seller disclosure start?
The mandatory scheme applies to relevant contracts entered into from 1 August 2025 under the Property Law Act 2023.

### Must the Form 2 be given before the buyer signs?
For an ordinary covered private sale, yes: the completed statement and prescribed certificates must be given before the buyer signs. Auctions use specific rules requiring the material to be given or made available before the hammer falls.

### Does the Form 2 disclose structural condition or flood history?
Queensland Government guidance excludes structural soundness, flooding history and previous building or development approvals from the general requirements.

### Can a buyer terminate for a wrong Form 2?
A conditional right may arise before settlement under a specific legal test. The seriousness of the error, what the buyer already knew and whether the truth would have changed the decision to sign all matter. Get legal advice before acting.

### How does the over-$10-million exception work?
The official summary describes a sale price over $10 million where the buyer waives disclosure. Have the waiver requirements checked for the transaction.

## Method
Built from the Queensland Government’s own scheme guide and its current cooling-off guidance, written while the scheme is still new enough to surprise people.

## Limitations
This is Queensland legal orientation. Whether a defective Form 2 lets you out depends on the Act, the defect and your circumstances, which is exactly the question for your solicitor.

## Sources
- [Seller disclosure scheme](https://www.qld.gov.au/housing/buying-owning-home/seller-disclosure-scheme) — Queensland Government; accessed 2026-07-19
- [Cooling-off period for residential property contracts](https://www.qld.gov.au/community/fair-trading/regulated-industries-licensing-and-legislation/property-industry-regulation/legal-requirements-for-the-property-industry/cooling-off-period-for-residential-property-contracts) — Queensland Government; accessed 2026-07-19

Canonical guide: https://homechecker.com.au/guides/seller-disclosure-qld

An inspection records accessible conditions, access gaps and issues needing specialist diagnosis. Use those findings to set the bid, discuss the contract or leave the auction.

**How findings should change the next step**

| Finding or limitation | Proportionate next step |
| --- | --- |
| Evidence of active timber pests or damage | Pest scope, extent assessment and repair advice before bidding |

| Roof or subfloor inaccessible | Arrange access, price the blind spot or reconsider bidding |
| Moisture evidence without a clear source | Targeted leak, drainage or moisture investigation |

guides.contentMarkdown:
# Is a building inspection worth it before auction?

Arrange an inspection whenever the condition of the building could change your decision or maximum bid. Do it early enough to understand the important findings and any areas the inspector could not reach. If the seller supplies a report, check who commissioned it, when it was done, what was accessed, whether the inspector carries professional indemnity insurance and whether you have a right to rely on it.

## Research note
Auction purchases are generally binding and cooling-off is usually unavailable. Complete physical checks and agree any contract changes before bidding. Victoria's official guidance explains [conditional offers and auction contracts](https://www.consumer.vic.gov.au/housing/buying-and-selling-property/buying-property/buying-property-by-private-sale).

## Opening
### Give yourself time to understand the building
- **Scope:** What the inspector could reach, and what they could not
- **Reliance:** Whose report it is, and who is allowed to lean on it
- **Escalate:** Anything flagged goes to a specialist before auction day

_Understand the report before it shapes your bid._

## Why auctions change the maths
At auction, the contract on display is generally the contract you accept by bidding, and cooling-off is usually unavailable. The seller may agree to documented changes before bidding. Complete the physical investigation while there is still time to act on it.

## The value case
An inspection records accessible conditions, access gaps and issues needing specialist diagnosis. Use those findings to set the bid, discuss the contract or leave the auction.

**How findings should change the next step**

| Finding or limitation | Proportionate next step |
| --- | --- |
| Evidence of active timber pests or damage | Pest scope, extent assessment and repair advice before bidding |
| Movement with associated distortion | Structural engineer for cause and significance |
| Roof or subfloor inaccessible | Arrange access, price the blind spot or reconsider bidding |
| Moisture evidence without a clear source | Targeted leak, drainage or moisture investigation |
| Old or suspect electrical installation | Licensed electrician for electrical condition and any quotation required |

Put a number on repairs once the cause and scope are understood. A guessed allowance is how budgets go quietly wrong. See [what drives inspection cost](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/building-and-pest-inspection-cost).

## Scope and blind spots
### Visual and non-invasive

A standard building inspection is a **visual, non-invasive** assessment to the agreed scope and Australian Standard. It covers accessible areas and leaves walls, fixed floor coverings and heavy stored goods in place.

### What can get missed

Concealed defects and inaccessible areas can escape a visual inspection. The report should record every access limitation. Movement, moisture or a suspected structural issue may justify targeted specialist work.

### Read findings and limitations together

Read the *significant items* and the *limitations* together. The report should show what was seen and identify inaccessible or excluded areas. Both belong in the bidding limit.

## Timing: book it early enough to act on it
Arrange access as soon as the property becomes serious. Leave time for clarification, a return visit or specialist advice. Obtain the contract and disclosure material at the same time, using the jurisdiction and contract to set the actual deadline.

## How to assess a vendor-supplied report
Check a seller-commissioned report for its date, property, scope, access restrictions, significant items, timber-pest scope, inspector, professional indemnity insurance and commissioning party. Ask whether the inspector offers assignment or purchaser reliance. Commission your own work where the report is stale, key access was blocked or reliance terms leave you exposed.

## How to focus your inspection spend
Every inspection on a house someone else wins is money you do not get back. An independent [desktop read](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/desktop-vs-physical-report) can triage a shortlist first, so the inspection spend lands on the strongest candidate.

> Note: Keep the report with later repairs, monitoring and photographs. That record helps the next property decision start from current evidence.

> Important: Complete the full auction plan: contract review, agreed changes, property-specific finance, deposit arrangements and a hard limit. Use [auction-day due diligence](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/auction-day-due-diligence) as the checklist.

## Frequently asked questions
### Is a building inspection worth it before auction?
Usually, yes, if the condition of the building could change your bid. The report gives you findings to act on, shows which areas could not be reached and leaves time for specialist advice before the contract becomes binding.

### Can I get out of an auction purchase if the building has problems?
Auction sales are generally unconditional and cooling-off is usually unavailable. Complete inspection and contract checks before bidding.

### What does a building and pest inspection cover?
It is a visual, non-invasive assessment of the agreed accessible areas and timber-pest scope. The report should record concealed and inaccessible areas as limitations.

### When should I book the inspection before an auction?
As soon as the property becomes serious, leaving time to read the report, clarify limitations and obtain specialist follow-up before bidding.

### Should I trust the building report the agent gives me?
Check date, scope, access, qualifications, insurance and your contractual right to rely on it. Commission more work where those answers leave material gaps.

### How do I reduce inspection spend on properties I may not win?
Use a low-cost desktop read to triage several properties, then commission physical inspections on the strongest candidates.

## Method
We read the official auction and inspection guidance side by side, because the timing rules and the report’s fine print only make sense together.

## Limitations
General Australian guidance only. Contracts, statutes, policies, site conditions and professional scopes vary; obtain advice for the property and decision in front of you.

## Sources
- [Buying property by private sale](https://www.consumer.vic.gov.au/housing/buying-and-selling-property/buying-property/buying-property-by-private-sale) — Consumer Affairs Victoria; accessed 2026-07-19
- [Inspection reports before buying property](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/buying-and-selling-property/buying-property-nsw/inspecting-a-property/inspection-reports) — NSW Government; accessed 2026-07-19

Canonical guide: https://homechecker.com.au/guides/building-inspection-before-auction

guides.question: How much does a building and pest inspection cost in Australia?
guides.title: Building and pest inspection cost in Australia: 2026 examples
guides.summary: Five providers publish their prices, and together they make a useful 2026 snapshot. Here is what those fees cover, and the questions worth asking before you book.
guides.answer: Published prices checked on 19 July 2026 were $499 plus GST in Perth, $500 plus GST in Melbourne and Brisbane, $595 including GST in Sydney, and $580 plus GST in Adelaide. Each example covers a slightly different job. Ask for an address-specific quote and make sure the roof space, subfloor, timber-pest inspection, written report and follow-up are clearly included.
guides.methodology: Government guidance on what an inspection covers, plus five real published prices from five cities, checked on the review date. Each figure keeps the GST basis and scope the provider stated.
guides.limitations: Every quote reflects a particular property, access and scope. Use the examples as bearings, then get the current inclusions, insurance and timing in writing.
guides.researchNote: Official buyer guidance covers inspection scope, qualifications, insurance and report limitations. Start with the [NSW Government inspection checklist](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/buying-and-selling-property/buying-property-nsw/inspecting-a-property/inspection-reports). The five city prices are provider-published examples accessed on 19 July 2026.

cluster.blurb: Sequence the checks, understand their limits and be ready before your offer becomes binding.

sections.heading: Opening
sections.markdown:
### What the inspection fee includes
- **Access:** Does the fee cover the roof space, the subfloor, the sheds?
- **Report:** Building and timber pests, in writing, with photos, on time
- **Assurance:** Qualified, insured, and answering the phone afterwards

_A low fee can reflect a narrow job._

sections.heading: Published price examples from five cities
sections.markdown:
We checked all five provider pages on 19 July 2026. Think of the figures as a useful snapshot, since the property, access and extras can all change the final quote.

**Provider-published combined building and pest inspection prices, accessed 19 July 2026**

| City | Published example | Scope or pricing note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sydney | [$595 including GST](https://csibuilding.com.au/prices/) | CSI lists an all-inclusive combined building and pest inspection price |
| Melbourne | [$500 plus GST](https://buildinginspectorsmelbourne.au/pricing/) | Residential house building and pest inspection |
| Brisbane | [$500 plus GST](https://buildingandpestinspectorsbrisbane.com.au/pricing/) | Residential house building and pest inspection |
| Adelaide | [$580 plus GST](https://aejbuildinginspections.com.au/prices/) | Residential combined building and pest inspection |
| Perth | [$499 plus GST](https://pierus.com.au/services/) | Combined inspection for a home up to 4 bedrooms by 2 bathrooms |

Ask for the fee at your actual address, because almost everything about a house can move it: the size, the storeys, the subfloor, the roof voids, the sheds, the age, the drive to get there, and how urgently you need the answer.

The [NSW Government advises buyers to check qualifications, professional indemnity insurance and report inclusions](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/buying-and-selling-property/buying-property-nsw/inspecting-a-property/inspection-reports).

sections.heading: The quote decoder
sections.markdown:
**Ask every inspector to answer the same fields**

| Field | What to ask | Why the answer changes value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Commissioning and reliance | Is the report addressed to me, and may I rely on it? | Reliance rights depend on the engagement terms |
| Building scope | Which structures and areas are included? | Garage, outbuildings, retaining walls, balconies and site may be excluded or limited |
| Timber-pest scope | Is a separate timber-pest inspection included, and to what scope? | Pest assessment needs an explicit scope |
| Access | Roof exterior, roof space, subfloor and restricted rooms, what is safely accessible? | Inaccessible areas remain blind spots |
| Methods | Visual inspection plus which meters or tools, used for what defined purpose? | Tools need access and defined interpretation |
| Report | Written report, photographs, significant items, limitations and delivery time? | A written report creates the decision record |
| Professional standing | Relevant qualification, state registration if applicable and professional indemnity insurance? | Requirements vary by state; insurance and competence need verification |
| Follow-up | Can I speak with the inspector, and is a reinspection available? | Clarification and changed access can matter before commitment |

sections.heading: What moves the quote
sections.markdown:
- **Property form and size:** apartment lot, freestanding house, multi-level home, acreage, ancillary structures.
- **Access and safety:** low subfloor, roof pitch, locked or stored areas, height, confined spaces and weather.
- **Construction complexity:** mixed eras, additions, retaining structures, balconies, unusual materials or multiple roof voids.
- **Scope:** building only, timber pests, pool, invasive testing, specialist diagnostics or strata records are separate questions.
- **Timing and travel:** urgent auction turnaround, remote call-out, return visit and report deadline.

The quote should reflect the actual accessible scope. For apartments, combine the lot inspection with a [strata or owners-corporation records inspection](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/reading-your-owners-corporation-report).

sections.heading: Understand the inspection limits
sections.markdown:
A conventional pre-purchase inspection is visual and non-invasive: the inspector looks hard at everything that can reasonably be reached, and opens nothing. Inside the walls, under fixed finishes, code compliance, full service testing and repair pricing all sit outside a typical scope. The report should identify its limitations and recommend further investigation for material issues.

Ask the inspector to name the agreed Australian Standard and scope in the engagement, then check that the report matches it. Standards documents themselves may require paid access.

sections.heading: Vendor reports: test the rights as well as the content
sections.markdown: For a vendor-supplied report, check its date, scope, access, commissioning party, inspector, professional indemnity insurance and purchaser-reliance or assignment terms. Commission your own inspection or specialist advice when reliance is absent, key areas were inaccessible or your concern sits outside scope.

sections.heading: Allow for specialist follow-up
sections.markdown: A good inspector states the limits of their scope clearly. Structural movement goes to an engineer, wiring to a licensed electrician, drainage to a plumber, suspect materials to a competent assessor, and air-quality questions to a defined indoor-environment scope. Leave time before the auction or the cooling-off deadline for that follow-up to happen.

sections.heading: Choose the inspector you can rely on
sections.markdown:
A clear scope, good access and a useful conversation after the report can be worth far more than a small saving on the fee. Write down any blind spots before you commit. For an auction, use the [five-gate due-diligence plan](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/auction-day-due-diligence); for early triage, read about [desktop and physical report scopes](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/desktop-vs-physical-report).

> Important: Licensing and registration differ by state. Confirm qualifications, insurance, engagement terms, access, standard, pest scope and delivery before booking.

faqs.question: How much does a building and pest inspection cost?
faqs.answer: In a five-city sample checked on 19 July 2026, published combined-inspection examples were $499 plus GST in Perth, $500 plus GST in Melbourne and Brisbane, $595 including GST in Sydney, and $580 plus GST in Adelaide. Confirm the current address-specific fee and inclusions.

faqs.question: Why do inspection prices vary?
faqs.answer: Property size, storeys, age, safe roof and subfloor access, outbuildings, timber-pest scope, travel, urgency, report depth and follow-up all affect the fee.

faqs.question: Is the cheapest inspection a bad one?
faqs.answer: A low fee can still buy a useful inspection. Trace the price back to the scope: what was accessed, whether pests are included, what the written report covers, the inspector’s qualifications and insurance, and whether they will take your call afterwards.

faqs.question: Does a building inspection include termites?
faqs.answer: Timber-pest assessment needs an explicit scope. Ask how its findings and limitations will be reported.

faqs.question: Is a vendor-supplied report useful?
faqs.answer: Check date, scope, access, inspector, insurance and your purchaser-reliance or assignment rights. Commission more work where those terms leave material gaps.

faqs.question: Does an apartment inspection cover the whole building?
faqs.answer: A typical inspection focuses on the lot and accessible areas. Use the registered plan and scheme records for common-property condition, funding, insurance, defects and works.

faqs.question: What extra inspections might be needed?
faqs.answer: Only those prompted by material evidence or the property: for example structural engineering, electrical, plumbing/drainage, hazardous material, pool or indoor-environment work.
