# Property cooling-off periods by state: the Australian comparison

The headline period is five business days in NSW and Queensland, five business days in the ACT, four business days in the NT, three clear business days in Victoria and two clear business days in South Australia. Ordinary private sales in WA and Tasmania have no general statutory period. Ask your conveyancer or solicitor to confirm when your clock starts, when it ends, what exceptions apply and how notice must be given.

## Research note
Cooling-off clocks use state-specific triggers. Victoria starts when the buyer signs, NSW starts at exchange, and Queensland starts when the buyer receives the fully signed contract. Compare the linked [Victorian](https://www.consumer.vic.gov.au/housing/buying-and-selling-property/buying-property/buying-property-by-private-sale), [NSW](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/buying-and-selling-property/buying-property-nsw/contracts-and-deposits) and [Queensland](https://www.qld.gov.au/community/fair-trading/regulated-industries-licensing-and-legislation/property-industry-regulation/legal-requirements-for-the-property-industry/cooling-off-period-for-residential-property-contracts) rules.

## Opening
### Know when your clock starts and stops
- **Trigger:** Signing, exchange or receipt: each state picks its own starting gun
- **Deadline:** Counted in clear, business or working days, and it matters which
- **Exceptions:** Auctions, waivers and edge cases can switch it off entirely

_Get your actual deadline, for your actual contract, in writing._

## The state-by-state orientation
This table covers the usual residential private-sale position for an individual buyer. Auctions, off-the-plan contracts, options, corporate buyers, rural or commercial land, written waivers and contract amendments can change the result. Have the actual deadline confirmed.

**Residential cooling-off orientation, legal review is still required for the actual contract**

| State / territory | Headline period | Typical consequence of withdrawal |
| --- | --- | --- |
| NSW | 5 business days after exchange; 10 business days for off-the-plan contracts | 0.25% of the purchase price |
| VIC | 3 clear business days, beginning when the buyer signs | The greater of $100 or 0.2% of the purchase price |
| QLD | 5 business days, triggered by the buyer receiving the fully signed contract | Seller may deduct up to 0.25% of the purchase price |
| ACT | 5 working days | 0.25% of the purchase price |
| NT | 4 business days in the usual eligible transaction | No statutory penalty stated in the standard government guidance |
| SA | 2 clear business days; the Form 1 timing matters | Seller generally retains the prescribed amount, commonly $100 |
| WA | No general statutory cooling-off period for an ordinary private sale | Any exit depends on negotiated contract conditions |
| TAS | No general statutory cooling-off period for an ordinary private sale | Any exit depends on negotiated contract conditions |

## Each state starts the clock differently
In Victoria, the [three-clear-business-day period begins on the date the buyer signs](https://www.consumer.vic.gov.au/housing/buying-and-selling-property/buying-property/buying-property-by-private-sale). In NSW, the [five-business-day period starts at exchange](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/buying-and-selling-property/buying-property-nsw/contracts-and-deposits) and ends at 5 pm on the fifth business day after the day of exchange. In Queensland, the [clock starts when the buyer receives the contract signed by both parties](https://www.qld.gov.au/community/fair-trading/regulated-industries-licensing-and-legislation/property-industry-regulation/legal-requirements-for-the-property-industry/cooling-off-period-for-residential-property-contracts).

In South Australia, cooling-off is connected to service of the statutory Form 1 and the contract. Ask your legal representative to state the deadline, time and notice method in writing.

## Auction and near-auction exceptions
A purchase made at auction generally has no cooling-off period. The edges differ. Victoria also excludes a private sale made within three clear business days before or after a publicly advertised auction. NSW excludes exchange on the auction day after the property is passed in. Queensland excludes a follow-up sale after an unsuccessful auction if it occurs before 5 pm on the second business day and the buyer was a registered bidder. Those rules are why an auction calendar can matter even when the final negotiation looks like a private sale.

If an auction is in the picture, finish the contract, finance and building work before you bid. Use the [auction due-diligence checklist](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/auction-day-due-diligence) and the narrower guide to [pre-auction building inspections](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/building-inspection-before-auction).

## Waiving, shortening or changing the period
Some regimes allow the buyer to waive or shorten the period through a prescribed mechanism. [NSW uses a section 66W certificate](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/buying-and-selling-property/buying-property-nsw/contracts-and-deposits) from the buyer's solicitor or conveyancer. [Queensland permits a written waiver or shortening](https://www.qld.gov.au/community/fair-trading/regulated-industries-licensing-and-legislation/property-industry-regulation/legal-requirements-for-the-property-industry/cooling-off-period-for-residential-property-contracts). A waiver removes or shortens the buyer's statutory cooling-off right, so the right to rescind may end as soon as the prescribed waiver takes effect.

## Contract conditions in WA and Tasmania
WA and Tasmania have no general statutory cooling-off period for ordinary private sales. Use appropriately drafted contract conditions for finance, building and pest, sale of another property or due diligence. The [WA Government advises buyers to understand the contract before signing](https://www.consumerprotection.wa.gov.au/buying-property-private-sale). Have each condition drafted or reviewed professionally.

## What to do inside a cooling-off window
1. **Have the contract and disclosure bundle reviewed**, including title, plan, easements, covenants, planning controls, notices and settlement terms.
2. **Confirm finance against this property**, including valuation or lender conditions still outstanding.
3. **Complete the physical checks** the property warrants within the available time.
4. **Escalate specific flags** to an engineer, electrician, plumber, strata specialist or other appropriate professional.
5. **Keep the deadline and notice method in writing**, using the method your legal representative confirms.

> Important: Cooling-off law is jurisdiction- and contract-specific. This comparison is current to 19 July 2026. Have a conveyancer or solicitor confirm eligibility, the exact expiry time, the required notice and the financial consequence.

## Frequently asked questions
### How long is the cooling-off period when buying a house?
It depends on the state and the contract: from five business days in NSW and Queensland down to none at all for ordinary private sales in WA and Tasmania. Have the trigger, the exact deadline and the exclusions confirmed for your contract.

### Is there a cooling-off period at auction?
Cooling-off is generally unavailable at auction. Some states also exclude defined transactions close to an auction.

### When does the cooling-off clock start?
Victoria starts when the buyer signs, NSW at exchange, and Queensland when the buyer receives the contract signed by both parties. South Australia’s Form 1 timing also matters.

### Can a cooling-off period be waived?
In some jurisdictions, yes, using a prescribed or written mechanism. NSW uses a section 66W certificate; Queensland permits written waiver or shortening. Take legal advice because a waiver can remove or shorten the buyer’s statutory right to rescind.

### What if the state has no statutory cooling-off period?
Negotiate appropriate conditions into the contract before signing and have them professionally drafted or reviewed. In WA and Tasmania, contract conditions usually do the protective work a statutory cooling-off period performs elsewhere.

## Method
Compiled state by state from current government and legislation sources, with each exception beside the headline number it changes.

## Limitations
Legal orientation only. Property type, buyer identity, auction timing, certificates, written waivers and contract terms can change the result.

## Sources
- [Buying property by private sale](https://www.consumer.vic.gov.au/housing/buying-and-selling-property/buying-property/buying-property-by-private-sale) — Consumer Affairs Victoria; accessed 2026-07-19
- [Contracts and deposits when buying property in NSW](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/buying-and-selling-property/buying-property-nsw/contracts-and-deposits) — NSW Government; accessed 2026-07-19
- [Cooling-off period for residential property contracts](https://www.qld.gov.au/community/fair-trading/regulated-industries-licensing-and-legislation/property-industry-regulation/legal-requirements-for-the-property-industry/cooling-off-period-for-residential-property-contracts) — Queensland Government; accessed 2026-07-19
- [Contract of sale](https://nt.gov.au/property/buying-and-selling-a-home/get-help-with-the-contract/contract-of-sale) — Northern Territory Government; accessed 2026-07-19
- [Cooling-off rights](https://lsc.sa.gov.au/handbook/ch23s08s08s01.php) — Legal Services Commission of South Australia; accessed 2026-07-19
- [Civil Law (Sale of Residential Property) Act 2003](https://www.legislation.act.gov.au/DownloadFile/a/2003-40/current/PDF/2003-40.PDF) — ACT Legislation Register; accessed 2026-07-19
- [Buying property by private sale](https://www.consumerprotection.wa.gov.au/buying-property-private-sale) — Consumer Protection Western Australia; accessed 2026-07-19

guides.question: What due diligence should I do before bidding at auction?
guides.title: Auction-day due diligence: the buyer's checklist
guides.summary: A good auction plan is finished before the crowd arrives. Clear the contract, building, finance, deposit and price-limit questions, then keep your written limit where you can see it.
guides.answer: Before you bid, have the contract and disclosure reviewed, put any agreed changes in writing and understand the building report, including the areas it could not cover. Ask your lender or broker how valuation, property type and the final price affect approval. Check how the deposit must be paid and write down a hard limit that already includes the immediate work and buying costs.
guides.methodology: A checklist built from the official contract, auction and inspection guidance, arranged as gates: things you finish before you let yourself bid.
guides.limitations: General Australian guidance only. Contracts, statutes, policies, site conditions and professional scopes vary; obtain advice for the property and decision in front of you.
guides.researchNote: Finish due diligence before auction day. Official guidance confirms that auction contracts are generally binding, cooling-off is usually unavailable and changes to terms require agreement before bidding. See [Consumer Affairs Victoria's auction guidance](https://www.consumer.vic.gov.au/housing/buying-and-selling-property/selling-property/selling-property-by-auction).

sections.heading: Opening
sections.markdown:
### Nothing important waits for the hammer
- **Contract:** Read properly, with any agreed changes in writing
- **Building:** The report understood, and every flag chased down
- **Money:** Finance for this property, the deposit ready, a limit you wrote down

_Bid only when every gate is green._

sections.heading: Why an auction is different
sections.markdown:
When the hammer falls, you are generally bound, and there is usually no cooling-off to save you. So the contract, the finance and the physical checks all get finished first.

In Victoria, the auction cooling-off exclusion also covers purchases within three clear business days before or after the scheduled auction. # Auction-day due diligence: the buyer's checklist

Before you bid, have the contract and disclosure reviewed, put any agreed changes in writing and understand the building report, including the areas it could not cover. Ask your lender or broker how valuation, property type and the final price affect approval. Check how the deposit must be paid and write down a hard limit that already includes the immediate work and buying costs.

## Research note
Finish due diligence before auction day. Official guidance confirms that auction contracts are generally binding, cooling-off is usually unavailable and changes to terms require agreement before bidding. See [Consumer Affairs Victoria's auction guidance](https://www.consumer.vic.gov.au/housing/buying-and-selling-property/selling-property/selling-property-by-auction).

## Opening
### Nothing important waits for the hammer
- **Contract:** Read properly, with any agreed changes in writing
- **Building:** The report understood, and every flag chased down
- **Money:** Finance for this property, the deposit ready, a limit you wrote down

_Bid only when every gate is green._

## Why an auction is different
When the hammer falls, you are generally bound, and there is usually no cooling-off to save you. So the contract, the finance and the physical checks all get finished first.

In Victoria, the auction cooling-off exclusion also covers purchases within three clear business days before or after the scheduled auction. Your state’s rules and your contract’s terms decide the rest. See [cooling-off periods by state](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/cooling-off-period-by-state).

## The checks to clear before you bid
1. **Contract & Section 32 reviewed** by your conveyancer or solicitor, see [how to read a Section 32](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/reading-a-section-32).
2. **Building report understood**, including the important findings, blind spots and any limits on your right to rely on it.
3. **Property-specific finance readiness**, lender conditions, valuation risk, funds to complete and buffer understood.
4. **Deposit mechanics confirmed**, the amount is set by the contract, with payment timing and method checked with the agent.
5. **Your maximum price set in writing**, with a plan to stop there, whatever the room does.

### Contract and Section 32

Have a conveyancer or solicitor review the vendor statement and contract early. Ask about title, settlement, deposit, inclusions, adjustments, default terms and special conditions. If the seller agrees to a change, have it recorded in the contract before you bid. Tell your legal adviser about any representation that affects your decision.

### Building and pest, done in advance

Understand the building before you bid. Check a vendor report's date, scope, access, inspector, insurance and buyer-reliance terms. Commission your own work if those details leave important gaps.

### Property-specific finance readiness

A pre-approval is usually conditional on valuation, final checks and an acceptable property. Give the lender or broker the property type, address, contract and intended price range. Confirm outstanding conditions, valuation-shortfall funding and the cash needed for deposit, duty, costs and settlement. Set a conservative limit and contingency.

### Deposit and your limit

The contract sets the deposit amount and due time. Confirm the agent's payment method and daily transfer limits, then record any negotiated change before bidding. Include acquisition costs, immediate work and a finance buffer in the maximum price.

## What happens if you win and can't settle
If you win and then cannot settle, the deposit is at risk and the seller’s losses, including any shortfall on a resale, can follow you home. That is the whole reason the gates come before the bidding.

> Important: Keep the written limit and the finished checks in front of you on the day. Have every agreed change recorded in the contract before bidding, and tell your legal adviser about any representation you relied on.

> Note: A [desktop read](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/desktop-vs-physical-report) can triage several properties before you commission physical inspections on the strongest candidates. If you buy, keep that evidence as the starting record for ownership.

## Frequently asked questions
### Can I make an auction purchase subject to finance or inspection?
A seller may agree to contract changes before the auction. Have each requested change negotiated and documented by the legal representatives before bidding.

### Is there a cooling-off period if I buy at auction?
Cooling-off is generally unavailable for auction purchases. In Victoria, the exclusion also covers purchases within three clear business days before or after the scheduled auction.

### Do I need a building inspection before auction?
If condition could change your decision or maximum bid, obtain an appropriately scoped inspection early enough to assess its findings and blind spots. Test any vendor report's date, access, commissioning party and purchaser-reliance terms.

### Is pre-approval enough to bid at auction?
Not by itself. Ask the lender what conditions remain, whether this property is acceptable to them, what happens if the valuation comes in short, and whether you hold the funds and buffer to complete at your intended price.

### What happens if I win and then can't settle?
You risk forfeiting the deposit and may be liable for the seller's losses, including a resale shortfall.

### How much deposit do I need at auction?
The contract sets the amount. Check the due time and payment method, and document any agreed change before bidding.

## Method
A checklist built from the official contract, auction and inspection guidance, arranged as gates: things you finish before you let yourself bid.

## Limitations
General Australian guidance only. Contracts, statutes, policies, site conditions and professional scopes vary; obtain advice for the property and decision in front of you.

## Sources

- [Contracts and deposits when buying property in NSW](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/buying-and-selling-property/buying-property-nsw/contracts-and-deposits) — NSW Government; accessed 2026-07-19

sections.heading: Opening
sections.markdown:

sections.heading: The era matrix
sections.markdown:
_[Illustration: Five detailed Australian house models progressing from a pre-1920s home through interwar, postwar, 1980s to 1990s and contemporary construction. Each era leaves its own clues in the roof, walls, footings, services and later alterations. The table below turns those clues into inspection questions.]_

**Inspection prompts by construction era**

| Era / form | Questions to put first | Evidence to seek |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pre-1920s | Actual footing/wall systems, roof/chimney, damp pathway, services, older coatings | Plans, footing and roof work, licensed service inspection, moisture diagnosis, lead-safe assessment |
| 1920s–40s | Regional construction, drainage/subfloor, roof and openings, services, later materials | Alteration dates, footing and drainage work, service records, pre-1990 material identification |
| 1950s–70s | Actual brick veneer/weatherboard/masonry system, asbestos screen, services, wet areas, movement | Material identification, licensed inspections, wet-area history, footing and crack evidence |
| 1980s–90s | Transition materials, wet-area evidence, roof/windows/services and actual installation dates | Permits, invoices, leak history, roof and service condition |
| 2000s onward, house | Approvals, drainage, roof/façade junctions, wet areas, workmanship and warranties | Completion records, reports, claims/notices and repair close-out |
| 2000s onward, apartment | Plan boundaries, common defects, external walls/cladding, fire, funding and insurance | Records inspection, engineering/fire reports, works plan, funds, litigation and policy schedule |

sections.heading: Hazards with useful date screens
sections.markdown:
### Asbestos-containing materials

The [national householders' guide](https://www.newaste.org.au/asbestos/assets/asbestos-guide-for-householders.pdf) says houses built or renovated before 1990 may contain asbestos products. All uses were prohibited nationally from 31 December 2003. Identify suspect material before drilling, sanding or demolition and follow the licensing and disposal rules for the material, amount and jurisdiction.

### Lead in older paint

Older paint, especially pre-1970s layers, may contain much higher lead concentrations than modern coatings. Before sanding, scraping or heat stripping, follow the [Australian Government Lead Alert](https://www.agriculture.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/lead-paint-fifth-edition.pdf), test where appropriate and use lead-safe controls.

sections.heading: Establish the age of each service
sections.markdown: A 1930 house may have 2020 wiring and mixed plumbing; a 2005 apartment may contain later unauthorised wet-area work. Ask for installation and alteration evidence, then have the relevant licensed trade assess the system within the available access and scope. Ceramic fuses, deteriorated insulation, galvanised pipe and old hot-water units are observable system clues.

sections.heading: Trace the water pathway
sections.markdown: Older masonry can show capillary moisture, bridged damp-proofing, rain penetration or plumbing leaks. Newer buildings can show failed junctions, drainage, membranes, façades or balconies. Trace source, path and damage using [the damp guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/damp-and-moisture-in-your-home).

sections.heading: Regional variation can outweigh decade
sections.markdown: Tropical elevated houses, cyclone-region homes, coastal masonry, alpine roofs, bushfire construction and southern clay-soil suburbs demand different questions. Add the property’s location to every era profile: climate, wind region, termites, flood and bushfire exposure, soil and salt.

sections.heading: Turn a red flag into a decision
sections.markdown:
1. **Name the clue:** record what was seen or disclosed without diagnosing it.
2. **Ask what would disprove the concern:** invoice, permit, material test, access or later report.
3. **Choose the discipline:** building inspector, engineer, electrician, plumber, hygienist, strata specialist or lawyer.
4. **Define consequence:** safety, scope, timing, contract condition, bid limit or decision not to proceed.
5. **Keep uncertainty visible:** record inaccessible and unverified areas clearly.

Where the clue is movement, use [the crack triage](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/cracks-structural-or-cosmetic). For a purchase, build the brief for the [physical inspection](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/building-inspection-before-auction); for ownership planning, use [the era evidence model](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/what-your-home-needs-by-decade).

> Note: A useful red flag changes the evidence you seek, the professional you engage or the decision you make.

# Property red flags by era: what deserves a closer look

Pre-1920s and interwar homes deserve close attention to footings, moisture, roofs, services and older coatings. Homes from the 1950s to the 1970s add a high-priority pre-1990 asbestos screen. The 1980s and 1990s span major material and standards changes. Newer houses bring approvals, drainage and workmanship into focus, while newer apartments add common property, cladding, fire systems, insurance and scheme funding. Region, construction and later alterations can change the picture completely.

## Research note
Age guides inspection priorities. Australian guidance says asbestos can be present in homes built or renovated before 1990 and all uses were prohibited nationally from 31 December 2003. Older paint can contain lead. See the [householders' asbestos guide](https://www.newaste.org.au/asbestos/assets/asbestos-guide-for-householders.pdf) and [Lead Alert](https://www.agriculture.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/lead-paint-fifth-edition.pdf).

## The era matrix
_[Illustration: Five detailed Australian house models progressing from a pre-1920s home through interwar, postwar, 1980s to 1990s and contemporary construction. | Era / form | Questions to put first | Evidence to seek |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pre-1920s | Actual footing/wall systems, roof/chimney, damp pathway, services, older coatings | Plans, footing and roof work, licensed service inspection, moisture diagnosis, lead-safe assessment |

| 1980s–90s | Transition materials, wet-area evidence, roof/windows/services and actual installation dates | Permits, invoices, leak history, roof and service condition |
| 2000s onward, house | Approvals, drainage, roof/façade junctions, wet areas, workmanship and warranties | Completion records, reports, claims/notices and repair close-out |
| 2000s onward, apartment | Plan boundaries, common defects, external walls/cladding, fire, funding and insurance | Records inspection, engineering/fire reports, works plan, funds, litigation and policy schedule |

## Hazards with useful date screens
### Asbestos-containing materials

The [national householders' guide](https://www.newaste.org.au/asbestos/assets/asbestos-guide-for-householders.pdf) says houses built or renovated before 1990 may contain asbestos products. All uses were prohibited nationally from 31 December 2003. Identify suspect material before drilling, sanding or demolition and follow the licensing and disposal rules for the material, amount and jurisdiction.

### Lead in older paint

Older paint, especially pre-1970s layers, may contain much higher lead concentrations than modern coatings. Before sanding, scraping or heat stripping, follow the [Australian Government Lead Alert](https://www.agriculture.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/lead-paint-fifth-edition.pdf), test where appropriate and use lead-safe controls.

## Establish the age of each service
A 1930 house may have 2020 wiring and mixed plumbing; a 2005 apartment may contain later unauthorised wet-area work. Ask for installation and alteration evidence, then have the relevant licensed trade assess the system within the available access and scope. Ceramic fuses, deteriorated insulation, galvanised pipe and old hot-water units are observable system clues.

## Trace the water pathway
Older masonry can show capillary moisture, bridged damp-proofing, rain penetration or plumbing leaks. Newer buildings can show failed junctions, drainage, membranes, façades or balconies. Trace source, path and damage using [the damp guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/damp-and-moisture-in-your-home).

## Turn a red flag into a decision
1. **Name the clue:** record what was seen or disclosed without diagnosing it.
2. **Ask what would disprove the concern:** invoice, permit, material test, access or later report.
3. **Choose the discipline:** building inspector, engineer, electrician, plumber, hygienist, strata specialist or lawyer.
4. **Define consequence:** safety, scope, timing, contract condition, bid limit or decision not to proceed.
5. **Keep uncertainty visible:** record inaccessible and unverified areas clearly.

> Note: A useful red flag changes the evidence you seek, the professional you engage or the decision you make.

## Frequently asked questions
### Which era of house has the most problems?
There is no winner. Construction, region, alterations and current condition matter far more than any decade ranking, and a well-kept 1920s house beats a neglected 2010s one comfortably.

### What is the asbestos screening date?

### Does an old home definitely have lead paint?
Older coatings are a high-priority screen, especially pre-1970s layers. Testing establishes presence and concentration. Use lead-safe methods before disturbance.

guides.question: Are cracks in the walls a dealbreaker? How do I tell structural from cosmetic?
guides.title: Wall cracks: which ones matter, and how to tell
guides.summary: Many wall cracks are minor. Width gives you a starting point; direction, location, nearby movement and change over time tell you when to call for help.
guides.answer: A hairline crack that stays still is often a monitoring job. Cracks around 5 mm or wider, diagonal or stepped patterns, visible growth, sticking openings, sloping floors or water entry deserve professional investigation. AS 2870 gives useful width categories, and an engineer can read those measurements in the context of the whole building and site.
guides.methodology: A triage approach: what the crack looks like, what surrounds it, and whether it is moving.
guides.limitations: A structural engineer can diagnose the significance and cause for the building in front of them. Visible progression or movement affecting doors, floors and openings deserves professional investigation.
guides.researchNote: Read crack width with direction, location, associated distortion and change over time. The [QBCC treats cracks wider than 5 mm as a sign that can warrant further investigation](https://qbcc.qld.gov.au/home-owner-hub/maintain-protect/protect-against-subsidence). A structural engineer should diagnose progressive movement or movement affecting doors, floors and openings.

cluster.label: Read the building
cluster.blurb: Use age and construction as a starting hypothesis, then test it against evidence and physical inspection.

sections.heading: Opening
sections.markdown:
### Width is the first clue
- **Geometry:** How wide, which way it runs, and where it sits
- **Context:** What is around it: openings, floors, drainage, the soil
- **Change:** Whether it is growing. Date it, measure it, come back.

_Read growth, width, direction, distortion and location together. Escalate concerning movement._

sections.heading: How serious is it? The damage categories
sections.markdown:
[AS 2870-2011, Residential slabs and footings](https://store.standards.org.au/product/as-2870-2011), classifies wall damage using crack width and typical effects. Use the categories with direction, location, associated distortion and change.

**AS 2870 damage categories for walls (indicative, an inspector or engineer confirms)**

| Category | Crack width | What it means |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | Less than 0.1 mm (hairline) | Negligible, no action |
| 1 | Up to about 1 mm (fine) | Very slight; monitor context and change |
| 2 | About 1–5 mm | Slight, noticeable, usually filled and monitored |
| 3 | About 5–15 mm | Moderate, doors and windows stick, pipes may fracture; investigate and repair |
| 4 | About 15–25 mm | Severe, frames distort, walls lean or bulge; major repair |
| 5 | More than about 25 mm | Very severe, with major structural effects; urgent engineering assessment |

Categories 0 and 1 are negligible to very slight, Category 2 is slight, and from Category 3 up the Standard’s own language runs moderate to severe, which is where professional investigation starts. The width is the entry point, not the verdict.

guides.contentMarkdown:
# Wall cracks: which ones matter, and how to tell

A hairline crack that stays still is often a monitoring job. Cracks around 5 mm or wider, diagonal or stepped patterns, visible growth, sticking openings, sloping floors or water entry deserve professional investigation. AS 2870 gives useful width categories, and an engineer can read those measurements in the context of the whole building and site.

## Research note
Read crack width with direction, location, associated distortion and change over time. The [QBCC treats cracks wider than 5 mm as a sign that can warrant further investigation](https://qbcc.qld.gov.au/home-owner-hub/maintain-protect/protect-against-subsidence). A structural engineer should diagnose progressive movement or movement affecting doors, floors and openings.

## Opening
### Width is the first clue
- **Geometry:** How wide, which way it runs, and where it sits
- **Context:** What is around it: openings, floors, drainage, the soil
- **Change:** Whether it is growing. Date it, measure it, come back.

_Read growth, width, direction, distortion and location together. Escalate concerning movement._

## How serious is it? The damage categories
[AS 2870-2011, Residential slabs and footings](https://store.standards.org.au/product/as-2870-2011), classifies wall damage using crack width and typical effects. Use the categories with direction, location, associated distortion and change.

**AS 2870 damage categories for walls (indicative, an inspector or engineer confirms)**

| Category | Crack width | What it means |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | Less than 0.1 mm (hairline) | Negligible, no action |
| 1 | Up to about 1 mm (fine) | Very slight; monitor context and change |
| 2 | About 1–5 mm | Slight, noticeable, usually filled and monitored |
| 3 | About 5–15 mm | Moderate, doors and windows stick, pipes may fracture; investigate and repair |
| 4 | About 15–25 mm | Severe, frames distort, walls lean or bulge; major repair |
| 5 | More than about 25 mm | Very severe, with major structural effects; urgent engineering assessment |

Categories 0 and 1 are negligible to very slight, Category 2 is slight, and from Category 3 up the Standard’s own language runs moderate to severe, which is where professional investigation starts. The width is the entry point, not the verdict.

## How to read a crack
_[Illustration: Architectural material study showing a fine plaster hairline, a diagonal crack from a window corner and stepped cracking along masonry joints. The pattern gives the first clue. Use the AS 2870 table above for width, then read direction, location, distortion and change.]_

Write down the width, the direction, where it sits, anything distorting nearby, and how it changes. Together those signals tell you which professional to call, and what to ask them.

**Reading the signals beyond width**

| Signal | Lower-concern pattern | Escalation pattern |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Direction | Vertical, fine, along joints | Diagonal from window/door corners; stepped through brick |
| Associated signs | Localised crack only | Sticking doors and windows, sloping floors, gaps at cornices |
| Where | Plaster or render surface | Through the structure, external brickwork, lintels |
| Over time | Stable, seasonal | Progressive, getting longer or wider |

## Why cracks appear
### Reactive clay and moisture

Cracks can arise from material shrinkage, seasonal movement, alterations or footing movement. Reactive clay soil swells and shrinks as moisture changes. AS 2870 uses site classifications including A, S, M, H1, H2, E and P. Use the classification with drainage, trees, services, footings and the observed building pattern.

### Drainage, trees and original footings

Moisture changes can drive footing movement. Check drainage at the foundations, leaking service pipes, downpipe discharge, large trees, root effects and the actual footing system.

## The single most useful test: time
Monitor cracks with dated photographs and a stable reference point. Record width, length, season, drainage conditions and associated changes to doors or floors. Visible growth raises concern, and width, direction, distortion and location still matter. Progression or associated movement is the point to seek professional investigation.

## When to bring in a structural engineer
Category 3 width, diagonal direction, sticking doors, sloping floors and visible progression justify professional investigation. A building inspection can flag the concern; a **structural engineer** can diagnose cause and scope. Use [the era guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/red-flags-by-era) for related construction questions.

> Note: Keep crack photographs, measurements, inspection findings and repair records together so change remains visible over time.

> Important: Fresh cosmetic work can obscure crack history. At auction, complete any required assessment before bidding. See [auction-day due diligence](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/auction-day-due-diligence).

## Frequently asked questions
### When should I investigate a wall crack?
Seek competent assessment where a crack is changing, relatively wide, stepped or diagonal, appears with sticking openings or floor movement, admits water, affects a structural element, or follows an event. Width categories are only one input; material, location, cause and change over time also matter.

### Are cracks in walls a dealbreaker when buying?
Cracks need context. Escalation signals include increasing width, diagonal cracking from openings, steps through masonry, sticking doors, sloping floors and related distortion. AS 2870 Category 3 starts at about 5 mm and describes moderate damage that warrants professional investigation.

### How wide does a crack need to be to worry?
AS 2870 classifies wall cracks by width: hairline under 0.1 mm and fine cracks up to about 1 mm are negligible; 1–5 mm is slight; 5–15 mm is moderate and worth professional investigation; 15–25 mm is severe. Also look at direction, location, associated distortion and progression.

### What causes structural cracks?
Most commonly movement in the footings, reactive clay soils swelling and shrinking with moisture, poor drainage at the foundations, leaking pipes, large trees, or shallow original footings. Much of southern Australia sits on reactive clay, which makes footing movement a recurring issue in older homes.

### Should I get an engineer or is a building inspection enough?
A building inspection can flag concerning cracking. A structural engineer can then diagnose cause, significance and repair scope where indicated.

### Is a hairline crack anything to worry about?
Hairline cracks fall within the negligible AS 2870 width category. Monitor progression and associated signs, especially around openings and floors.

## Method
A triage approach: what the crack looks like, what surrounds it, and whether it is moving.

## Limitations
A structural engineer can diagnose the significance and cause for the building in front of them. Visible progression or movement affecting doors, floors and openings deserves professional investigation.

## Sources
- [AS 2870-2011 Residential slabs and footings](https://store.standards.org.au/product/as-2870-2011) — Standards Australia; accessed 2026-07-19
- [Protect against subsidence](https://qbcc.qld.gov.au/home-owner-hub/maintain-protect/protect-against-subsidence) — Queensland Building and Construction Commission; accessed 2026-07-20
- [Due diligence checklist for home buyers](https://www.consumer.vic.gov.au/housing/buying-and-selling-property/checklists/due-diligence) — Consumer Affairs Victoria; accessed 2026-07-19
- [Brickwork and blockwork](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/materials/brickwork-and-blockwork) — YourHome, Australian Government; accessed 2026-07-19

sections.heading: Opening
sections.markdown:
### You are joining the building too
- **Lot:** Your four walls: condition, services, alterations
- **Common property:** Everyone’s walls: the fabric and systems the plan makes shared
- **Scheme:** The scheme: its money, its minutes, its decisions

_Start with the registered plan, then read it with the legislation and scheme records._

sections.heading: Read the lot and the scheme together
sections.markdown:
The registered plan and state law define the lot/common-property boundary. Inspect the lot, understand owner alterations, and read scheme records for shared fabric, services, finances, insurance, disputes and decisions. Use the [shared-building risk guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/strata-risks-for-owners) to connect each issue to its boundary, decision maker and funding path. Check:

- **Maintenance / sinking fund balance:** is there enough set aside for the building’s age and the works it will need?
- **Special levies:** any raised recently, or foreshadowed in the meeting minutes?
- **Quarterly fees:** the ongoing cost, and the trend. Are they rising, and why?
- **Insurance:** what does the scheme policy insure, for what declared value, with which excesses, exclusions, claims and valuation basis?
- **Disputes & defects:** litigation, building-defect claims, or major works on the horizon.
- **By-laws / rules:** restrictions on pets, renovations or short-term letting that may affect how you use or rent the apartment.

sections.heading: Where to find it
sections.markdown: Available documents and disclosure routes differ by state. In Victoria, relevant owners-corporation information forms part of the [Section 32 process](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/reading-a-section-32); elsewhere, certificates, searches or records inspections take different forms. Commission the appropriate search early enough to review minutes, financials, maintenance plans, insurance, defects, disputes, notices and correspondence. Missing or thin records are a substantive evidence gap worth investigating.

sections.heading: The funding gap is the tell
sections.markdown: A fund balance has meaning only beside the building's forecast and known works, levy income, arrears, liabilities and timing. A low balance may be appropriate after completed work or inadequate for imminent work; a high balance may still be insufficient for a large program. Liability for a special levy can turn on the resolution, instalment due dates, state law, disclosure, contract and settlement adjustments. Have the legal representative map each known or proposed amount to this contract.

sections.heading: Then check the building itself
sections.markdown:
Use scheme records for boundaries, decisions, funding, insurance and known projects. Use a physical inspection for the lot and accessible common areas. Three recurring apartment questions deserve attention:

### Waterproofing and balcony membranes

Failed waterproofing in bathrooms and balconies is a recurring apartment defect category. Repair can cross common property and multiple lots, with costs funded through the scheme.

### Combustible cladding

For towers and mid-rise buildings constructed in the 2000s–2010s, combustible cladding is a live issue. Check the owners-corporation records for a cladding assessment, any rectification works, and whether a related special levy has been raised or is foreshadowed. Cladding replacement is rarely cheap.

### Builder defects

Newer buildings carry the risk of original builder defects, waterproofing, fire separation, structural and services issues that emerge in the first years. The minutes will often show whether defects have been identified, pursued, and resolved, or are still in dispute. See [red flags by era](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/red-flags-by-era) for what newer buildings tend to hide.

> Note: Read the apartment, the shared building and the scheme together. A records inspection, legal review and physical inspection each answer a different part of the purchase.

faqs.answer: In the owners-corporation certificate and meeting minutes disclosed with the contract; in Victoria that means inside the Section 32 vendor statement. You can also commission a specialist strata report.

# What to check before buying an apartment: strata and owners corporation

Get the right records inspection for your state, read several years of minutes and finances, compare the works plan with available funds, and check insurance and active defects. Ask your legal representative to explain how any current or proposed levy affects the contract.

## Research note
An apartment purchase includes the lot and an interest in shared property and governance. The registered plan and state law establish common property. - **Special levies:** any raised recently, or foreshadowed in the meeting minutes?
- **Quarterly fees:** the ongoing cost, and the trend. Are they rising, and why?
- **Insurance:** what does the scheme policy insure, for what declared value, with which excesses, exclusions, claims and valuation basis?
- **Disputes & defects:** litigation, building-defect claims, or major works on the horizon.
- **By-laws / rules:** restrictions on pets, renovations or short-term letting that may affect how you use or rent the apartment.

## Where to find it
Available documents and disclosure routes differ by state. Have the legal representative map each known or proposed amount to this contract.

## Then check the building itself

### Waterproofing and balcony membranes

Failed waterproofing in bathrooms and balconies is a recurring apartment defect category. Repair can cross common property and multiple lots, with costs funded through the scheme.

### Combustible cladding

> Note: Read the apartment, the shared building and the scheme together. A records inspection, legal review and physical inspection each answer a different part of the purchase.

## Frequently asked questions
### What should I check before buying an apartment?
Check the registered plan, owners-corporation records, maintenance or capital-works plan, funds, levies, insurance, by-laws, disputes and defects. Add a physical inspection of the lot and accessible common areas.

### What is a special levy and why does it matter?
It is an additional contribution resolved under the applicable strata or owners-corporation process. Existing and proposed levies can materially change ownership cost; responsibility around a sale depends on the resolution, due dates, law, disclosure and contract.

### Where do I find the owners-corporation information?

## Limitations

guides.question: Does my home's condition affect my insurance?
guides.title: Home condition and insurance: describe the risk accurately
guides.summary: Your home's age, construction and condition can shape the cover you are offered. A clear description, sensible rebuild figure and good records make insurance easier to understand and use.
guides.answer: Insurers may consider construction, age, condition, claims history, occupancy and local hazards when setting cover, terms and price. Describe the property and its alterations accurately, keep the rebuild figure current, read the exclusions and maintenance obligations, and get a quote before you buy. Dated photographs, invoices and reports can be invaluable if you ever need to make a claim.
guides.methodology: We followed the policy the way an insurer reads it: how the property is described, what it is insured for, what is excluded, what upkeep it expects, and what evidence a claim will need.
guides.limitations: No record guarantees cover, a cheaper premium or a paid claim. The policy wording and the insurer’s assessment decide; good records just make sure your side of the story is on the table.
guides.researchNote: Insurance is policy-specific. Moneysmart recommends checking exclusions, rebuilding cost, excesses and the Product Disclosure Statement; it also warns that inadequate sums insured can leave a gap. See [choosing home insurance](https://moneysmart.gov.au/home-insurance/choosing-home-insurance) and [avoiding underinsurance](https://moneysmart.gov.au/home-insurance/underinsurance-what-it-is-and-how-to-avoid-it).

cluster.label: Own, maintain and change
cluster.blurb: Keep useful records, maintain the fabric safely and plan works without over-promising what condition can prove.

sections.heading: Opening
sections.markdown:
### Tell the story of your home clearly
- **Describe:** Describe it straight: construction, occupancy, works, hazards
- **Insure:** Know what it is insured for, and what the fine print excludes
- **Document:** Keep dated evidence before anything goes wrong

_The policy wording has the final word. Make sure you have read it._

sections.heading: How condition can affect cover and price
sections.markdown: An insurer may use construction, roof type, age, visible condition, maintenance, occupancy, claims history and local hazards when deciding whether to offer cover and on what terms. The effect on premium varies by insurer and property. Ask for an address-specific quote, disclose known information accurately and read the exclusions and conditions in the Product Disclosure Statement.

sections.heading: Five insurance questions
sections.markdown:
**Where property evidence fits into an insurance decision**

| Question | Evidence to prepare | What controls the outcome |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Will the insurer offer cover? | Address, use, construction, age, condition, hazards and claims history | Insurer underwriting criteria |
| What events and property are covered? | Building description, listed items and optional covers | Policy wording, schedule and exclusions |
| How much should be insured? | Dimensions, construction, finishes, site and demolition/rebuild allowances | Chosen cover basis, calculator or professional estimate and policy limits |
| What must the owner do? | Maintenance, vacancy, security, notification and works history | Policy conditions and general insurance law |
| What supports a claim? | Before-and-after photos, invoices, reports, contents evidence and communications | Cause of loss, policy response, evidence and insurer assessment |

sections.heading: Describe the actual home
sections.markdown:
Answer the proposal and renewal questions straight, because the policy is only as honest as the answers underneath it. Construction type, roof material, year built, occupancy, business use, short-term letting, security, renovations, pools, solar systems and past losses can all be relevant. Use plans, reports or qualified assessment to identify the wall system where it matters.

If buying, seek an insurance quote before committing, especially for flood, bushfire, cyclone, heritage fabric, an older roof, unusual construction or unresolved defects. Check eligibility, exclusions, excesses and price for the specific property.

sections.heading: Read exclusions and maintenance conditions
sections.markdown:
Policies distinguish insured events from wear, corrosion, gradual deterioration, building defects, vermin, ground movement and maintenance-related loss. Wording varies. [Moneysmart recommends comparing the Product Disclosure Statement, exclusions, excesses and limits](https://moneysmart.gov.au/home-insurance/choosing-home-insurance). Read the definitions for storm and water damage in the actual policy.

Maintenance can reduce avoidable damage. Read the policy’s maintenance and wear exclusions, then ask the insurer in writing how a specific measure may affect cover, underwriting or price before spending for an insurance outcome.

sections.heading: Set the rebuild basis
sections.markdown: Set the insured amount from demolition and rebuild cost. Include site access, slope, professional fees, debris removal, code upgrades, materials and temporary accommodation where relevant. [Moneysmart warns that underinsurance can leave a household unable to fully rebuild](https://moneysmart.gov.au/home-insurance/underinsurance-what-it-is-and-how-to-avoid-it). Retain the calculation inputs and consider a professional estimate for complex, heritage, high-value or unusual buildings.

sections.heading: Keep useful evidence
sections.markdown:
- **Baseline:** dated exterior, roof-from-ground, room and service photographs; plans and specifications where available.
- **Work:** contracts, invoices, permits, certificates, warranties, product details and before/during/after photographs.

guides.contentMarkdown:
# Home condition and insurance: describe the risk accurately

Insurers may consider construction, age, condition, claims history, occupancy and local hazards when setting cover, terms and price. Describe the property and its alterations accurately, keep the rebuild figure current, read the exclusions and maintenance obligations, and get a quote before you buy. Dated photographs, invoices and reports can be invaluable if you ever need to make a claim.

## Research note
Insurance is policy-specific. Moneysmart recommends checking exclusions, rebuilding cost, excesses and the Product Disclosure Statement; it also warns that inadequate sums insured can leave a gap. See [choosing home insurance](https://moneysmart.gov.au/home-insurance/choosing-home-insurance) and [avoiding underinsurance](https://moneysmart.gov.au/home-insurance/underinsurance-what-it-is-and-how-to-avoid-it).

## Opening
### Tell the story of your home clearly
- **Describe:** Describe it straight: construction, occupancy, works, hazards
- **Insure:** Know what it is insured for, and what the fine print excludes
- **Document:** Keep dated evidence before anything goes wrong

_The policy wording has the final word. Make sure you have read it._

## How condition can affect cover and price
An insurer may use construction, roof type, age, visible condition, maintenance, occupancy, claims history and local hazards when deciding whether to offer cover and on what terms. The effect on premium varies by insurer and property. Ask for an address-specific quote, disclose known information accurately and read the exclusions and conditions in the Product Disclosure Statement.

## Five insurance questions
**Where property evidence fits into an insurance decision**

| Question | Evidence to prepare | What controls the outcome |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Will the insurer offer cover? | Address, use, construction, age, condition, hazards and claims history | Insurer underwriting criteria |
| What events and property are covered? | Building description, listed items and optional covers | Policy wording, schedule and exclusions |
| How much should be insured? | Dimensions, construction, finishes, site and demolition/rebuild allowances | Chosen cover basis, calculator or professional estimate and policy limits |
| What must the owner do? | Maintenance, vacancy, security, notification and works history | Policy conditions and general insurance law |
| What supports a claim? | Before-and-after photos, invoices, reports, contents evidence and communications | Cause of loss, policy response, evidence and insurer assessment |

## Describe the actual home
Answer the proposal and renewal questions straight, because the policy is only as honest as the answers underneath it. Construction type, roof material, year built, occupancy, business use, short-term letting, security, renovations, pools, solar systems and past losses can all be relevant. Use plans, reports or qualified assessment to identify the wall system where it matters.

If buying, seek an insurance quote before committing, especially for flood, bushfire, cyclone, heritage fabric, an older roof, unusual construction or unresolved defects. Check eligibility, exclusions, excesses and price for the specific property.

## Read exclusions and maintenance conditions
Policies distinguish insured events from wear, corrosion, gradual deterioration, building defects, vermin, ground movement and maintenance-related loss. Wording varies. [Moneysmart recommends comparing the Product Disclosure Statement, exclusions, excesses and limits](https://moneysmart.gov.au/home-insurance/choosing-home-insurance). Read the definitions for storm and water damage in the actual policy.

Maintenance can reduce avoidable damage. Read the policy’s maintenance and wear exclusions, then ask the insurer in writing how a specific measure may affect cover, underwriting or price before spending for an insurance outcome.

## Set the rebuild basis
Set the insured amount from demolition and rebuild cost. Include site access, slope, professional fees, debris removal, code upgrades, materials and temporary accommodation where relevant. [Moneysmart warns that underinsurance can leave a household unable to fully rebuild](https://moneysmart.gov.au/home-insurance/underinsurance-what-it-is-and-how-to-avoid-it). Retain the calculation inputs and consider a professional estimate for complex, heritage, high-value or unusual buildings.

## Keep useful evidence
- **Baseline:** dated exterior, roof-from-ground, room and service photographs; plans and specifications where available.
- **Work:** contracts, invoices, permits, certificates, warranties, product details and before/during/after photographs.
- **Condition:** inspection reports, repair recommendations, moisture or crack monitoring and completion evidence.
- **Insurance:** proposals, schedules, PDS versions, endorsements, renewal notices and written answers from the insurer or broker.
- **Loss:** photographs before clean-up where safe, emergency-work invoices, damaged-item evidence and a contemporaneous event timeline.

These records establish what existed, when the work happened and how a loss unfolded. Whether that adds up to a paid claim still turns on the cause, the cover and the policy’s words. Build the record described in [keeping a record of your home](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/keeping-a-record-of-your-home).

## Notify before renovations and material changes
Renovations can change occupancy, security, construction risk, value and the boundary between domestic building insurance and home insurance. Before work starts, tell the insurer or broker what is planned and ask in writing whether the policy continues, needs endorsement or excludes part of the work. Do the same for extended vacancy, letting or another material change required by the policy.

## Hazard cover is specific
Flood, storm, bushfire, cyclone and actions of the sea have specific policy definitions, exclusions, excesses and optional covers. [Moneysmart's storm, flood and fire guide](https://moneysmart.gov.au/home-insurance/storm-flood-and-fire-insurance) explains how the event definition connects with the local hazard. Follow property-specific authority or professional advice for resilience work, then ask the insurer how it affects underwriting.

> Important: The policy schedule, PDS, endorsements, insurer questions and applicable law determine cover. Confirm property-specific terms with the insurer or a licensed insurance broker.

## Frequently asked questions
### Does my home's condition affect my insurance premium?
Condition can affect underwriting, terms or price alongside location, hazard, rebuild cost, claims history, construction, occupancy and insurer appetite.

### Will maintenance lower my premium?
It may, depending on the insurer, the property and the measure. Ask what the insurer recognises and what evidence it wants. The clearer benefit is reducing avoidable damage and attending to any maintenance obligations in your own policy.

### Does a condition report guarantee a claim will be paid?
A report can support evidence about the property and timing. The event, cause, policy wording, exclusions and insurer assessment control the claim.

### Should I get an insurance quote before buying?
Yes, particularly for hazard-exposed, older, heritage, unusual or defect-affected properties. Check cover, excesses, exclusions, conditions and premium.

### How do I avoid underinsurance?
Use the policy’s rebuild basis, keep dimensions and construction information accurate, review the amount after works and cost changes, and consider a professional estimate for a complex property.

## Method
We followed the policy the way an insurer reads it: how the property is described, what it is insured for, what is excluded, what upkeep it expects, and what evidence a claim will need.

## Limitations
No record guarantees cover, a cheaper premium or a paid claim. The policy wording and the insurer’s assessment decide; good records just make sure your side of the story is on the table.

## Sources
- [Choosing home insurance](https://moneysmart.gov.au/home-insurance/choosing-home-insurance) — Moneysmart, Australian Securities and Investments Commission; accessed 2026-07-19
- [Underinsurance: what it is and how to avoid it](https://moneysmart.gov.au/home-insurance/underinsurance-what-it-is-and-how-to-avoid-it) — Moneysmart, Australian Securities and Investments Commission; accessed 2026-07-19
- [Storm, flood and fire insurance](https://moneysmart.gov.au/home-insurance/storm-flood-and-fire-insurance) — Moneysmart, Australian Securities and Investments Commission; accessed 2026-07-19

sections.heading: Opening
sections.markdown:
### Make the useful things easy to find
- **What:** Plans, permits, invoices, warranties, photos, reports
- **Where:** Tied to a room, an element, a product, a name
- **When:** Dated: done, checked, fixed, and due again

_Keep the originals. And when you are not sure, write down that you are not sure._

sections.heading: Build a record you will use
sections.markdown:
A useful record is retrievable by any future reader. Every item should answer four fields: **date**, **element or location**, **event or work**, and **source**. Keep the original file with a descriptive filename.

**The minimum home record**

| Folder | Keep | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 01 Property and title | Title, deposited/registered plan, survey, easements, covenants, planning and hazard reports | Defines the land, restrictions and property context |
| 02 Approvals | Planning and building permits, endorsed plans, inspections, occupancy and trade certificates | Records the approval pathway and approved scope |
| 03 Works and products | Contracts, quotes, variations, invoices, warranties, manuals, model numbers, colours and materials | Explains what was installed, by whom and on what terms |
| 04 Condition and reports | Building, pest, engineering, plumbing, electrical, roof, moisture, strata and other reports | Creates dated professional observations and limitations |
| 05 Photographs | Wide and close views before, during and after work; concealed services before closing | Locates evidence and preserves what later becomes hidden |
| 06 Maintenance and monitoring | Service dates, filters, treatments, cleaning, crack or moisture logs and next review | Shows change and keeps recurring tasks visible |
| 07 Insurance and incidents | Schedules, PDS versions, valuations, claims, loss photos and insurer correspondence | Preserves the wording and evidence relevant to a loss |
| 08 Shared building | Plan, by-laws/rules, minutes, budgets, funds, insurance, levies and scheme correspondence | Connects the lot to common-property decisions and costs |
| 09 Contacts | Designer, builder, certifier/surveyor, engineer, trades, insurer, strata manager and warranties | Makes follow-up and responsibility traceable |

sections.heading: Use filenames that sort themselves
sections.markdown: Use ISO dates and plain language: 2026-07-19_roof_north-valley_leak-photo_01.jpg or 2026-08-04_bathroom-waterproofing_certificate.pdf. Add a one-page index with the element, current known status, latest evidence and next action. Keep a cloud copy and a separate backup, with sensitive identity and financial material protected.

sections.heading: Take photographs that will still help later
sections.markdown:
1. **Orient:** one wide photograph showing the room, elevation or element.
2. **Locate:** a mid-range view connecting the issue to a window, corner, joint or service.
3. **Detail:** a clear close view with a scale where dimension matters.
4. **Date and describe:** weather/event, direction, dimensions and whether the condition changed.
5. **During work:** capture framing, membranes, flashings, pipes and cables before they are concealed.
6. **Close out:** finished work, invoice, specification, certificate and warranty in the same indexed folder.

sections.heading: Record uncertainty explicitly
sections.markdown: Write 'installation date unknown' or 'reported by previous owner, unverified' where appropriate. A receipt records a purchase; a permit records an approval; a photograph records what the frame caught that day. Let each document say only what it truly knows.

sections.heading: Update at decision moments
sections.markdown:
- **On purchase:** save the contract/disclosure, reports and a dated baseline.
- **Before work:** save approvals, condition photos, service locations and insurer advice.
- **During work:** variations, concealed work and inspection evidence.
- **At completion:** certificates, final plans, warranties, manuals and a next-maintenance date.
- **After an event:** safe pre-clean-up evidence, emergency work and the claim timeline.
- **At sale:** copy the releasable, accurate set for legal review; retain sensitive or irrelevant material separately.

sections.heading: The limits of a home record
sections.markdown:
A good record shortens every future search and supports the insurance, maintenance, renovation and sale decisions to come. Verify current condition and legal effect for the decision in front of you. For insurance-specific use, read [home condition and insurance](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/home-condition-and-insurance); for works, read [planning a renovation](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/planning-a-renovation).

> Note: The best record is modest and precise: original evidence, clear dates, known limits and an explicit next action. That is more credible than a polished history that hides uncertainty.

# The home record: what to keep, how to name it, when to update it

Keep enough information for someone to answer five questions: what is here, where is it, when did it change, who did the work and what proves it? Save the title and plans, permits, certificates, contracts, invoices, warranties, dated photographs, product details, inspection reports, repair records, insurance documents and useful contacts. Keep the originals, use filenames you can understand at a glance and add a one-page index.

## Research note
A useful home record preserves permits, plans, invoices, warranties, dated photographs, materials, reports, maintenance and insurer correspondence. Current condition and legal compliance still require the relevant property-specific checks.

## Opening
### Make the useful things easy to find
- **What:** Plans, permits, invoices, warranties, photos, reports
- **Where:** Tied to a room, an element, a product, a name
- **When:** Dated: done, checked, fixed, and due again

_Keep the originals. And when you are not sure, write down that you are not sure._

## Build a record you will use
A useful record is retrievable by any future reader. Every item should answer four fields: **date**, **element or location**, **event or work**, and **source**. Keep the original file with a descriptive filename.

**The minimum home record**

| Folder | Keep | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 01 Property and title | Title, deposited/registered plan, survey, easements, covenants, planning and hazard reports | Defines the land, restrictions and property context |
| 02 Approvals | Planning and building permits, endorsed plans, inspections, occupancy and trade certificates | Records the approval pathway and approved scope |
| 03 Works and products | Contracts, quotes, variations, invoices, warranties, manuals, model numbers, colours and materials | Explains what was installed, by whom and on what terms |
| 04 Condition and reports | Building, pest, engineering, plumbing, electrical, roof, moisture, strata and other reports | Creates dated professional observations and limitations |
| 05 Photographs | Wide and close views before, during and after work; concealed services before closing | Locates evidence and preserves what later becomes hidden |
| 06 Maintenance and monitoring | Service dates, filters, treatments, cleaning, crack or moisture logs and next review | Shows change and keeps recurring tasks visible |
| 07 Insurance and incidents | Schedules, PDS versions, valuations, claims, loss photos and insurer correspondence | Preserves the wording and evidence relevant to a loss |
| 08 Shared building | Plan, by-laws/rules, minutes, budgets, funds, insurance, levies and scheme correspondence | Connects the lot to common-property decisions and costs |
| 09 Contacts | Designer, builder, certifier/surveyor, engineer, trades, insurer, strata manager and warranties | Makes follow-up and responsibility traceable |

## Use filenames that sort themselves
Use ISO dates and plain language: 2026-07-19_roof_north-valley_leak-photo_01.jpg or 2026-08-04_bathroom-waterproofing_certificate.pdf. Add a one-page index with the element, current known status, latest evidence and next action. Keep a cloud copy and a separate backup, with sensitive identity and financial material protected.

## Take photographs that will still help later
1. **Orient:** one wide photograph showing the room, elevation or element.
2. **Locate:** a mid-range view connecting the issue to a window, corner, joint or service.
3. **Detail:** a clear close view with a scale where dimension matters.
4. **Date and describe:** weather/event, direction, dimensions and whether the condition changed.
5. **During work:** capture framing, membranes, flashings, pipes and cables before they are concealed.
6. **Close out:** finished work, invoice, specification, certificate and warranty in the same indexed folder.

## Record uncertainty explicitly
Write 'installation date unknown' or 'reported by previous owner, unverified' where appropriate. A receipt records a purchase; a permit records an approval; a photograph records what the frame caught that day. Let each document say only what it truly knows.

## Update at decision moments
- **On purchase:** save the contract/disclosure, reports and a dated baseline.
- **Before work:** save approvals, condition photos, service locations and insurer advice.
- **During work:** variations, concealed work and inspection evidence.
- **At completion:** certificates, final plans, warranties, manuals and a next-maintenance date.
- **After an event:** safe pre-clean-up evidence, emergency work and the claim timeline.
- **At sale:** copy the releasable, accurate set for legal review; retain sensitive or irrelevant material separately.

## The limits of a home record
A good record shortens every future search and supports the insurance, maintenance, renovation and sale decisions to come. Verify current condition and legal effect for the decision in front of you. For insurance-specific use, read [home condition and insurance](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/home-condition-and-insurance); for works, read [planning a renovation](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/planning-a-renovation).

> Note: The best record is modest and precise: original evidence, clear dates, known limits and an explicit next action. That is more credible than a polished history that hides uncertainty.

## Frequently asked questions
### What records should I keep for my house?
Title and plans; approvals and certificates; contracts, invoices and warranties; product details; dated photographs; condition reports; maintenance and monitoring; insurance documents; shared-building records; and professional contacts.

### How should I name home files?
Start with an ISO date, then element/location, event and file type, for example 2026-07-19_roof_north-valley_leak-photo_01.jpg.

### How long should I keep renovation documents?
Keep the core property, approval, completion, warranty and concealed-work evidence for the life of your ownership, and check legal or warranty retention requirements for the jurisdiction and work.

### Do records prove work is compliant?
A complete approval and certificate chain is useful evidence. Current condition and legal compliance may still require authority or professional verification.

### Should I give every record to a buyer?
Have the sale and disclosure set reviewed legally. Provide accurate, relevant material while protecting unrelated sensitive information.

## Method
A practical system for the paperwork of a home: what to keep, how to date it, where it belongs, and the decisions it will one day have to support.

## Limitations
Records can be incomplete, and occasionally wrong. For permits, title, boundaries and present condition, the authority or the professional is the source of truth; the record is your map to them.

## Sources
- [Choosing home insurance](https://moneysmart.gov.au/home-insurance/choosing-home-insurance) — Moneysmart, Australian Securities and Investments Commission; accessed 2026-07-19
- [When is a building permit required?](https://www.bpc.vic.gov.au/resource-hub/practice-notes/bp-01-when-is-a-building-permit-required) — Building and Plumbing Commission Victoria; accessed 2026-07-19

guides.question: What does a home need as it ages, decade by decade?
guides.title: What your home needs by decade, and how to plan ahead
guides.summary: Your home's age leaves clues about how it was built and what may be coming due. Use those clues with its records and present condition to plan ahead without guessing.
guides.answer: Start with the build date, then look for the work that has happened since. Plans, invoices and alteration dates can save you from assuming everything is original. Keep a simple picture of the roof, wet areas, exterior, hot-water equipment, wiring, plumbing, drainage and structure, because each ages on its own timetable.
guides.methodology: The era sets expectations; the records, the visible evidence and a physical inspection tell you how this particular home has kept to them.
guides.limitations: Regional archetypes differ. Confirm the actual material, installation date and condition before budgeting work.
guides.researchNote: A build date narrows the questions. Set replacement planning from the installed system, its condition, exposure, maintenance and alteration history. For date-linked hazards, use the [pre-1990 asbestos screening rule](https://www.newaste.org.au/asbestos/assets/asbestos-guide-for-householders.pdf) and [Lead Alert](https://www.agriculture.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/lead-paint-fifth-edition.pdf).

cluster.label: Read the building
cluster.blurb: Use age and construction as a starting hypothesis, then test it against evidence and physical inspection.

sections.heading: Opening
sections.markdown:
### Age guides the first questions
- **Original fabric:** What might still be original, quietly ageing
- **Later work:** What later work added, including its own risks
- **Current evidence:** What the condition and records say to do next

_Budget from the installed systems, their age and their condition._

sections.heading: The four-step era model
sections.markdown:
1. **Prior:** build date, region, building type and construction suggest likely systems and questions.
2. **Records:** plans, permits, invoices and photographs show what changed and when.
3. **Evidence:** materials, defects, repairs, exposure and performance show the current direction.
4. **Confirmation:** building or specialist inspection resolves the questions that affect safety, scope or money.

Put a date on every major system and alteration, because the façade lies. A 1910 frontage can hide a 2018 roof and three eras of wiring; a 2018 apartment can carry defects older than its paint.

sections.heading: How long do houses last?

The [Australian Government's YourHome guidance says many homes built today will still be in use in 50 or 100 years](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/live-adapt).
