# What your home needs by decade, and how to plan ahead

Start with the build date, then look for the work that has happened since. Plans, invoices and alteration dates can save you from assuming everything is original. Keep a simple picture of the roof, wet areas, exterior, hot-water equipment, wiring, plumbing, drainage and structure, because each ages on its own timetable.

## Research note
A build date narrows the questions. Set replacement planning from the installed system, its condition, exposure, maintenance and alteration history. For date-linked hazards, use the [pre-1990 asbestos screening rule](https://www.newaste.org.au/asbestos/assets/asbestos-guide-for-householders.pdf) and [Lead Alert](https://www.agriculture.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/lead-paint-fifth-edition.pdf).

## Opening
### Age guides the first questions
- **Original fabric:** What might still be original, quietly ageing
- **Later work:** What later work added, including its own risks
- **Current evidence:** What the condition and records say to do next

_Budget from the installed systems, their age and their condition._

## The four-step era model
1. **Prior:** build date, region, building type and construction suggest likely systems and questions.
2. **Records:** plans, permits, invoices and photographs show what changed and when.
3. **Evidence:** materials, defects, repairs, exposure and performance show the current direction.
4. **Confirmation:** building or specialist inspection resolves the questions that affect safety, scope or money.

Put a date on every major system and alteration, because the façade lies. A 1910 frontage can hide a 2018 roof and three eras of wiring; a 2018 apartment can carry defects older than its paint.

## How long do houses last?
The [Australian Government's YourHome guidance says many homes built today will still be in use in 50 or 100 years](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/live-adapt). Continued use depends on maintenance, adaptation and renewal of individual systems. Roof coverings, membranes, coatings, services and equipment each follow their own cycle. Structure and foundations also need investigation when movement, water or deterioration appears.

A useful forecast starts with what was installed and when, then adds its exposure, maintenance history, present condition and the likely consequence of failure. Give each element a review date, and get an assessment or quote when the evidence says work is getting close.

## The questions each broad era prompts
**Screening questions only, regional construction and alterations can change every row**

| Era | Useful first questions | Evidence that changes the prior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pre-1920s | Actual footings and walls? Damp pathway? Roof/chimney condition? Service upgrades? Older coatings? | Restumping/underpinning records, damp diagnosis, roof invoices, electrical/plumbing evidence, lead testing |
| 1920s–40s | Which regional construction? Footings and drainage? Roof and timber openings? Pre-1990 alterations? | Plan, footing work, service dates, roof/joinery work, asbestos register or test |
| 1950s–70s | Brick veneer, weatherboard or masonry? Slab or raised floor? Pre-1990 materials? Wet-area and service renewal? | Material identification, licensed service inspection, bathroom/roof records, movement history |
| 1980s–90s | Which materials and standard transitions apply? Are wet areas, roof, windows or services original? | Actual installation dates, leak evidence, roof condition, product and approval records |
| 2000s onward, house | Approvals complete? Drainage and junctions performing? Defect or warranty history? Later alterations? | Completion and inspection records, reports, warranty notices, repair close-out evidence |
| 2000s onward, apartment | Common-property defects? External wall/cladding? Fire systems? Funding and developer pathways? | Plan, records inspection, engineering/fire reports, scheme funds, insurance and rectification status |

## Date-linked hazards need careful cut-offs
For asbestos, the national householders' screen is that homes built or renovated before 1990 may contain asbestos-containing material; all uses were prohibited nationally from 31 December 2003. Older paint and coatings, especially pre-1970s layers, may contain higher lead levels. Testing establishes the material before disturbance. Read the [asbestos householders' guide](https://www.newaste.org.au/asbestos/assets/asbestos-guide-for-householders.pdf) and [Lead Alert](https://www.agriculture.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/lead-paint-fifth-edition.pdf).

## The parts that set the renewal plan
**Track each element by date, evidence and consequence**

| Element | Evidence to find | Signals for assessment or renewal planning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Roof and rainwater system | Material, installation invoice, repair history and safe-access inspection | Corrosion, cracked tiles, failed fixings, leaking junctions, ponding or recurring overflow |
| Wet-area waterproofing | Renovation date, permits, certificates, product and repair records | Loose finishes, swelling, staining, failed junctions, moisture readings or leakage below |
| Exterior coating and cladding | Product, application date, substrate and exposure | Chalking, peeling, open joints, exposed end grain, corrosion or water entry |
| Hot-water equipment | Model, manufacture and installation date, warranty and service history | Leaks, corrosion, unreliable temperature, rising energy use or repeated repair |
| Electrical and plumbing services | Material, upgrade date, certificates and licensed inspection | Faults, leakage, corrosion, inadequate capacity, unsafe components or undocumented alterations |
| Footings, subfloor and drainage | Construction type, past movement, drainage works and dated monitoring | Changing cracks, distortion, persistent subfloor moisture, timber decay or water collecting near footings |

[YourHome recommends a regular maintenance schedule and expert advice for leaks, cracks, settlement, damp, salt and termites](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/buy-build-renovate/repairs-and-maintenance). Use manufacturer guidance and qualified assessment for the installed system.

## Turn evidence into a capital plan
**A simple evidence-led capital register**

| Field | Example entry |
| --- | --- |
| Element | North roof slope and box gutter |
| Known date / source | Roof invoice dated 2004; gutter date unknown |
| Current evidence | No internal stain; corrosion at two gutter joints |
| Uncertainty / access | Valley concealed from ground; no recent roof inspection |
| Next action | Roof plumber inspection and defined repair scope before winter |
| Budget status | Investigation allowance now; quotation after scope |

Keep two budgets: one for routine upkeep, one for the big renewals. Build both from the register, real quotes where you can get them, and a contingency sized to what you genuinely do not yet know. The safe framework is in [the maintenance guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/the-maintenance-that-prevents-the-big-bills).

## Add regional construction and exposure
Regional construction changes the era profile. Tropical, cyclone, coastal, alpine, bushfire and remote-area housing use different materials, ventilation, tie-down, termite and moisture strategies. Add climate zone, local hazards, soil, proximity to coast and construction type.

> Note: An era guide identifies the questions that deserve attention first. Records and inspection establish what the home needs now.

## Frequently asked questions
### How long do houses last?
Australian Government guidance says many homes built today will remain in use for 50 or 100 years. Continued use depends on maintenance, adaptation and renewal of the roof, membranes, services, finishes and other components over time.

### How long do the main parts of a house last?
Less uniformly than the folklore suggests. The useful date comes from the actual product installed, its record, its exposure and its condition now, which is why tracking each element separately beats any generic lifespan table.

### Can a build date tell me what needs replacing?
A build date targets likely questions. Set a replacement plan from the actual system, installation or alteration date, exposure, maintenance and current evidence.

### How should I budget by era?
Create an element register with known dates, current condition, uncertainty, next action and quotations. Separate routine maintenance from capital renewal.

### What is the asbestos date for an Australian home?
Homes built or renovated before 1990 may contain asbestos-containing materials. All uses were prohibited nationally from 31 December 2003. Identify suspect material before disturbance.

### Does an older home always cost more?
Renewed older homes can have modest near-term needs. Budget from actual condition, installed systems, completed work and shared-building obligations.

### How do regional differences affect era patterns?
Region, climate, hazard, soil, construction type and alterations can materially change the profile. Combine era with these property-specific inputs.

## Method
The era sets expectations; the records, the visible evidence and a physical inspection tell you how this particular home has kept to them.

## Limitations
Regional archetypes differ. Confirm the actual material, installation date and condition before budgeting work.

## Sources
- [Asbestos: a guide for householders and the general public](https://www.newaste.org.au/asbestos/assets/asbestos-guide-for-householders.pdf) — Australian Government / enHealth; accessed 2026-07-19
- [Lead Alert: the six step guide to painting your home](https://www.agriculture.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/lead-paint-fifth-edition.pdf) — Australian Government; accessed 2026-07-19
- [Brickwork and blockwork](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/materials/brickwork-and-blockwork) — YourHome, Australian Government; accessed 2026-07-19
- [Live and adapt](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/live-adapt) — YourHome, Australian Government; accessed 2026-07-19

sections.markdown:
### Help the house shed, drain and dry
- **Shed:** The roof, flashings and cladding turning water away
- **Drain:** Gutters, downpipes and falls carrying it off the block
- **Dry:** Air moving, clearances kept, leaks fixed the week you find them

_Maintenance can extend service life and reduce avoidable damage. Keep renewal in the plan._

sections.heading: Maintenance, inspection and renewal are different
sections.markdown:
**Name the job correctly before budgeting it**

| Job | Purpose | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Observe | Notice change without unsafe access or diagnosis | Photograph a stain, crack or overflowing downpipe with a date |
| Maintain | Keep a serviceable element operating as intended | Clean an accessible drain or renew a failed seal with the correct system |
| Inspect / service | Use a competent person to test or access a risk area | Roof inspection, termite inspection or licensed electrical check |
| Renew | Replace an element that has failed, is obsolete or has reached condition-based end of service | Re-roofing, switchboard upgrade, membrane replacement or footing repair |

Routine maintenance slows avoidable deterioration. Capital renewal covers major work driven by age, condition and evidence: re-roofing, wiring upgrades, renewed membranes or footing repairs where they are needed. Budget it separately because its timing and cost behave differently.

sections.heading: Follow the water path
sections.markdown: Trace rain from the roof surface through valleys, flashings, gutters, downpipes, stormwater connection, surface falls and lawful discharge. Then check walls, openings, balconies, wet areas, plumbing and subfloor. Investigate staining, salt, soft timber, corrosion, musty odour, lifted finishes or ponding using [the damp and moisture guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/damp-and-moisture-in-your-home).

sections.heading: A safe rhythm that works
sections.markdown:
**Adapt intervals to exposure, material and manufacturer guidance**

| Element | Owner observation | Professional or trade trigger |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Roof and rainwater goods | From ground after heavy rain: overflow, sagging, displaced material, staining | Unsafe access, leaks, storm damage, deteriorated flashings or unclear roof condition |
| Ground and drainage | Ponding, erosion, blocked grates, discharge toward the building | Persistent water, subsidence, failed drains or a change needing hydraulic/civil advice |
| Wet areas and plumbing | Loose finishes, failed sealant, swelling, stains, odour or unexplained meter use | Recurring moisture, suspected concealed leak or waterproofing failure |
| Timber and subfloor | Vent openings clear; no obvious soil contact or new damage from safe areas | Restricted/unsafe access, pest evidence, damp timber or structural change |
| Electrical and fire safety | Use test buttons and replace alarms as required by local rules/manufacturer | Any electrical defect, shock, heat, burning smell, old installation concern or required licensed work |
| Cracks and movement | Dated photos with a stable reference point; note doors, floors and weather | Progression, displacement, repeated repair failure or associated distortion |

sections.heading: Keep maintenance work safe
sections.markdown: Use licensed or appropriately competent people for roof access, ladders, electrical systems, confined or contaminated subfloors, termite treatment and asbestos-containing materials. Before drilling, sanding or demolition in a home built or renovated before 1990, screen for possible asbestos.

sections.heading: Budget from the asset register
sections.markdown:
Build a short asset register covering roof, drainage, exterior, openings, wet areas, services, structure and shared property. Record known age, observed condition, last work, next review and quotation ranges for defined scopes.

Keep a routine annual allowance and a capital-renewal reserve. Update both when evidence changes. The [home record guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/keeping-a-record-of-your-home) provides the structure; [the era planning guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/what-your-home-needs-by-decade) helps set inspection priorities.

sections.heading: An escalation rule that stays useful
sections.markdown:
1. **Record:** date, location, weather or event, dimensions and photographs.
2. **Make safe:** isolate water or power only if safe and within your competence; use emergency help where needed.
3. **Find the cause:** engage the discipline that owns the pathway behind the damaged finish.
4. **Define the work:** diagnosis and scope before comparing repair prices.
5. **Close the record:** invoice, permits or certificates, photos, warranty and next review date.

> Note: Maintenance reduces avoidable deterioration and helps catch change early. Keep capital renewal visible in the same plan.

faqs.question: What maintenance prevents expensive repairs?
faqs.answer: Manage water pathways, repair leaks promptly, maintain safe clearances and drainage, and observe change early. Fund age- and condition-driven renewal separately.

faqs.question: How much should I budget each year?
faqs.answer: Build an element register, keep a routine-maintenance allowance and separately fund capital renewal from evidence and quotations.

faqs.question: Can I inspect the roof and subfloor myself?
faqs.answer: Observe from safe, accessible locations. Roofs, ladders and confined or contaminated subfloors can be hazardous; use appropriately competent professionals when access or work is unsafe.

faqs.question: What does clearing gutters help prevent?
faqs.answer: Overflow and the damage it can feed, including damp walls, rotting eaves and water pooling near footings. Roof renewal still follows the roof’s material, exposure and condition.

faqs.question: What should I record after maintenance?
faqs.answer: The date, element, observed issue, diagnosis, work scope, contractor, invoice, photos, product, permits or certificates, warranty and next review date.

# The maintenance that reduces avoidable repair bills

The most valuable routine is simple: help the house shed water, drain it away and dry out. > Note: Maintenance reduces avoidable deterioration and helps catch change early. Keep capital renewal visible in the same plan.

## Frequently asked questions
### What maintenance prevents expensive repairs?
Manage water pathways, repair leaks promptly, maintain safe clearances and drainage, and observe change early. Fund age- and condition-driven renewal separately.

### How much should I budget each year?
Build an element register, keep a routine-maintenance allowance and separately fund capital renewal from evidence and quotations.

### Can I inspect the roof and subfloor myself?
Observe from safe, accessible locations. Roofs, ladders and confined or contaminated subfloors can be hazardous; use appropriately competent professionals when access or work is unsafe.

### What does clearing gutters help prevent?
Overflow and the damage it can feed, including damp walls, rotting eaves and water pooling near footings. Roof renewal still follows the roof’s material, exposure and condition.

### What should I record after maintenance?
The date, element, observed issue, diagnosis, work scope, contractor, invoice, photos, product, permits or certificates, warranty and next review date.

## Method
We drew the line between what you can safely watch, what you can routinely do, what a professional should inspect, and what simply wears out and gets replaced.

## Limitations
Timing depends on exposure, material and manufacturer guidance. Leave roof access, electrical work and confined subfloors to properly equipped professionals.

guides.contentMarkdown:
# How to read owners-corporation and strata records

Begin with the registered plan so you know where the lot ends and common property begins. Then read several years of minutes beside the works plan, current budget, funds, liabilities, arrears, insurance and legal matters. The gap between planned work and available money is the tell. Ask a strata records inspector and your legal representative to explain what current or proposed levies could mean for this purchase.

## Research note
Read fund balances with the maintenance or capital-works plan, current liabilities and known projects. Boundaries, levy liability and insurance responsibilities depend on the registered plan, state law and contract. See [NSW strata roles](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/strata/roles) and [Victorian guidance](https://www.consumer.vic.gov.au/housing/owners-corporations/buying-into-an-owners-corporation/what-is-an-owners-corporation).

## Opening
### The funding gap is the tell
- **Plan:** What the building says it will need, and when
- **Money:** Available funds after debts and arrears
- **Gap:** The distance between planned work and available money

_The funding gap shapes the next decision: levy, loan, staged work, recovery or changed scope._

## Begin with the registered plan
The registered plan and state legislation define lot and common-property boundaries. Read the plan and any by-law or rule granting exclusive use or responsibility before assigning a balcony leak, window, service pipe, slab, roof or courtyard. Compare [NSW strata roles](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/strata/roles) with the equivalent guidance in the property's state.

## The records stack
**Read each record for its specific evidence value**

| Record | Useful question | Watch for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Registered plan and scheme documents | What is lot, common property or exclusive use? | Use the plan to establish each boundary |
| Minutes over multiple years | Which issues recur, escalate, disappear or are deferred? | Vague references, missing attachments and open decisions |
| Maintenance / capital-works plan | What work, timing and forecast cost are recognised? | A stale plan, omitted major systems or unsupported costs |
| Budgets and financial statements | What income, operating cost, liabilities and fund movements exist? | One-off underspends, unpaid bills, loans or transfers masking the trend |
| Levy and arrears schedule | Who is paying, what has been struck and what remains unpaid? | High arrears, repeated special levies or collection disputes |
| Insurance | What building and liability cover exists, with what excesses and exclusions? | Obtain the schedule, valuation basis and known coverage issues |
| Defect, fire, cladding and legal material | What investigation, order, claim or limitation period is active? | Open reports, expired rights or unfunded rectification |

## The funding gap is the tell
Put the maintenance or capital-works plan beside the current balance, forecast contributions, existing liabilities, cash restrictions and near-term projects. Check whether the plan is current and its cost assumptions reflect actual scopes and quotes. Calculate the timing and size of any unfunded gap.

A scheme has only so many moves: a special levy, a loan, staged work, an insurance or developer recovery, or quietly shrinking the scope. The minutes are where you watch it choose.

## Trace recurring issues through the minutes
Trace a recurring leak, façade investigation or lift breakdown from first report through investigation, decision, funding, completion and warranty. Ask for missing reports or explanations where the chain breaks. Recent and unresolved issues may sit outside the formal minutes.

## Insurance boundaries vary
The scheme generally insures building or common-property interests required by state law. Lot owners may need contents, improvements, landlord, liability or other cover. Check the plan, legislation, policy schedule, insured value, excesses, exclusions, claims history and responsibility for lot improvements.

## Special levies and settlement need legal review
Special-levy liability can turn on the resolution date, instalment due dates, sale contract, disclosure and settlement adjustments. Ask the legal representative to identify existing resolutions, proposed motions and post-contract decisions, then allocate each amount under the contract.

## A ten-question close-out
1. What does the registered plan define as lot and common property for the elements I care about?
2. Which physical issues recur across at least three years of minutes?
3. What reports, orders or quotations sit behind those references?
4. Is the maintenance or capital-works plan current and complete for this building?
5. What near-term work is planned, and what evidence supports the cost?
6. How much unrestricted money is available after liabilities and committed work?
7. What levies, loans, arrears or special contributions exist or are being discussed?
8. What does the full insurance schedule cover and exclude, with what excess?
9. What defects, disputes, cladding, fire-safety or legal limitation issues remain open?
10. How does the sale contract allocate current and proposed levy liability?

> Important: Terminology and legal responsibilities differ across Australian states and schemes. Use state-specific strata and legal advice, then inspect the lot and accessible building separately.

## Frequently asked questions
### What should I look for in strata minutes?
Trace recurring issues from first report through investigation, decision, funding, completion and warranty. Ask for missing reports or attachments where the chain breaks.

### How much should a capital-works or maintenance fund hold?
Compare the balance and future contributions with the current plan, liabilities, committed work and evidence-based project costs.

### Who pays a special levy when an apartment is sold?
It depends on state law, the resolution and due dates, the contract, disclosure and settlement adjustments. Have the legal representative allocate each current or proposed amount.

### Does strata insurance cover the inside of my apartment?
The boundary depends on the plan, legislation and policy. Contents, improvements and owner-installed items may require separate cover.

### What can clean records tell me about defects?
Records can be incomplete, delayed or silent. Read them with a physical inspection and ask about recent events still outside the formal minutes.

## Method
We read the minutes, plans, budgets and funds across several years, because the story of a building lives in the gaps between what was planned and what was paid for.

## Limitations
The records only hold what someone wrote down, so recent or unresolved issues can be missing. A state-specific records inspection and legal advice on adjustments and levies close that gap.

## Sources
- [Who is responsible for what in strata](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/strata/roles) — NSW Government; accessed 2026-07-19
- [Changes to strata laws](https://www.nsw.gov.au/departments-and-agencies/fair-trading/news/changes-to-strata-laws) — NSW Fair Trading; accessed 2026-07-19
- [What is an owners corporation?](https://www.consumer.vic.gov.au/housing/owners-corporations/buying-into-an-owners-corporation/what-is-an-owners-corporation) — Consumer Affairs Victoria; accessed 2026-07-19

sections.markdown:
### Follow the water
- **Source:** Where it comes from: rain, pipes, ground or the air indoors
- **Path:** How it gets in: roof, wall, opening, service or soil
- **Damage:** What it leaves behind: stains, salts, rot, mould

_Fix the source first. A repaint over live moisture is a countdown._

sections.heading: Why damp is the problem behind the problems
sections.markdown: Moisture can contribute to rot, mould, coating failure, salt-damaged masonry and ground movement. A visible symptom can have several possible sources. Before selecting a treatment, record timing and location, check urgent electrical or health risk, and investigate rain, plumbing, drainage, indoor humidity and ground moisture.

sections.heading: The four kinds of damp, and how to tell them apart
sections.markdown:
_[Illustration: Architectural house cutaway showing ground moisture and salt bloom, rain penetration, condensation and a localised roof or plumbing leak. The mark is a clue. Its location, timing and relationship to rain, plumbing, ventilation and ground conditions help trace the source.]_

**The tell-tale signs of each source**

| Type | Where it comes from | Typical signs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rising damp | Groundwater drawn up through porous masonry | A tide mark up to roughly a metre on a wall, salt deposits (white, powdery), worse at the base |
| Penetrating / lateral damp | Water entering sideways through walls | Damp patches that worsen after rain, often near a leaking gutter, cracked render or a wall below ground level |
| Condensation | Moist indoor air meeting cold surfaces | Mould in corners, behind furniture and on window reveals; worse in winter, bathrooms and kitchens |
| Leaks | Plumbing, roof or shower failures | A localised, often growing patch unrelated to weather or season; may track from above |

### Rising damp

Capillary moisture can move from the ground through porous masonry. Low-wall staining, salts or a tide-like mark also occur with bridged damp-proofing, rain, plumbing, condensation and historic salts. Work out the pathway before anyone sells you an injection, a drain, a fan or a repaint. The treatments only work on the problem they were built for.

### Penetrating and lateral damp

Rain can enter through cracked render, failed pointing, leaking gutters or downpipes, and walls below external ground level. A pattern that appears or worsens after rain can help locate the external pathway.

### Condensation

Condensation forms when warm, moist indoor air meets a cold surface. It commonly appears in corners, behind furniture against external walls and on window reveals, especially in winter or poorly ventilated rooms. [YourHome explains how ventilation, insulation, thermal bridges and indoor moisture loads interact](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/passive-design/condensation). The response should suit the climate, construction and confirmed source.

### Leaks

A plumbing, roof or wet-area leak can produce a localised mark, while water may travel before becoming visible. Investigation may need moisture mapping, safe access, service testing or owner-approved opening-up.

sections.heading: Why the diagnosis is the whole job
sections.markdown: Match the repair to the confirmed moisture pathway. Fix the source first, allow the materials to dry properly, then restore the finishes. If movement or deterioration is also present, use the [cracks guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/cracks-structural-or-cosmetic) to frame the next professional question.

sections.heading: Keeping water where it belongs
sections.markdown:
Keep gutters and downpipes clear, direct drainage away from the house, maintain wet-area seals and provide suitable ventilation. The [maintenance guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/the-maintenance-that-prevents-the-big-bills) sets out the wider water-management routine.

> Note: Record the moisture location, timing, weather, source investigation, repair and drying evidence. Recurrence then becomes easier to trace.

> Important: Persistent damp and extensive mould warrant property-specific investigation. Seek health advice for symptoms and qualified building advice for the moisture source.

faqs.answer: Mould needs moisture. Sources include indoor humidity and condensation, rain entry, plumbing, drainage and combinations of these pathways. Building repair, ventilation, heating, source control and health precautions depend on the cause.

# Planning a renovation: the checks before you start

Before design gets too far, check the title and planning controls, likely approvals, licensed-trade requirements, possible pre-1990 hazardous materials, and the capacity of the existing structure and services. Tell the home insurer about relevant work and get the cover position in writing. Keep a contingency for the things no one can see until the building is opened up.

## Research note
Planning and building permits are different approvals, and requirements turn on the proposal, site and jurisdiction. Victoria's official guides explain [planning permits](https://www.planning.vic.gov.au/guides-and-resources/guides/guide-to-victorias-planning-system/planning-permits) and [when a building permit is required](https://www.bpc.vic.gov.au/resource-hub/practice-notes/bp-01-when-is-a-building-permit-required).

## Opening
### Clear the path while change is still cheap
- **Site:** What the title, easements and overlays already decided
- **Approval:** Planning approval and a building permit: separate questions
- **Delivery:** Licensed hands, insured work, inspections passed, records kept

_Settle the pathway while the design is still a pencil sketch._

## Reduce uncertainty before design hardens
Run the early checks on title, planning, hazards, structure and services while the design can still bend around what they find. Then write down the assumptions you are still carrying, decide whether it is worth opening anything up to test them, and make the contract say who owns the risk of what nobody could see.

## Approvals for the proposed work
Planning permits, building permits, trade licences and compliance certificates serve different purposes. Requirements vary by state, council, site and scope. In Victoria, use the official guides to [planning permits](https://www.planning.vic.gov.au/guides-and-resources/guides/guide-to-victorias-planning-system/planning-permits) and [building permits](https://www.bpc.vic.gov.au/resource-hub/practice-notes/bp-01-when-is-a-building-permit-required). Ask the relevant authority and building surveyor to confirm the pathway before design is locked.

## Hazardous materials: know before you disturb
Renovation can disturb hazardous materials. Screen the property before drilling, sanding or demolition.

### Asbestos

If the home was built or renovated before 1990, the [national householders' guidance](https://www.newaste.org.au/asbestos/assets/asbestos-guide-for-householders.pdf) says asbestos-containing materials may be present. All uses were prohibited nationally from 31 December 2003, while existing products remain. Identify suspect material before disturbance and follow state licensing and disposal rules.

### Lead paint

Homes painted before the 1970s are very likely to carry lead paint, and ones built before 1997 may still have it under newer coats. Sanding, scraping or heat-stripping releases lead dust, with particular risk around young children. Test first and follow lead-safe methods.

## Structure and services: what the building can take
### Load-bearing walls and structure

Establish the load-bearing structure before removing or opening a wall. Structural changes need engineering and an appropriately sized support. Where the home already shows movement, read [the guide to wall cracks](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/cracks-structural-or-cosmetic) and obtain professional assessment before adding load.

### Wiring, plumbing and the switchboard

A new kitchen, bathroom or extension may require switchboard, wiring, plumbing or drainage upgrades. Assess the installed services while planning and budget coordinated work while walls are open. The [era planning guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/what-your-home-needs-by-decade) helps identify the first questions.

## Title and planning: what you are allowed to build
Check the title and planning information before commissioning a detailed design. An **easement** may require authority consent for building work. A **restrictive covenant** can control height, materials or dwelling numbers. **Overlays** add controls to the zone. These are the same layers covered in a Victorian [Section 32](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/reading-a-section-32).

## Build the homework into the budget
Link the contingency to recorded assumptions and the decision points that could change scope. Before work begins, notify the home insurer or broker and confirm how renovation, vacancy, security and contract works affect cover.

> Note: A current home record gives the design team the best available picture of the structure, services, prior work and unresolved questions.

> Important: Confirm permit requirements with your local council or a building surveyor. Use licensed asbestos professionals and a qualified engineer for structural change.

## Frequently asked questions
### What should I check before renovating my home?
Check approvals, hazardous materials, structure, services, title constraints, planning controls and insurance before the design is locked. Decide which plans, photographs, certificates and invoices you will keep as the work unfolds.

### Do I need a permit to renovate?
It depends on the proposal, site and jurisdiction. Planning and building permits are separate, and licensed plumbing or electrical work is a separate compliance question again. Confirm the pathway before design is locked.

### How do I know if my home has asbestos before renovating?
For a home built or renovated before 1990, treat suspect material as potentially asbestos-containing until appropriately identified. Follow your state’s licensing and disposal requirements before disturbance.

### How do I know if a wall is load-bearing?
Establish the structural system from plans and professional assessment before removal. Load-bearing changes need engineering and an appropriately sized support.

### Will my switchboard and wiring handle a renovation?
Have a licensed electrician assess the proposed load, switchboard, safety switches and installed wiring during planning.

### Can I build an extension anywhere on my land?
Easements, restrictive covenants, overlays, setbacks and approval rules can limit the location and form. Check title and planning information before design.

## Method
A national sequence of decisions, with Victorian examples clearly labelled as Victorian, and the pre-1990 hazard screen built in before any demolition talk.

## Limitations
Approval, licensing, insurance and disclosure obligations vary. Confirm them before design or demolition with the relevant authority and insurer.

## Sources
- [Planning permits](https://www.planning.vic.gov.au/guides-and-resources/guides/guide-to-victorias-planning-system/planning-permits) — Victorian Government; accessed 2026-07-19
- [When is a building permit required?](https://www.bpc.vic.gov.au/resource-hub/practice-notes/bp-01-when-is-a-building-permit-required) — Building and Plumbing Commission Victoria; accessed 2026-07-19
- [Asbestos: a guide for householders and the general public](https://www.newaste.org.au/asbestos/assets/asbestos-guide-for-householders.pdf) — Australian Government / enHealth; accessed 2026-07-19

sections.heading: Inspection priorities

### Rising damp

Low-wall damp can come from capillary rise, bridged or deteriorated damp-proofing, rain, plumbing, condensation, ground levels or salts remaining after an old event. Identify wiring, switchboard, water, sewer, gas and hot-water materials and upgrade dates from records and licensed inspection. Use the installed condition to set any rewire or replumb scope.

Slate and terracotta roofs can provide long service when flashings, valleys and pointing are maintained. Chimneys need sound flashing and brickwork, including where the fireplace is decorative. Failure at these junctions is how a small roof problem becomes a whole-house one.

# Period homes (pre-1920s): what to expect and what they need

With a pre-1920s home, first find out how it is standing and how water moves around it. Check the footings, walls, roof, drainage and subfloor, then look for renewed wiring, plumbing and wet areas, later alterations, older coatings and possible pre-1990 hazardous materials. Victorian, Edwardian and Federation describe styles, and the construction behind those labels varies across Australia.

## Research note
Period homes cover many Australian construction systems. Footings, damp-proofing, wall fabric and services vary by region and alteration history. Later works may also introduce pre-1990 asbestos and older lead paint.

## Opening
### Find out how this house stands
- **Structure:** What holds it up after a century of change
- **Water:** How the roof, walls and ground details shed water today
- **Alterations:** A century of changes: services, wet areas, old materials

_"Renovated" is a claim. Records and inspection make it a fact._

## Pre-1920s construction varies widely
Pre-1920s homes include terraces, freestanding masonry houses, timber-framed homes and region-specific forms on timber or concrete stumps, piers, strip footings or mixed later foundations. Roof and wall materials also vary. Let the date write the first inspection brief. Then find out what this particular house is made of, and what a century of owners have done to it.

## Inspection priorities
### Stumps and footings

Identify the footing system and any later underpinning or restumping. Timber stumps can decay; masonry piers can settle; strip footings and mixed additions can move differently. Assess soil reactivity, drainage, trees, alterations and prior work. Where distortion or progressive cracking appears, use [the crack triage](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/cracks-structural-or-cosmetic) and an engineer where indicated.

### Rising damp

Low-wall damp can come from capillary rise, bridged or deteriorated damp-proofing, rain, plumbing, condensation, ground levels or salts remaining after an old event. Diagnose the source and pathway using [damp and moisture in your home](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/damp-and-moisture-in-your-home).

### Lead paint

Older coats may contain substantial lead, including on later renovations and joinery. Test or use lead-safe methods before sanding, scraping or heat work, following the [Australian Government Lead Alert](https://www.agriculture.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/lead-paint-fifth-edition.pdf).

### Original wiring and plumbing

Identify wiring, switchboard, water, sewer, gas and hot-water materials and upgrade dates from records and licensed inspection. Use the installed condition to set any rewire or replumb scope.

### Roof, chimneys and pointing

Slate and terracotta roofs can provide long service when flashings, valleys and pointing are maintained. Chimneys need sound flashing and brickwork, including where the fireplace is decorative. Failure at these junctions is how a small roof problem becomes a whole-house one.

## Heritage controls
Many period homes sit under a heritage overlay that controls alterations, particularly to the street-facing exterior. Check the property's planning information and Victorian [Section 32](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/reading-a-section-32) before design.

## Confirm the property’s current condition
Confirm the footing, services, roof, drainage, damp management and completed renewals for the specific property. The broader sequence appears in [the era planning guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/what-your-home-needs-by-decade).

> Note: Keep restumping, damp work, services and roof renewals in the property record with dates, scopes and warranties.

## Frequently asked questions
### What should I check in a pre-1920s home?
Actual footing and wall systems, roof and drainage, subfloor and low-wall moisture, service materials and upgrade records, alterations, hazardous coatings/materials and any heritage controls.

### How do I know if an old home needs restumping?
First identify the footing system, because restumping applies to stumps. Then assess movement, decay, drainage, soil conditions and any earlier work.

### Is rising damp common in period homes?
Low-wall damp is a common investigation question. Possible sources include capillary rise, bridged damp-proofing, rain, plumbing, condensation and historic salts. Diagnose the pathway before choosing treatment.

### Does my period home have lead paint?
Older coatings may contain lead. Test before disturbance and use lead-safe methods.

### Can I renovate a heritage-listed period home?
Renovation is often possible within property-specific heritage controls. Confirm the overlay, schedule, statement of significance and approval pathway before design.

### What makes a period home a sound purchase?
One where the big questions have answers: the footings, the damp, the services, the roof, the alterations, the hazards, the heritage controls. A period home with its evidence in order is a purchase. One without is a hopeful guess.

## Method
The era opens the questions; the actual construction, the region, the alterations and the inspection evidence answer them.

## Limitations
Confirm stump type, damp-proof course, wiring age and hazardous materials through records and physical evidence.

## Sources
- [Asbestos: a guide for householders and the general public](https://www.newaste.org.au/asbestos/assets/asbestos-guide-for-householders.pdf) — Australian Government / enHealth; accessed 2026-07-19
- [Lead Alert: the six step guide to painting your home](https://www.agriculture.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/lead-paint-fifth-edition.pdf) — Australian Government; accessed 2026-07-19
- [Brickwork and blockwork](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/materials/brickwork-and-blockwork) — YourHome, Australian Government; accessed 2026-07-19

sections.heading: Opening
sections.markdown:
### A practical shell with decades of changes
- **Fabric:** Which shell is present: veneer, boards, masonry or mixed
- **Services:** When the wiring and plumbing were renewed, with proof
- **Hazards:** Anything pre-1990 gets screened before anyone drills into it

_The wiring in place sets the electrical question. Find its age and alteration history._

sections.heading: The houses that built the suburbs
sections.markdown: Postwar expansion produced brick veneer, weatherboard, masonry and mixed systems on slabs, stumps, piers and strip footings, with strong regional variation. Many homes have also had several generations of wet-area, service and extension work. Treat the decade as the opening question, then go and meet the actual building.

sections.heading: Inspection priorities
sections.markdown:
### Asbestos, the defining check

Use the national pre-1990 screening rule, identify suspect material before cutting or demolition, and follow state-specific licensing and disposal requirements. The material, amount and jurisdiction determine the removal pathway.

### Ageing wiring and the switchboard

Have a licensed electrician assess the wiring, alterations, capacity and safety devices behind the switchboard. Their inspection defines the need and scope for any upgrade.

### Dated wet areas and waterproofing

Original and later wet areas use varied construction. Look for swelling, staining, loose finishes, failed junctions and dampness below. If the bathroom could change your decision or budget, arrange the right moisture investigation before you commit.

### Slab and footing movement

Reactive clay soils common across much of southern Australia move as moisture changes. Read crack pattern, progression and associated distortion using [the crack guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/cracks-structural-or-cosmetic). Maintain roof-water disposal and ground drainage around the footings.

### Lead paint and tired finishes

Homes painted before the 1970s may carry lead in older coats. Test before sanding or stripping. Also assess metal-framed windows, insulation, kitchens, services and wet areas by current condition.

sections.heading: Renovating a postwar home: check, then build
sections.markdown: Identify suspect asbestos-containing materials before demolition. Coordinate any service and waterproofing upgrades while walls are open. The broader sequence is in [planning a renovation](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/planning-a-renovation).

sections.heading: Confirm the property’s current condition
sections.markdown:
Confirm the property's materials, services, wet areas, footings and completed renewals. The overview across all eras is [the era planning guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/what-your-home-needs-by-decade).

> Note: Keep hazardous-material identification, service upgrades and wet-area work in the property record.

> Important: Have suspect asbestos-containing materials identified before work and use the licensed removal pathway required in your state.

faqs.question: What problems do 1950s–70s homes have?
faqs.answer: Priority checks include asbestos-containing materials, wiring and switchboards, wet areas, footing movement, drainage and older lead paint.

faqs.question: Does my brick-veneer home from the 1960s have asbestos?
faqs.answer: It may. Identify suspect sheeting, eaves, vinyl floor backing, roofing and later alterations before work, then follow state removal rules.

faqs.question: Do postwar homes need rewiring?
faqs.answer: A licensed electrician should identify the installation, alterations, safety devices, defects and capacity before scope is set.

faqs.question: Why do bathrooms in older homes leak?
faqs.answer: Water can escape through plumbing, junctions, shower screens, drainage, finishes or waterproofing. Look at what is happening now and ask when the room was last renewed.

faqs.question: Is cracking in a brick-veneer home serious?

# Postwar homes (1950s–70s): what to expect and what they need

With a 1950s to 1970s home, begin by identifying how it was built and what has changed since. Screen pre-1990 materials for possible asbestos before any disturbance. Find the wiring and plumbing upgrade dates, inspect the roof, drainage and footings, and look for present leakage or reliable renewal records in wet areas. Regional practice varied, so treat the decade as a clue and inspect the systems in this home.

## Research note
Postwar housing spans many systems and regions. The reliable date-linked screen is that homes built or renovated before 1990 may contain asbestos; material identification and removal rules require competent assessment. See the [national householders' guide](https://www.newaste.org.au/asbestos/assets/asbestos-guide-for-householders.pdf).

## Opening
### A practical shell with decades of changes
- **Fabric:** Which shell is present: veneer, boards, masonry or mixed
- **Services:** When the wiring and plumbing were renewed, with proof
- **Hazards:** Anything pre-1990 gets screened before anyone drills into it

_The wiring in place sets the electrical question. Find its age and alteration history._

## The houses that built the suburbs
Postwar expansion produced brick veneer, weatherboard, masonry and mixed systems on slabs, stumps, piers and strip footings, with strong regional variation. Many homes have also had several generations of wet-area, service and extension work. Treat the decade as the opening question, then go and meet the actual building.

## Inspection priorities
### Asbestos, the defining check

Use the national pre-1990 screening rule, identify suspect material before cutting or demolition, and follow state-specific licensing and disposal requirements. The material, amount and jurisdiction determine the removal pathway.

### Ageing wiring and the switchboard

Have a licensed electrician assess the wiring, alterations, capacity and safety devices behind the switchboard. Their inspection defines the need and scope for any upgrade.

### Dated wet areas and waterproofing

Original and later wet areas use varied construction. Look for swelling, staining, loose finishes, failed junctions and dampness below. If the bathroom could change your decision or budget, arrange the right moisture investigation before you commit.

### Slab and footing movement

Reactive clay soils common across much of southern Australia move as moisture changes. Read crack pattern, progression and associated distortion using [the crack guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/cracks-structural-or-cosmetic). Maintain roof-water disposal and ground drainage around the footings.

### Lead paint and tired finishes

Homes painted before the 1970s may carry lead in older coats. Test before sanding or stripping. Also assess metal-framed windows, insulation, kitchens, services and wet areas by current condition.

## Renovating a postwar home: check, then build
Identify suspect asbestos-containing materials before demolition. Coordinate any service and waterproofing upgrades while walls are open. The broader sequence is in [planning a renovation](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/planning-a-renovation).

## Confirm the property’s current condition
Confirm the property's materials, services, wet areas, footings and completed renewals. The overview across all eras is [the era planning guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/what-your-home-needs-by-decade).

> Note: Keep hazardous-material identification, service upgrades and wet-area work in the property record.

> Important: Have suspect asbestos-containing materials identified before work and use the licensed removal pathway required in your state.

## Frequently asked questions
### What problems do 1950s–70s homes have?
Priority checks include asbestos-containing materials, wiring and switchboards, wet areas, footing movement, drainage and older lead paint.

### Does my brick-veneer home from the 1960s have asbestos?
It may. Identify suspect sheeting, eaves, vinyl floor backing, roofing and later alterations before work, then follow state removal rules.

### Do postwar homes need rewiring?
A licensed electrician should identify the installation, alterations, safety devices, defects and capacity before scope is set.

### Why do bathrooms in older homes leak?
Water can escape through plumbing, junctions, shower screens, drainage, finishes or waterproofing. Look at what is happening now and ask when the room was last renewed.

### Is cracking in a brick-veneer home serious?
Read width, direction, location, associated distortion and change over time. Check roof-water disposal, ground drainage, plumbing leaks, trees and the footing system, then obtain professional assessment for escalation patterns.

### Are postwar homes a good buy?
A postwar home can offer practical proportions and well-understood construction. Identify suspect asbestos-containing materials before work, check wiring and wet areas, inspect drainage and footings, and budget from the property’s current evidence and completed renewals.

## Method
The era suggests what to expect; the alteration history, service records and physical condition of this particular house decide what is true.

## Limitations
Confirm the age of services, wet areas, footings and hazardous materials through records and physical evidence.

## Sources
- [Asbestos: a guide for householders and the general public](https://www.newaste.org.au/asbestos/assets/asbestos-guide-for-householders.pdf) — Australian Government / enHealth; accessed 2026-07-19
- [Lead Alert: the six step guide to painting your home](https://www.agriculture.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/lead-paint-fifth-edition.pdf) — Australian Government; accessed 2026-07-19
- [Brickwork and blockwork](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/materials/brickwork-and-blockwork) — YourHome, Australian Government; accessed 2026-07-19

### Every shared problem has a decision and a bill

- **Boundary:** Whose side of the plan it falls on

_In a shared building, the committee is part of the structure._

sections.heading: Shared-building exposure
sections.markdown: Apartment ownership connects a private lot to common property and collective decisions. The registered plan and state law establish the precise boundary. Shared systems, building defects, insurance, contracts and scheme finances can affect an owner even where the lot interior looks sound. Recent events, poor recordkeeping and inaccessible areas can leave gaps in the records.

sections.heading: The risks that land on owners
sections.markdown:
### Special levies from an underfunded reserve

A scheme may resolve an additional or special levy when available funds fall short of an approved need. Assess the fund beside the maintenance plan, the quotes, the contracts, the liabilities, the arrears and the levy schedule. Who ends up paying around a sale comes down to the contract and the state.

### Combustible cladding

For mid-rise and high-rise buildings of roughly the 2000s–2010s, combustible cladding remains a live risk. The exposures are the cost of assessment, the cost of rectification, and the effect on insurance and resale in the meantime. The records should show whether a cladding assessment has been done and whether any rectification, and its levy, is on the books.

### Builder defects

Newer buildings carry the risk of original construction defects, waterproofing, fire separation, structural and services issues that surface in the early years. They can be expensive to rectify and slow to resolve where they end up in dispute or a warranty claim. The minutes usually reveal whether defects have been identified and pursued, or are still unresolved.

### Waterproofing and balcony membranes

Failed waterproofing, particularly in balcony membranes, is consistently one of the leading defect categories in apartment buildings, and an expensive one because the repair usually crosses common property and multiple lots. It is a frequent trigger for special levies, and a recurring line in the minutes of buildings that have it.

### Underinsurance of the building

Scheme insurance obligations and the boundary between building, common-property, lot-owner and contents cover vary by jurisdiction, plan and policy. Review the current schedule, valuation basis, declared value, excesses, exclusions, claims and responsibility for owner improvements. The event and policy determine any coverage gap.

### A poorly run owners corporation

Thin minutes, high arrears, deferred decisions, missing close-out evidence or long-running disputes are investigation signals. Compare several reporting periods and trace material issues from proposal to resolution, funding, completion and warranty.

sections.heading: Buying in? You inherit all of this on day one
sections.markdown: A buyer acquires the lot within the scheme's continuing physical, financial and governance position. The contract and state law determine treatment of existing levies and disclosure. Use the records to identify exposure and uncertainty, then have legal and technical advisers explain their effect. The companion checklist is [what to check before buying an apartment](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/buying-an-apartment-strata).

sections.heading: How to stay ahead of them
sections.markdown:
Read financial statements, the maintenance-fund balance and minutes as they arrive. Compare the same signals year on year using [the owners-corporation records guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/reading-your-owners-corporation-report).

> Note: Track shared-building condition, decisions, funds and levies alongside the records for your lot.

> Important: Strata rules, terminology and owners’ rights vary by state: an owners corporation in Victoria, a strata scheme in New South Wales, a body corporate in Queensland. For a dispute, a levy challenge or a major decision, check the scheme in your state and consider strata-specialist or legal advice.

guides.contentMarkdown:
# Strata risks: what every apartment owner should watch for

Apartment risk lives across the lot, the shared building and the scheme that runs it. Read the maintenance plan beside the funds and liabilities, then follow the minutes for water, façade, fire, defect and legal issues. Work out who makes each decision and who pays. Recent problems may not have reached the minutes yet, so thin or delayed records deserve a question.

## Research note
Strata risk is a building-and-governance system: common property, budgets, maintenance plans, insurance, by-laws and records interact. Responsibilities differ across jurisdictions and plans; start with [NSW strata roles](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/strata/roles) or the equivalent authority in your state.

## Opening
### Every shared problem has a decision and a bill
- **Issue:** The problem itself: a leak, a crack, a lift, a façade
- **Boundary:** Whose side of the plan it falls on
- **Response:** Who decides, who pays, and where that gets written down

_In a shared building, the committee is part of the structure._

## Shared-building exposure
Apartment ownership connects a private lot to common property and collective decisions. The registered plan and state law establish the precise boundary. Shared systems, building defects, insurance, contracts and scheme finances can affect an owner even where the lot interior looks sound. Recent events, poor recordkeeping and inaccessible areas can leave gaps in the records.

## The risks that land on owners
### Special levies from an underfunded reserve

A scheme may resolve an additional or special levy when available funds fall short of an approved need. Assess the fund beside the maintenance plan, the quotes, the contracts, the liabilities, the arrears and the levy schedule. Who ends up paying around a sale comes down to the contract and the state.

### Combustible cladding

For mid-rise and high-rise buildings of roughly the 2000s–2010s, combustible cladding remains a live risk. The exposures are the cost of assessment, the cost of rectification, and the effect on insurance and resale in the meantime. The records should show whether a cladding assessment has been done and whether any rectification, and its levy, is on the books.

### Builder defects

Newer buildings carry the risk of original construction defects, waterproofing, fire separation, structural and services issues that surface in the early years. They can be expensive to rectify and slow to resolve where they end up in dispute or a warranty claim. The minutes usually reveal whether defects have been identified and pursued, or are still unresolved.

### Waterproofing and balcony membranes

Failed waterproofing, particularly in balcony membranes, is consistently one of the leading defect categories in apartment buildings, and an expensive one because the repair usually crosses common property and multiple lots. It is a frequent trigger for special levies, and a recurring line in the minutes of buildings that have it.

### Underinsurance of the building

Scheme insurance obligations and the boundary between building, common-property, lot-owner and contents cover vary by jurisdiction, plan and policy. Review the current schedule, valuation basis, declared value, excesses, exclusions, claims and responsibility for owner improvements. The event and policy determine any coverage gap.

### A poorly run owners corporation

Thin minutes, high arrears, deferred decisions, missing close-out evidence or long-running disputes are investigation signals. Compare several reporting periods and trace material issues from proposal to resolution, funding, completion and warranty.

## Buying in? You inherit all of this on day one
A buyer acquires the lot within the scheme's continuing physical, financial and governance position. The contract and state law determine treatment of existing levies and disclosure. Use the records to identify exposure and uncertainty, then have legal and technical advisers explain their effect. The companion checklist is [what to check before buying an apartment](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/buying-an-apartment-strata).

## How to stay ahead of them
Read financial statements, the maintenance-fund balance and minutes as they arrive. Compare the same signals year on year using [the owners-corporation records guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/reading-your-owners-corporation-report).

> Note: Track shared-building condition, decisions, funds and levies alongside the records for your lot.

> Important: Strata rules, terminology and owners’ rights vary by state: an owners corporation in Victoria, a strata scheme in New South Wales, a body corporate in Queensland. For a dispute, a levy challenge or a major decision, check the scheme in your state and consider strata-specialist or legal advice.

## Frequently asked questions
### What are the strata risks for apartment buyers?
The same ones owners carry, inherited in full at settlement: special levies from an underfunded maintenance fund, combustible cladding, builder defects, failed waterproofing, underinsurance and weak governance. For a buyer they are a pricing exercise: every one is visible in the owners-corporation records before you commit, which is why reading those records is the core pre-purchase check.

### What are the biggest risks of owning an apartment?
Mostly building-wide ones: a special levy from an underfunded maintenance fund, combustible cladding, builder defects, failed waterproofing, an underinsured building, and poor owners-corporation governance. Each can land a large, unplanned cost on you regardless of your own unit’s condition.

### What is a special levy in strata?
An additional contribution resolved under the applicable scheme process. Its purpose, amount, instalments and responsibility around a sale must be read from the resolution, state law, disclosure and contract.

### How do I avoid a surprise strata levy?
Read the building’s records as they arrive, the financial statements, the sinking-fund balance against the building’s age, and the minutes for deferred major works. A large, deferred work is usually a special levy in waiting, and reading the papers turns it from a shock into a date you can plan for.

### Is combustible cladding still a risk for apartment owners?
For buildings of roughly the 2000s–2010s it can be, through the cost of assessment and rectification and the effect on insurance and resale. Check the owners-corporation records for any cladding assessment and whether a rectification levy is on the books.

### What should I check about scheme insurance?
Check the current policy, valuation basis, declared value, excesses, exclusions, claims and the boundary between scheme and lot-owner cover. Obligations and shortfalls depend on state law, the plan, policy and actual event.

### How can I tell if my owners corporation is well run?
Look for a current works plan, aligned funding, manageable arrears, clear minutes, appropriate insurance and closed-out disputes.

## Method
For each physical problem, we traced the same four questions: whose side of the boundary, who decides, who pays, and where the evidence lives.

## Limitations
General Australian strata guidance. Use the registered plan, scheme documents and state-specific professional advice.

## Sources
- [Who is responsible for what in strata](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/strata/roles) — NSW Government; accessed 2026-07-19
- [Changes to strata laws](https://www.nsw.gov.au/departments-and-agencies/fair-trading/news/changes-to-strata-laws) — NSW Fair Trading; accessed 2026-07-19
- [What is an owners corporation?](https://www.consumer.vic.gov.au/housing/owners-corporations/buying-into-an-owners-corporation/what-is-an-owners-corporation) — Consumer Affairs Victoria; accessed 2026-07-19

sections.heading: Opening
sections.markdown:
### Know the house before you sell it
- **Know:** What you have, what it is in, what is still unanswered
- **Decide:** Fix it, investigate it, price it in, or leave it honestly visible
- **Disclose:** Tell what your state requires. Concealment ages badly.

_Preparation removes doubt. The market still sets the price._

sections.heading: Get the house story straight before the styling
sections.markdown:
- **Legal bundle:** title, plan, state disclosure, contract, planning, rates and owners-corporation/body-corporate material.
- **Works history:** permits, endorsed plans, certificates, owner-builder material, invoices and warranties.
- **Condition evidence:** relevant reports, recurring repairs, insurance claims and unresolved recommendations.
- **Product and service information:** manuals, service dates, keys, access and transferable warranties.

The exact disclosure duty differs by state. Victoria uses the [Section 32](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/reading-a-section-32); Queensland's [Form 2 scheme](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/seller-disclosure-qld) applies from 1 August 2025; NSW places prescribed material in the contract for sale. Use a conveyancer or solicitor in the property's jurisdiction.

sections.heading: Make a decision register
sections.markdown:
**A calm way to decide what happens before marketing**

| Condition | Possible decision | Evidence needed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Active leak or safety issue | Make safe, diagnose cause and repair competently | Report, scope, invoice, photos and certificate where relevant |
| Known material defect with uncertain scope | Investigate, price with the evidence, or disclose and leave | Professional diagnosis and legal disclosure advice |
| Cosmetic wear only | Repair for presentation or leave visible | Clear distinction from structural or moisture concerns |
| Historic repair | Assemble proof and current status | Before/during/after photos, invoice, warranty and later inspection |
| Unapproved or unclear work | Authority/legal investigation before making a claim about it | Plans, searches, permit advice and contract treatment |

sections.heading: Fix the cause before the finish
sections.markdown: Diagnose the cause before painting a stain, filling a moving crack or covering damaged material. Keep the close-out record for completed repairs. For unresolved items, obtain disclosure advice and keep marketing claims consistent with the evidence.

sections.heading: A pre-sale inspection is a strategic choice
sections.markdown:
A seller-commissioned inspection can identify issues before a buyer does, help define repairs and support a more orderly auction campaign. It can also create knowledge that needs legal consideration, cost money for issues you may not change, and fail to give buyers a right of reliance unless the inspector offers appropriate terms. Before commissioning, agree on scope, access, report ownership, distribution, professional indemnity and whether purchaser reliance or assignment will be available.

If you share a report, share its fine print with it: the date, the scope, the limits, and whether a buyer may rely on it. Leave buyers free to commission their own inspection.

sections.heading: Apartments need building-level preparation
sections.markdown: For a lot in a scheme, organise current certificates and records. Identify resolved or proposed levies, defects, disputes, cladding, fire-safety, insurance and major works, then have the contract allocate amounts correctly. Use [the owners-corporation records guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/reading-your-owners-corporation-report) to assemble the evidence.

sections.heading: Prepare for an informed sale
sections.markdown:
Accurate records, competent repairs and straight answers shrink a buyer’s doubt, and doubt is exactly what buyers price against you. The market, the contract and the building still write the final number.

> Important: Have the contract, disclosure material, known issues and any pre-sale report reviewed by the property's conveyancer or solicitor before finalising marketing claims.

faqs.question: Should I fix defects before selling?
faqs.answer: Fix urgent safety issues and active causes competently. For other defects, compare investigation and repair cost with accurate disclosure and pricing, using legal and agent advice.

faqs.question: Should I get a building inspection before selling?
faqs.answer: A seller inspection can define issues and repair scope. It also creates information and reliance questions. Agree scope, distribution and buyer-reliance terms and obtain legal advice before commissioning.

faqs.question: Will maintenance records increase my sale price?
faqs.answer: They can reduce uncertainty and support accurate answers. Price still depends on the property, contract and market.

faqs.question: Can I paint over a stain or crack before sale?
faqs.answer: Only after understanding and addressing the cause where required. Concealing evidence without repair or appropriate disclosure can create legal and trust problems.

faqs.question: What documents should I prepare?
faqs.answer: The state legal disclosure and contract material, title and plan, approvals and certificates, works and warranty records, relevant condition reports, shared-building records and accurate evidence of repairs.

Diagnose the cause before painting a stain, filling a moving crack or covering damaged material. Keep the close-out record for completed repairs. For unresolved items, obtain disclosure advice and keep marketing claims consistent with the evidence.

## A pre-sale inspection is a strategic choice
A seller-commissioned inspection can identify issues before a buyer does, help define repairs and support a more orderly auction campaign. It can also create knowledge that needs legal consideration, cost money for issues you may not change, and fail to give buyers a right of reliance unless the inspector offers appropriate terms. Before commissioning, agree on scope, access, report ownership, distribution, professional indemnity and whether purchaser reliance or assignment will be available.

If you share a report, share its fine print with it: the date, the scope, the limits, and whether a buyer may rely on it. Leave buyers free to commission their own inspection.

## Apartments need building-level preparation
For a lot in a scheme, organise current certificates and records. Identify resolved or proposed levies, defects, disputes, cladding, fire-safety, insurance and major works, then have the contract allocate amounts correctly. Use [the owners-corporation records guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/reading-your-owners-corporation-report) to assemble the evidence.

## Prepare for an informed sale
Accurate records, competent repairs and straight answers shrink a buyer’s doubt, and doubt is exactly what buyers price against you. The market, the contract and the building still write the final number.

> Important: Have the contract, disclosure material, known issues and any pre-sale report reviewed by the property's conveyancer or solicitor before finalising marketing claims.

## Frequently asked questions
### Should I fix defects before selling?
Fix urgent safety issues and active causes competently. For other defects, compare investigation and repair cost with accurate disclosure and pricing, using legal and agent advice.

### Should I get a building inspection before selling?
A seller inspection can define issues and repair scope. It also creates information and reliance questions. Agree scope, distribution and buyer-reliance terms and obtain legal advice before commissioning.

### Will maintenance records increase my sale price?
They can reduce uncertainty and support accurate answers. Price still depends on the property, contract and market.

### Can I paint over a stain or crack before sale?
Only after understanding and addressing the cause where required. Concealing evidence without repair or appropriate disclosure can create legal and trust problems.

### What documents should I prepare?
The state legal disclosure and contract material, title and plan, approvals and certificates, works and warranty records, relevant condition reports, shared-building records and accurate evidence of repairs.

## Method
We put the obligations first and the styling last: what the law requires you to disclose, what evidence to prepare, what to fix, and only then how to present it.

## Limitations
Selling obligations vary by state and contract. A pre-sale report may create information that requires legal consideration before marketing.

A damp-proof course may be present, altered, bridged or ineffective. Low-wall moisture can also come from rain, plumbing, condensation or salts from an old event. Diagnose the pathway using [damp and moisture in your home](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/damp-and-moisture-in-your-home).

### Lead paint

Older coatings may contain lead. Test before disturbance and follow lead-safe methods for sanding, scraping or heat work.

### The first asbestos

Asbestos-containing materials may be original or introduced by later renovation. The national householders' screen is practical: if the home was built or renovated before 1990, suspect materials may contain asbestos. Identify them before disturbance and follow state licensing and disposal requirements.

### Ageing wiring, plumbing and roofs

Identify wiring, switchboard, water and sewer materials and upgrade records through licensed inspection. Assess roofs, flashings, valleys, windows and joinery by material and condition, including later replacements.

## Heritage and character controls
Interwar homes in established suburbs may sit under a heritage or character overlay, especially at the street frontage. Confirm the controls before design. For Victorian purchases, check the planning information and [Section 32](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/reading-a-section-32).

## Confirm the property’s current condition
Confirm current footings, services, damp management, hazardous materials and completed renewals. Compare adjacent eras in [period homes](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/period-homes-pre-1920s), [postwar homes](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/postwar-homes-1950s-70s) and the broader [era planning guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/what-your-home-needs-by-decade).

## Frequently asked questions
### What should I investigate in a 1920s–40s home?
Identify the footing, wall, roof, drainage and damp-management systems; establish service upgrade history; assess later wet areas and alterations; and screen pre-1990 suspect materials before disturbance.

### Do interwar homes have a damp-proof course?
Confirm whether one exists, remains effective or has been bridged. Diagnose low-wall moisture against the construction, levels, rain, plumbing, condensation and salts.

### Does a Californian bungalow have asbestos?
It may, either in original fabric or later alterations. Australian household guidance uses a pre-1990 screening threshold; identify suspect material before disturbance.

### How do I know if an interwar home needs restumping?
Identify the actual footings and assess decay, movement, soil, drainage and prior work before defining a repair.

### Can I renovate an interwar home in a heritage area?
Usually, with conditions. These homes often sit under heritage or character overlays that shape what you can alter, especially to the street frontage. Confirm the overlay and what it allows before designing a renovation around it.

## Method
The era sketches the house; the records, alterations and a physical inspection fill in this one.

## Limitations
Confirm footing, wall, service and damp-proofing condition through records and physical evidence.

Detached houses and apartments use different evidence systems. For a house, the owner usually controls the fabric and records. For an apartment, add common property, scheme governance, developer history and shared funding.

### Builder defects

Original construction issues can involve waterproofing, fire separation, structure, drainage, façade or services. Trace each issue through diagnosis, scope, completed work and remaining items. Warranty and statutory pathways vary by state and date, so obtain current jurisdiction-specific advice.

Wet areas, balconies and façades rely on coordinated falls, drainage, membranes, flashings, joints and penetrations. Trace any leak through the complete water path and obtain a defined rectification scope before pricing work.

Some multi-storey buildings use combustible external-wall products and have been subject to state assessment or rectification programs. Obtain the external-wall assessment, authority correspondence, fire-engineering advice, work status, funding, warranty and insurance response. Check the current program in the building's state.

For an apartment, compare physical issues with the plan, minutes, capital-works plan, current funds, liabilities, insurance and proposed recovery from builders or developers. A fund balance only makes sense against planned obligations. A newer home has less history to read, which makes the history it does have matter more: the build quality, the waterproofing, the drainage, the approvals, and any defects already on the record. Apartment buyers add the shared building, its governance and its money.

## First split: house or shared building
