guides.question: How do I prepare my home for storms, floods and bushfire?
guides.title: Preparing your home for extreme weather: people first, hazard by hazard
guides.summary: A safer home starts with the people in it. Make the plan, know where warnings come from and leave early when advised, then work through the property risks that apply to your address.
guides.answer: Know your official warning source, practise a household plan and include medication, pets, communication and more than one route. Leave early when emergency authorities advise it. For the home itself, storm preparation centres on the roof, openings, drainage and loose objects. Flood work must reflect local water behaviour, while bushfire work should follow the property’s BAL and local authority guidance. Ask the insurer before spending money for a promised insurance benefit.
guides.methodology: The order is deliberate: people first, official warnings second, and only then the property, the works, the records and the insurance conversation.
guides.limitations: This is a national resilience guide. During an event, follow your emergency service. BAL ratings, flood levels and engineering require site-specific assessment.
guides.researchNote: Life safety comes before fabric. Follow the emergency service and hazard authority for your location, make a household plan, and leave early when directed. Building work should follow property-specific flood, storm or bushfire advice; start with the [NSW RFS survival plan](https://www.rfs.nsw.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0003/36597/BFSP-Complete.pdf) and [VICSES storm guidance](https://www.ses.vic.gov.au/plan-and-stay-safe/emergencies/storm).

cluster.label: Own, maintain and change
cluster.blurb: Keep useful records, maintain the fabric safely and plan works without over-promising what condition can prove.

sections.heading: Opening
sections.markdown:
### Protect people first
- **People:** A household plan: people, pets, medication, and when to leave
- **Warnings:** One source of truth: your local emergency authority
- **Property:** Then the property, with hazard-specific advice and competent hands

_When they say leave, leave. The house is the replaceable part._

sections.heading: The order is people, warnings, property
sections.markdown:
1. **People:** decide who does what, where you will go, when you will leave and how children, older people, disability, medication and pets are supported.
2. **Warnings:** use the official emergency service and hazard authority for your location; understand warning levels before the event.
3. **Property:** assess the specific storm, flood or bushfire mechanism and complete competent work in calm conditions.
4. **Records and insurance:** keep photographs and invoices, update the rebuild basis, and ask the insurer about cover, excesses and recognised mitigation.

The [NSW Rural Fire Service survival plan](https://www.rfs.nsw.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0003/36597/BFSP-Complete.pdf) says leaving early is the safest option and calls for a prepared plan. Follow the current authority for your state or territory during an event.

sections.heading: Storm and wind
sections.markdown:
Before storm season, use safe ground-level observation and competent inspection to identify loose roof material, deteriorated flashings, blocked or failing rainwater goods, vulnerable openings, hazardous trees and unsecured outdoor objects. [VICSES advises maintaining the home and yard, clearing gutters and securing loose items](https://www.ses.vic.gov.au/plan-and-stay-safe/emergencies/storm). Use trained, equipped people for roof access. Stay clear of fallen powerlines and floodwater.

**Who should check each part of the home before a storm**

| Signal | Action in calm weather | Who may be needed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Roof movement, leaks or damaged flashings | Arrange condition assessment and repair scope | Roof plumber, builder or engineer as appropriate |
| Overflowing gutters or failed downpipes | Clear safely; repair falls, joints and lawful discharge | Roof plumber or drainage professional |
| Tree defect or contact risk | Obtain risk-based pruning or removal advice | Qualified arborist; council/utility where relevant |
| Vulnerable garage door, shutters or openings | Assess against local wind region and product suitability | Engineer, builder or product specialist |

sections.heading: Flood
sections.markdown:
Flood depth, velocity, duration, contamination, access and warning time vary street by street. Start with the council, catchment or state flood authority and property-specific flood information. Loss shrinks with simple moves: valuables and electricals up high, the shut-off procedures known before you need them, the critical records protected, and recoverable materials chosen whenever you are renovating anyway. Use professional and authority advice for barriers, pumps, drainage changes and structural measures.

Stay out of floodwater and follow official power-safety advice. After inundation, treat water and affected materials as potentially contaminated and follow emergency, electrical and public-health instructions before re-entry.

sections.heading: Bushfire and ember attack
sections.markdown:
Begin with a survival plan and the local fire authority. Determine whether the property is in bushfire-prone land and whether a Bushfire Attack Level or planning control applies. Building measures depend on the assessed exposure, construction and local rules.

Preparation can include lawful fuel and vegetation management, clear gutters, maintained decks and subfloors, sealed gaps and compliant non-combustible mesh at openings. Keep required ventilation paths, cavity drainage and weep holes clear. On catastrophic or extreme conditions, follow official advice and leave early.

guides.contentMarkdown:
# Preparing your home for extreme weather: people first, hazard by hazard

Know your official warning source, practise a household plan and include medication, pets, communication and more than one route. Leave early when emergency authorities advise it. For the home itself, storm preparation centres on the roof, openings, drainage and loose objects. Flood work must reflect local water behaviour, while bushfire work should follow the property’s BAL and local authority guidance. Ask the insurer before spending money for a promised insurance benefit.

## Research note
Life safety comes before fabric. Follow the emergency service and hazard authority for your location, make a household plan, and leave early when directed. Building work should follow property-specific flood, storm or bushfire advice; start with the [NSW RFS survival plan](https://www.rfs.nsw.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0003/36597/BFSP-Complete.pdf) and [VICSES storm guidance](https://www.ses.vic.gov.au/plan-and-stay-safe/emergencies/storm).

## Opening
### Protect people first
- **People:** A household plan: people, pets, medication, and when to leave
- **Warnings:** One source of truth: your local emergency authority
- **Property:** Then the property, with hazard-specific advice and competent hands

_When they say leave, leave. The house is the replaceable part._

## The order is people, warnings, property
1. **People:** decide who does what, where you will go, when you will leave and how children, older people, disability, medication and pets are supported.
2. **Warnings:** use the official emergency service and hazard authority for your location; understand warning levels before the event.
3. **Property:** assess the specific storm, flood or bushfire mechanism and complete competent work in calm conditions.
4. **Records and insurance:** keep photographs and invoices, update the rebuild basis, and ask the insurer about cover, excesses and recognised mitigation.

The [NSW Rural Fire Service survival plan](https://www.rfs.nsw.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0003/36597/BFSP-Complete.pdf) says leaving early is the safest option and calls for a prepared plan. Follow the current authority for your state or territory during an event.

## Storm and wind
Before storm season, use safe ground-level observation and competent inspection to identify loose roof material, deteriorated flashings, blocked or failing rainwater goods, vulnerable openings, hazardous trees and unsecured outdoor objects. [VICSES advises maintaining the home and yard, clearing gutters and securing loose items](https://www.ses.vic.gov.au/plan-and-stay-safe/emergencies/storm). Use trained, equipped people for roof access. Stay clear of fallen powerlines and floodwater.

**Who should check each part of the home before a storm**

| Signal | Action in calm weather | Who may be needed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Roof movement, leaks or damaged flashings | Arrange condition assessment and repair scope | Roof plumber, builder or engineer as appropriate |
| Overflowing gutters or failed downpipes | Clear safely; repair falls, joints and lawful discharge | Roof plumber or drainage professional |
| Tree defect or contact risk | Obtain risk-based pruning or removal advice | Qualified arborist; council/utility where relevant |
| Vulnerable garage door, shutters or openings | Assess against local wind region and product suitability | Engineer, builder or product specialist |

## Flood
Flood depth, velocity, duration, contamination, access and warning time vary street by street. Start with the council, catchment or state flood authority and property-specific flood information. Loss shrinks with simple moves: valuables and electricals up high, the shut-off procedures known before you need them, the critical records protected, and recoverable materials chosen whenever you are renovating anyway. Use professional and authority advice for barriers, pumps, drainage changes and structural measures.

Stay out of floodwater and follow official power-safety advice. After inundation, treat water and affected materials as potentially contaminated and follow emergency, electrical and public-health instructions before re-entry.

## Bushfire and ember attack
Begin with a survival plan and the local fire authority. Determine whether the property is in bushfire-prone land and whether a Bushfire Attack Level or planning control applies. Building measures depend on the assessed exposure, construction and local rules.

Preparation can include lawful fuel and vegetation management, clear gutters, maintained decks and subfloors, sealed gaps and compliant non-combustible mesh at openings. Keep required ventilation paths, cavity drainage and weep holes clear. On catastrophic or extreme conditions, follow official advice and leave early.

## Confirm insurance outcomes in writing
Before major resilience work, ask the insurer or broker what evidence it requires, whether the measure changes cover or excess, and whether construction must be notified. Review flood, storm, bushfire, actions-of-the-sea and temporary-accommodation definitions using [Moneysmart's hazard insurance guide](https://moneysmart.gov.au/home-insurance/storm-flood-and-fire-insurance).

## The property record to keep
- Official hazard maps, BAL or flood information and the date accessed.
- Emergency plan, contacts, routes, medication and pet arrangements.
- Dated photographs of roof, elevations, drainage, openings, yard and critical equipment.
- Inspection reports, design advice, approvals, invoices, product specifications and warranties for resilience work.
- Insurance schedule, PDS version, endorsements and written insurer responses about mitigation.

> Important: Follow current official warnings and call emergency services where life or property is in immediate danger. Use property-specific engineering, flood or bushfire assessment for building work.

## Frequently asked questions
### What is the first step in extreme-weather preparation?
Prepare the household plan and official warning sources before the building. Include routes, communication, medication, disability needs and pets, and leave early when authorities advise it.

### What should I do before storm season?
From safe locations, check for roof, drainage, tree, opening and loose-object risks; arrange competent inspection and repair where needed. Never work on a roof during a storm or approach fallen powerlines.

### Should I install flood barriers?
Only after property-specific flood and professional advice. Depth, velocity, duration, contamination and drainage interactions matter, and a barrier can redirect water or fail if misapplied.

### How do I protect vents and weep holes from embers?
Use bushfire-compliant, non-combustible mesh and details suited to the assessed exposure without blocking required drainage or ventilation. Confirm the applicable BAL, standard and local requirements.

### Will resilience work lower my insurance premium?
Ask the insurer what it recognises, what evidence it needs and whether cover or excess changes before spending for an insurance outcome.

## Method
The order is deliberate: people first, official warnings second, and only then the property, the works, the records and the insurance conversation.

## Limitations
This is a national resilience guide. During an event, follow your emergency service. BAL ratings, flood levels and engineering require site-specific assessment.

## Sources
- [Bush Fire Survival Plan](https://www.rfs.nsw.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0003/36597/BFSP-Complete.pdf) — NSW Rural Fire Service; accessed 2026-07-19
- [Plan and stay safe in a storm](https://www.ses.vic.gov.au/plan-and-stay-safe/emergencies/storm) — Victoria State Emergency Service; accessed 2026-07-19
- [Storm, flood and fire insurance](https://moneysmart.gov.au/home-insurance/storm-flood-and-fire-insurance) — Moneysmart, Australian Securities and Investments Commission; accessed 2026-07-19

sections.markdown:
### A time of mixed materials and systems
- **Materials:** Identify the installed materials and systems
- **Wet areas:** Age, renewal history and evidence of leaks
- **Envelope:** The roof, windows and joints as they stand today

_The waterproofing membrane is the quiet one to ask about._

sections.heading: The transition era
sections.markdown: 1980s and 90s housing commonly includes brick veneer, concrete slabs, concrete tile roofs, aluminium-framed windows and varied wet-area systems. The era spans the pre-1990 asbestos screening threshold and several decades of later alterations. Identify the installed materials and systems before planning renewal; these two decades mixed them freely.

sections.heading: Inspection priorities
sections.markdown:
### The tail of asbestos

Use the national pre-1990 screen: homes built or renovated before 1990 may contain asbestos products. All uses were prohibited nationally from 31 December 2003. Renovations can mix dates, so identify suspect material before disturbance.

### Wet areas and waterproofing

Wet-area construction, products and workmanship vary, and later bathrooms may replace the original system. Look for staining, swelling, loose finishes, failed joints, drainage behaviour and evidence of renewal. Use appropriate moisture investigation where warranted.

### Roofs, windows and services of an age

Identify the roof material and repair history; inspect tiles or sheeting, flashings, valleys, gutters and coatings by condition. Assess window joints, drainage and glazing units. Use records and licensed inspection for wiring, switchboard, plumbing and hot-water age.

### Movement on clay soils

Reactive clay soils common across much of southern Australia move as moisture changes. Read crack pattern and progression with [the crack guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/cracks-structural-or-cosmetic). Maintain roof-water disposal and ground drainage around the footings.

sections.heading: Confirm the property’s current condition
sections.markdown:
The build date gives you a useful first list of questions. The records and the home itself provide the answers. Separate original work from later renovations, then look at each element by material, exposure and present condition. The overview is [what your home needs by decade](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/what-your-home-needs-by-decade), and the eras either side are [postwar homes](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/postwar-homes-1950s-70s) and [modern homes](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/modern-homes-2000s-on).

> Note: Record installed systems, renewal dates, condition and the pre-1990 asbestos screen for relevant work.

faqs.question: Why do bathrooms from this era leak?
faqs.answer: Potential causes include plumbing, junctions, drainage, screens, finishes and waterproofing. Identify current evidence and whether the room is original or later.

faqs.question: Do concrete tile roofs need maintenance?
faqs.answer: Yes. Pointing, bedding, flashings and any coating age in place. Inspect them periodically and respond to their condition before a ceiling stain makes the announcement.

# 1980s–90s homes: what to expect and what they need

A home built or renovated before 1990 may contain asbestos, so identify suspect materials before any disturbance. Then check the wet areas, roof covering, windows, services, footings and alteration dates. These decades contain plenty of mixed systems, and the safest budget comes from what is installed and how it is performing today.

## Research note
Homes from the 1980s and 1990s span changing materials and standards. A pre-1990 build or renovation may contain asbestos. Establish membrane, roof, glazing and service condition through property-specific evidence.

## Opening
### A time of mixed materials and systems
- **Materials:** Identify the installed materials and systems
- **Wet areas:** Age, renewal history and evidence of leaks
- **Envelope:** The roof, windows and joints as they stand today

_The waterproofing membrane is the quiet one to ask about._

## The transition era
1980s and 90s housing commonly includes brick veneer, concrete slabs, concrete tile roofs, aluminium-framed windows and varied wet-area systems. The era spans the pre-1990 asbestos screening threshold and several decades of later alterations. Identify the installed materials and systems before planning renewal; these two decades mixed them freely.

## Inspection priorities
### The tail of asbestos

Use the national pre-1990 screen: homes built or renovated before 1990 may contain asbestos products. All uses were prohibited nationally from 31 December 2003. Renovations can mix dates, so identify suspect material before disturbance.

### Wet areas and waterproofing

Wet-area construction, products and workmanship vary, and later bathrooms may replace the original system. Look for staining, swelling, loose finishes, failed joints, drainage behaviour and evidence of renewal. Use appropriate moisture investigation where warranted.

### Roofs, windows and services of an age

Identify the roof material and repair history; inspect tiles or sheeting, flashings, valleys, gutters and coatings by condition. Assess window joints, drainage and glazing units. Use records and licensed inspection for wiring, switchboard, plumbing and hot-water age.

### Movement on clay soils

Reactive clay soils common across much of southern Australia move as moisture changes. Read crack pattern and progression with [the crack guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/cracks-structural-or-cosmetic). Maintain roof-water disposal and ground drainage around the footings.

## Confirm the property’s current condition
The build date gives you a useful first list of questions. The records and the home itself provide the answers. Separate original work from later renovations, then look at each element by material, exposure and present condition. The overview is [what your home needs by decade](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/what-your-home-needs-by-decade), and the eras either side are [postwar homes](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/postwar-homes-1950s-70s) and [modern homes](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/modern-homes-2000s-on).

> Note: Record installed systems, renewal dates, condition and the pre-1990 asbestos screen for relevant work.

## Frequently asked questions
### What problems do 1980s–90s homes have?
Priority checks include pre-1990 asbestos-containing materials, wet areas, concrete tile roofs, aluminium windows, services and movement on reactive soils.

### Does a 1980s home have asbestos?
It may. Australian household guidance treats homes built or renovated before 1990 as potentially containing asbestos products. Identify suspect material before disturbance.

### Why do bathrooms from this era leak?
Potential causes include plumbing, junctions, drainage, screens, finishes and waterproofing. Identify current evidence and whether the room is original or later.

### Do concrete tile roofs need maintenance?
Yes. Pointing, bedding, flashings and any coating age in place. Inspect them periodically and respond to their condition before a ceiling stain makes the announcement.

### What makes an 1980s–90s home a sound purchase?
Clear evidence about wet areas, roof, services, alterations, drainage and any pre-1990 asbestos-containing materials supports informed budgeting.

## Method
The era narrows the questions; installation dates, renovation records and inspection evidence settle them.

## Limitations
Identify the installed membrane and roof systems, then assess their condition before setting renewal timing.

- [Brickwork and blockwork](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/materials/brickwork-and-blockwork) — YourHome, Australian Government; accessed 2026-07-19

guides.question: What should I check in a weatherboard home?
guides.title: Weatherboard homes: read the whole water-shedding system
guides.summary: The paint is part of the weatherproofing, and the small junctions do the quiet work. Read the boards, flashings, openings, drainage and subfloor as one connected system.
guides.answer: Start with the boards and coating, then follow every place water can get in or linger: end grain, fixings, joints, windows, doors, penetrations, roof and gutter junctions, ground clearance and splashback. Check the wall wrap or sarking where it can be seen, and identify the footing and subfloor arrangement. Repaint timing depends on preparation, product, colour, orientation and exposure, so the most weathered side usually tells the story first.
guides.methodology: We followed the water the way the house has to: from the roof edge, down the boards and junctions, all the way to the ground.
guides.limitations: Weatherboard homes may use stump, pier, strip footing or slab systems. Confirm the actual assembly and safe access before work.
guides.researchNote: Paint protects timber cladding. The weatherproofing system also depends on flashings, wraps or sarking, junctions, drainage, ground clearance and maintenance. Exposure, coating and preparation determine recoating intervals.

sections.heading: Opening
sections.markdown:
### The paint is part of the weatherproofing
- **Face:** The boards and their coat, down to the end grain
- **Junctions:** The corners, openings and flashings where water tries first
- **Below:** Clearance from the ground, and air moving underneath

_Paint starts the job. Flashings and drainage finish it._

sections.heading: Start with exposure and condition
sections.markdown: North- and west-facing walls, coastal salt, shade, wind-driven rain, garden irrigation and low clearances can make one elevation deteriorate much faster than another. Walk every side in consistent light and compare the bottom boards, corners, window sills, meter boxes, decks, pipes and roof-to-wall junctions.

sections.heading: The envelope checklist
sections.markdown:
**What each layer is doing**

| Layer | Look for | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Boards and coating | Peeling, checking, open laps, splitting, softness, exposed end grain and failed filler | The outer layer sheds weather and protects the substrate |
| Openings and penetrations | Missing or failed flashings, sealant-only repairs, sill damage and staining | Water concentrates at interruptions in the wall |
| Wrap / sarking and cavity | Records, visible edges at alterations, blocked drainage or incompatible additions | The secondary drainage and air-control layer may be concealed |
| Ground and paving | Low boards, soil contact, mulch, splashback and paving falling toward walls | Persistent wetting raises decay, pest and concealed-moisture risk |
| Subfloor or footing | Actual slab, stump, pier or strip system; ventilation, damp and movement evidence | Confirm the foundation separately from the cladding |
| Roof and rainwater goods | Overflow paths, downpipes, apron flashings and staining | Many wall problems begin above the wall |

sections.heading: Paint within the weatherproofing system
sections.markdown:
A compatible, well-prepared coating protects timber from ultraviolet and moisture cycling. Missing flashing, soil contact, failed joints and trapped water need their own repairs. Repeated early paint failure usually points to an underlying moisture, preparation or detailing problem. Find the cause before repainting.

Manufacturer guidance, coating type, preparation, timber or sheet substrate, colour and exposure determine inspection and recoating. Record the product and colour, inspect the most exposed elevation first, and plan work from current condition.

sections.heading: Movement and decay need different questions
sections.markdown: Gaps, sticking openings and out-of-level floors can relate to footings, moisture, alterations or local timber damage. Soft boards, fungal decay or pest evidence relate to material and moisture pathways. Use [the movement guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/cracks-structural-or-cosmetic) and a competent building inspection where associated distortion or progression exists.

sections.heading: Renovating older weatherboards
sections.markdown:
Before sanding, drilling or removing cladding on a home built or renovated before 1990, screen for asbestos-containing sheet products and older lead paint. Later recladding may also hide mixed substrates, missing wrap or non-compliant junctions. Identify the assembly before specifying repair.

For ongoing care, follow the water-path approach in [the maintenance guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/the-maintenance-that-prevents-the-big-bills) and keep the product, repair and photo record described in [the home record](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/keeping-a-record-of-your-home).

> Note: A weatherboard wall is credible when every layer has a job: coating protects, boards shed, flashings drain, wrap backs up, clearances keep splash and soil away, and the roof and ground send water elsewhere.

faqs.question: How often should weatherboards be painted?
faqs.answer: Inspect by condition and follow the coating manufacturer, with closer attention to exposed orientations, dark colours, coastal sites and weak prior preparation.

faqs.question: Is paint the waterproofing system?
faqs.answer: Paint is one protective layer. Boards, joints, flashings, wrap or sarking, penetrations, roof junctions, clearance and drainage complete the weatherproofing system.

faqs.question: What foundations do weatherboard homes use?
faqs.answer: They can use timber or concrete stumps, piers, strip footings or slabs, and alterations may mix systems. Confirm the actual foundation.

faqs.question: Where does weatherboard rot usually start?
faqs.answer: At persistent wetting points such as bottom boards, end grain, sills, joints, penetrations, low clearances, splashback and roof or gutter failures.

faqs.question: What hazards matter before sanding old boards?
faqs.answer: Older lead paint and, in pre-1990 work, possible asbestos-containing sheet products. Identify suspect materials and use the required safe methods before disturbance.

> Note: A weatherboard wall is credible when every layer has a job: coating protects, boards shed, flashings drain, wrap backs up, clearances keep splash and soil away, and the roof and ground send water elsewhere.

## Frequently asked questions
### How often should weatherboards be painted?
Inspect by condition and follow the coating manufacturer, with closer attention to exposed orientations, dark colours, coastal sites and weak prior preparation.

### Is paint the waterproofing system?
Paint is one protective layer. Boards, joints, flashings, wrap or sarking, penetrations, roof junctions, clearance and drainage complete the weatherproofing system.

### What foundations do weatherboard homes use?
They can use timber or concrete stumps, piers, strip footings or slabs, and alterations may mix systems. Confirm the actual foundation.

### Where does weatherboard rot usually start?
At persistent wetting points such as bottom boards, end grain, sills, joints, penetrations, low clearances, splashback and roof or gutter failures.

### What hazards matter before sanding old boards?
Older lead paint and, in pre-1990 work, possible asbestos-containing sheet products. Identify suspect materials and use the required safe methods before disturbance.

## Method
We followed the water the way the house has to: from the roof edge, down the boards and junctions, all the way to the ground.

## Limitations
Weatherboard homes may use stump, pier, strip footing or slab systems. Confirm the actual assembly and safe access before work.

## Sources

- [Brickwork and blockwork](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/materials/brickwork-and-blockwork) — YourHome, Australian Government; accessed 2026-07-19

sections.heading: Same look, different building
sections.markdown:
Two brick homes can use different structural systems. In **brick veneer**, a timber or steel frame carries the load and an outer brick skin acts as cladding. **Cavity masonry**, often called double brick, uses masonry leaves for structural and weather roles. Confirm the actual wall system through plans and physical evidence.

**How the two compare**

|  | Brick veneer | Double brick |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What carries the load | The internal timber/steel frame | The masonry walls themselves |
| Load-bearing system | Timber or steel frame | Masonry leaves |
| Thermal mass | Lower, frame inside, brick outside | Higher, masonry holds heat and cool |
| Reading a crack | Outer-leaf movement is possible; confirm the full pattern | Masonry may carry load; confirm the full pattern |
| Altering / opening up | Generally easier, frame is workable | Harder and costlier, masonry is structural |
| Main vulnerabilities | Frame rot and termites if water gets in | Damp bridging the cavity; cracking |

sections.heading: Why the difference matters to you
sections.markdown:
### Reading cracks

Cracking reads differently in the two systems. In brick veneer, the outer brick leaf is a weather skin and may crack as that leaf moves. In double brick, a cracked masonry leaf may also carry structural load. Width, direction, location, associated distortion and change over time remain central. Use the full pattern in [cracks: structural or cosmetic](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/cracks-structural-or-cosmetic), then confirm the wall system.

### Comfort and insulation

Cavity masonry brings thermal mass; brick veneer leans on insulation within the framed wall. Comfort depends on climate, orientation, insulation, ventilation and the full wall assembly.

### Renovating and altering

Altering brick veneer means working with a frame. Altering double brick can mean cutting into walls that hold the house up, which is a different engineering job with a different support sequence. Establish the load path before anyone talks about removing a wall, using the process in [planning a renovation](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/planning-a-renovation).

sections.heading: How to tell which you have
sections.markdown:
Useful clues include the plans, wall thickness at a window reveal, brick bond and observations from safely accessible roof or subfloor spaces. A tap on the inside face can offer a clue, though linings, insulation and later alterations can change the sound. Have a building professional confirm the system where it affects a decision. Add the era context from [what your home needs by decade](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/what-your-home-needs-by-decade).

> Note: Record the wall system with plans, photographs and any inspection evidence. It will inform later crack, insulation, moisture and renovation decisions.

# Brick veneer and double brick: what each means for your home

In brick veneer, a timber or steel frame carries the house and the outer brick skin keeps out the weather. In cavity masonry, often called double brick, the masonry also does structural work. That difference changes how you read cracks, moisture and insulation, and how you plan an opening or extension. Plans and an inspection can settle which system you have.

## Research note
Brick veneer and cavity masonry manage structure, insulation and moisture differently. The [Australian Government's YourHome guide](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/materials/brickwork-and-blockwork) explains the roles of masonry, cavities, ties, damp-proof courses and weep holes.

## Opening
### The bricks may be doing different jobs
- **Veneer:** The frame carries the building; the outer brick leaf manages weather
- **Cavity masonry:** Two masonry leaves sit across a cavity, with roles set by the design
- **Both:** Cavities, ties, flashings and weep holes manage moisture and stability

_A tap can offer a clue. Plans and physical inspection confirm the system._

## Same look, different building
Two brick homes can use different structural systems. In **brick veneer**, a timber or steel frame carries the load and an outer brick skin acts as cladding. **Cavity masonry**, often called double brick, uses masonry leaves for structural and weather roles. Confirm the actual wall system through plans and physical evidence.

**How the two compare**

|  | Brick veneer | Double brick |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What carries the load | The internal timber/steel frame | The masonry walls themselves |
| Load-bearing system | Timber or steel frame | Masonry leaves |
| Thermal mass | Lower, frame inside, brick outside | Higher, masonry holds heat and cool |
| Reading a crack | Outer-leaf movement is possible; confirm the full pattern | Masonry may carry load; confirm the full pattern |
| Altering / opening up | Generally easier, frame is workable | Harder and costlier, masonry is structural |
| Main vulnerabilities | Frame rot and termites if water gets in | Damp bridging the cavity; cracking |

## Why the difference matters to you
### Reading cracks

Cracking reads differently in the two systems. In brick veneer, the outer brick leaf is a weather skin and may crack as that leaf moves. In double brick, a cracked masonry leaf may also carry structural load. Width, direction, location, associated distortion and change over time remain central. Use the full pattern in [cracks: structural or cosmetic](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/cracks-structural-or-cosmetic), then confirm the wall system.

### Comfort and insulation

Cavity masonry brings thermal mass; brick veneer leans on insulation within the framed wall. Comfort depends on climate, orientation, insulation, ventilation and the full wall assembly.

### Renovating and altering

Altering brick veneer means working with a frame. Altering double brick can mean cutting into walls that hold the house up, which is a different engineering job with a different support sequence. Establish the load path before anyone talks about removing a wall, using the process in [planning a renovation](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/planning-a-renovation).

## How to tell which you have
Useful clues include the plans, wall thickness at a window reveal, brick bond and observations from safely accessible roof or subfloor spaces. A tap on the inside face can offer a clue, though linings, insulation and later alterations can change the sound. Have a building professional confirm the system where it affects a decision. Add the era context from [what your home needs by decade](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/what-your-home-needs-by-decade).

> Note: Record the wall system with plans, photographs and any inspection evidence. It will inform later crack, insulation, moisture and renovation decisions.

## Frequently asked questions
### What is the difference between brick veneer and double brick?
In brick veneer, a timber or steel frame carries the structure and the outer brick leaf acts as cladding. In cavity masonry, masonry leaves carry structural and weather roles. The systems have different load paths, water paths, thermal behaviour and alteration methods.

### How do double brick and brick veneer compare?
Cavity masonry has higher thermal mass and can be harder to alter. Brick veneer is easier to modify and relies more on cavity insulation. Climate, comfort priorities and renovation plans determine the fit.

### How do I know if my house is brick veneer or double brick?
Use plans, wall thickness at openings, brick bond, roof-space or subfloor views and inspection evidence to identify the relationship between frame and masonry.

### Does it matter for cracks?
Yes. A brick-veneer crack may sit in the outer weather leaf. A cavity-masonry crack may affect masonry carrying structural load. Confirm the system, then read width, direction, location, distortion and change over time.

### How does the wall system affect renovation?
Brick-veneer work follows a framed load path. Cavity-masonry work may involve load-bearing masonry. Establish the structure and engineering sequence before planning an opening or wall removal.

## Method
A comparison built around what differs between the wall systems: load paths, moisture management, wall behaviour and observable clues.

## Limitations
Confirm cavity construction, tie condition and concealed moisture through plans and physical evidence.

## Sources
- [Brickwork and blockwork](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/materials/brickwork-and-blockwork) — YourHome, Australian Government; accessed 2026-07-19
- [Due diligence checklist for home buyers](https://www.consumer.vic.gov.au/housing/buying-and-selling-property/checklists/due-diligence) — Consumer Affairs Victoria; accessed 2026-07-19

sections.heading: Four layers that people often collapse into one
sections.markdown:
**The approval stack for a heritage property in Victoria**

| Layer | Where it comes from | What to establish |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Heritage Overlay | Local planning scheme, Clause 43.01 and map | The overlay number and core permit triggers |
| Schedule and heritage material | Schedule, statement of significance, policy and incorporated documents | Property-specific controls, significance and decision guidance |
| Victorian Heritage Register | Heritage Act and Heritage Victoria | Whether state-level registration and separate approvals apply |
| Title and building controls | Registered title, covenant, easement and building legislation | Private restrictions and separate building-permit requirements |

A local Heritage Overlay, the Victorian Heritage Register and a restrictive covenant on title are separate control layers. Check each one that applies.

sections.heading: Read Clause 43.01 with the schedule
sections.markdown:
The [Heritage Overlay clause](https://planning-schemes.app.planning.vic.gov.au/Knox/ordinance/43.01) sets the framework. The schedule identifies controls for a specific place, which can include internal alterations, trees, outbuildings, fences and property-specific exemptions.

Obtain the property report and planning map, note the Heritage Overlay reference, then read the matching schedule row and cited heritage material. Ask council which version is current and whether a proposed change is exempt, needs a planning permit or would benefit from pre-application advice.

sections.heading: Classify the proposed work
sections.markdown: Ordinary repair and alteration can follow different approval paths. Replacing fabric, changing appearance or using a materially different detail may require permission. Painting a previously unpainted surface can be controlled; controls for an already-painted surface depend on the scheme and proposal. Demolition, removal and subdivision have their own tests. Bring council the specifics: the exact work, the material, the colour, where it sits and who can see it. Vague questions get cautious answers.

sections.heading: Plan a change from significance outward
sections.markdown:
1. **Identify significance:** which building, view, material, tree or precinct characteristic is protected and why.
2. **Confirm every control layer:** overlay schedule, register, title, easements, zone and other overlays.
3. **Survey actual fabric and condition:** distinguish original, significant, altered and failed material.
4. **Test the proposal early:** seek council or heritage advice before resolving a design around an unacceptable move.
5. **Coordinate approvals:** planning permit, building permit, trade compliance and any Heritage Victoria consent.
6. **Record the result:** approvals, endorsed plans, specifications, colours, photographs and completion certificates.

sections.heading: Assess value through the specific property
sections.markdown:
A Heritage Overlay can protect a valued place and constrain change. Its effect on price, cost, insurance and the buyer pool depends on the property's significance, controls, condition, development expectations and market. Evaluate the actual property and intended use.

For a Victorian purchase, the overlay should be read with the [Section 32](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/reading-a-section-32). For works, continue with [planning a renovation](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/planning-a-renovation).

> Important: This is Victorian planning orientation. Planning schemes change, and the property-specific schedule and council interpretation matter. Obtain current planning information and professional advice before buying on an assumption or commissioning design.

faqs.answer: Yes, where the schedule applies internal alteration controls to a particular place. Read the schedule entry and property-specific heritage material.

faqs.question: Is a Heritage Overlay the same as the Victorian Heritage Register?
faqs.answer: No. The overlay is a planning-scheme control; the Register is a state heritage regime. A property can be affected by one or both, with separate approval pathways.

faqs.question: Can I repaint a heritage home?
faqs.answer: It depends on the surface, existing treatment, schedule and proposal. Painting a previously unpainted surface may be controlled. Confirm the exact work and colour/material proposal with council.

faqs.question: Can I renovate in a Heritage Overlay?
faqs.answer: Renovation is often possible when the design and approval pathway respond to the identified significance and property-specific controls. Seek early planning and heritage advice.

faqs.question: Does a Heritage Overlay reduce property value?
faqs.answer: There is no reliable generic answer. Controls, significance, condition, intended development and the local market all affect the outcome.

# Living in a Victorian Heritage Overlay: how to read the schedule

In Victoria, land within a Heritage Overlay is controlled through Clause 43.01 and the local schedule. Read the map, schedule entry, statement of significance, heritage policy and incorporated documents for your address. External changes, demolition, subdivision, fences, trees or painting may need approval, and some schedules also control interiors. Check the Victorian Heritage Register, title covenants and ordinary building approvals as well.

## Research note
A Victorian Heritage Overlay is a planning control. The schedule can activate additional controls, including internal alteration controls for a particular place. Read [Clause 43.01 and the applicable schedule](https://planning-schemes.app.planning.vic.gov.au/Knox/ordinance/43.01) before planning interior work.

## Opening
### The schedule tells you what applies here
- **Overlay:** Clause 43.01 sets the frame every overlay hangs from
- **Schedule:** The schedule is where your address gets its own rules
- **Other layers:** The Register, the title and building approvals sit on top

_Four layers, one address. Check all four before you sketch anything._

## Four layers that people often collapse into one
**The approval stack for a heritage property in Victoria**

| Layer | Where it comes from | What to establish |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Heritage Overlay | Local planning scheme, Clause 43.01 and map | The overlay number and core permit triggers |
| Schedule and heritage material | Schedule, statement of significance, policy and incorporated documents | Property-specific controls, significance and decision guidance |
| Victorian Heritage Register | Heritage Act and Heritage Victoria | Whether state-level registration and separate approvals apply |
| Title and building controls | Registered title, covenant, easement and building legislation | Private restrictions and separate building-permit requirements |

A local Heritage Overlay, the Victorian Heritage Register and a restrictive covenant on title are separate control layers. Check each one that applies.

## Read Clause 43.01 with the schedule
The [Heritage Overlay clause](https://planning-schemes.app.planning.vic.gov.au/Knox/ordinance/43.01) sets the framework. The schedule identifies controls for a specific place, which can include internal alterations, trees, outbuildings, fences and property-specific exemptions.

Obtain the property report and planning map, note the Heritage Overlay reference, then read the matching schedule row and cited heritage material. Ask council which version is current and whether a proposed change is exempt, needs a planning permit or would benefit from pre-application advice.

## Classify the proposed work
Ordinary repair and alteration can follow different approval paths. Replacing fabric, changing appearance or using a materially different detail may require permission. Painting a previously unpainted surface can be controlled; controls for an already-painted surface depend on the scheme and proposal. Demolition, removal and subdivision have their own tests. Bring council the specifics: the exact work, the material, the colour, where it sits and who can see it. Vague questions get cautious answers.

## Plan a change from significance outward
1. **Identify significance:** which building, view, material, tree or precinct characteristic is protected and why.
2. **Confirm every control layer:** overlay schedule, register, title, easements, zone and other overlays.
3. **Survey actual fabric and condition:** distinguish original, significant, altered and failed material.
4. **Test the proposal early:** seek council or heritage advice before resolving a design around an unacceptable move.
5. **Coordinate approvals:** planning permit, building permit, trade compliance and any Heritage Victoria consent.
6. **Record the result:** approvals, endorsed plans, specifications, colours, photographs and completion certificates.

## Assess value through the specific property
A Heritage Overlay can protect a valued place and constrain change. Its effect on price, cost, insurance and the buyer pool depends on the property's significance, controls, condition, development expectations and market. Evaluate the actual property and intended use.

For a Victorian purchase, the overlay should be read with the [Section 32](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/reading-a-section-32). For works, continue with [planning a renovation](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/planning-a-renovation).

> Important: This is Victorian planning orientation. Planning schemes change, and the property-specific schedule and council interpretation matter. Obtain current planning information and professional advice before buying on an assumption or commissioning design.

## Frequently asked questions
### Can a Victorian Heritage Overlay control interiors?
Yes, where the schedule applies internal alteration controls to a particular place. Read the schedule entry and property-specific heritage material.

### Is a Heritage Overlay the same as the Victorian Heritage Register?
No. The overlay is a planning-scheme control; the Register is a state heritage regime. A property can be affected by one or both, with separate approval pathways.

### Can I repaint a heritage home?
It depends on the surface, existing treatment, schedule and proposal. Painting a previously unpainted surface may be controlled. Confirm the exact work and colour/material proposal with council.

### Can I renovate in a Heritage Overlay?
Renovation is often possible when the design and approval pathway respond to the identified significance and property-specific controls. Seek early planning and heritage advice.

### Does a Heritage Overlay reduce property value?
There is no reliable generic answer. Controls, significance, condition, intended development and the local market all affect the outcome.

## Method
We untangled the four layers people usually collapse into one: the overlay, its schedule, the Heritage Register and anything on the title.

## Limitations
Victorian planning guidance only. Confirm the property-specific schedule, incorporated documents and council interpretation before design.

## Sources

- [Planning permits](https://www.planning.vic.gov.au/guides-and-resources/guides/guide-to-victorias-planning-system/planning-permits) — Victorian Government; accessed 2026-07-19
- [Due diligence checklist for home buyers](https://www.consumer.vic.gov.au/housing/buying-and-selling-property/checklists/due-diligence) — Consumer Affairs Victoria; accessed 2026-07-19
